The backend uses --nodeps because language builds and their tool checks have already been performed before staging; declared runtime dependencies remain in the package. No dependencies are installed into the host. makepkg requires an unprivileged user. The output uses .pkg.tar.gz, a native makepkg-supported compression choice. BUILDDIR is confined to this build's private directory, overriding host-wide temporary-build settings without changing them. See makepkg, ALPM package contents and PKGINFO. architecture = "all" (Debian) and architecture = "any" (Arch) are suitable for architecture-independent payloads. Select the actual architecture for compiled binaries. Package metadata does not cross-compile the executable. Python, Rust and JavaScript Python artifacts use the normal PEP 517 frontend and the project's declared build backend. Install build in the Python environment that runs zdistro. Isolation is enabled by default; isolation = false is available when the user has already provisioned the backend. Metadata is read from the built archive, not synthesized by zdistro. See Python packaging flow and wheel format. Cargo source packages are made with cargo package, including its normal verification build. The normalized Cargo.toml must match the unified package name and version. Select a single package project for each target. See Cargo package. npm packages use npm pack --ignore-scripts; explicit language builds can run npm run <script> before native packaging. build.install = true runs npm ci --ignore-scripts in the private project copy first. Source manifests and lockfiles are preserved. See npm pack. Browser extensions extension creates a ZIP with manifest.json at its root. xpi uses the same WebExtension layout with an XPI suffix. The validator checks manifest version, name/version and declared local script/page/icon resources. Browser API compatibility and store policy validation remain browser-specific; run that browser's linter and runtime tests in your build recipe when required. Chrome accepts an extension ZIP for upload. Firefox distribution normally involves Mozilla signing. The built-in XPI output is unsigned. See Chrome preparation, WebExtension manifest and Mozilla extension signing. macOS and Windows PKG and DMG adapters run on macOS. PKG files use the declared package identifier and install the staged relative paths under /. DMG files use a read-only UDZO image. They are left unsigned for an explicit signing/notarization workflow. Apple describes the distinction between containers, signing and distribution in Packaging Mac software. MSI packages are generated from staged files through WiX's native schema and CLI. The installer uses a per-machine Program Files directory. Verification decodes the MSI database; it does not perform an installation or the full ICE suite. See WiX CLI and WiX validation. MSIX requires a real staged Windows PE executable at targets.msix.executable. The backend generates a desktop manifest, neutral template icons, block map and package through MakeAppx. Specify the correct publisher and identity for later signing. The generated manifest requests runFullTrust for a Win32 executable. See MakeAppx. Android Android receipts record the actual application_id, version_name, and version_code read from the artifact. targets.apk / targets.aab can set these expected values explicitly; application ID otherwise uses the explicitly declared package.identifier, and version name uses package.version. A mismatch fails the build and re-verification. This also checks independently configured Gradle application IDs and flavors; the package display name is never used to guess an ID. The APK template builds a small no-code Android package with AAPT2 and an installed SDK platform. For an existing Android app, select mode = "gradle", point project at its source, and declare the task and relative output artifact. The Gradle wrapper must be complete. SDK paths come from ANDROID_HOME or ANDROID_SDK_ROOT; platform = "android-35" can choose an installed platform. No SDK is downloaded or configured by zdistro. AAB can link the manifest/resources as protobuf through AAPT2, assemble the standard base-module ZIP layout, and call bundletool build-bundle. Existing Gradle apps can use mode = "gradle" with a task and output path. Both routes validate the resulting bundle with bundletool. Provide bundletool_jar or the BUNDLETOOL_JAR environment variable. Missing Gradle projects, tools and SDK components are reported by doctor. The checked-in CI reuses its existing SDK and provisions a pinned, checksum-verified bundletool JAR in the workspace. It builds actual APK/AAB artifacts and records prerequisite checks; the contract tests also exercise the missing-SDK failure. See Android command-line builds, AAPT2 and bundletool. Containers Docker uses an explicit Buildx docker or oci exporter to write an archive. Both formats need a driver that supports archive export, such as docker-container. The classic docker driver lacks these exporters unless its worker reports the containerd snapshotter. doctor inspects the selected builder without bootstrapping or creating it and reports the missing capability before a build begins. You can create a dedicated builder once: docker buildx create --name zdistro-packages --driver docker-container Select it explicitly in the manifest; the global default builder stays unchanged: [targets.docker] project = "container" engine = "docker" builder = "zdistro-packages" archive = "oci" files = [] When builder is omitted, Docker's existing selection, including BUILDX_BUILDER, applies. The formal Linux workflow creates and removes its own builder in the disposable runner. See Docker/OCI exporters and Buildx inspection. Podman builds a unique local image, saves the selected archive format and removes only that build's unique tag. No image is pushed to a registry by the backend. Verification follows archive references and validates SHA-256/size for recursively referenced OCI blobs using bounded reads. Docker image archives are checked for a valid manifest, configuration and uncompressed layer digests. See Docker exporters, Docker save and the OCI image layout. Extension contract A custom backend declares hosts, tool names, literal build argv arrays, an output path and literal verify argv arrays. Success requires both command groups and a nonempty regular artifact inside the assigned output directory. Receipts label these results recipe, keeping the supplied verifier's scope explicit. Add new language tools through build.kind = "command"; JSON/TOML and compression stay with standard libraries and ecosystem tools. Staging supports regular files and rejects escaping paths, file collisions and unsupported links. Source trees containing application-specific symlink layouts can use an explicit native recipe. Build scripts remain executable project code; this utility provides isolated working directories, not an operating-system sandbox.

title: 概览
body: 预览、应用、备份与恢复 dotfiles 部署。 zdot Small, explicit dotfile deployments and Git synchronization. zdot links files from a repository into your home directory. You preview the changes, apply them, and can restore any originals you chose to back up. The native Linux executable uses Rust no_std, Project Z's zclap, and direct system calls. It has no allocator, libc dependency, daemon, or background network activity. Install Download a matching archive and SHA256SUMS from Releases, verify the checksum, and extract it into ~/.local. The archive contains bin/zdot, its manual, completion, and license. Linux x86_64 and aarch64 are supported. From source, install Rust 1.100 and a C-compatible linker, then: make check make install PREFIX="$HOME/.local" The linker produces a static ELF; no C library is linked. Use make uninstall PREFIX="$HOME/.local" to remove the installed program, manual and completion. Remove deployments separately with zdot remove. Use zdot init --root "$HOME/dotfiles" cp "$HOME/.zshrc" "$HOME/dotfiles/files/zshrc" printf 'files/zshrc\t.zshrc\n' > "$HOME/dotfiles/profile.zdot" zdot plan --root "$HOME/dotfiles" --target "$HOME" --json zdot apply --root "$HOME/dotfiles" --target "$HOME" --backup zdot status --root "$HOME/dotfiles" --target "$HOME" zdot remove --root "$HOME/dotfiles" --target "$HOME" Each profile line has source<TAB>destination. Paths are relative to the repository and target respectively. Files, whole directories, spaces and Unicode names work. Empty lines and # comments are ignored. plan only reads. apply refuses existing files unless --backup is explicit. Repeated application keeps matching links. remove uses the saved deployment profile, restores originals, and refuses to remove a destination you replaced. Edits made through a managed symlink edit the repository's source file. Keep recovery data in XDG state Use one stable, private state directory for a deployment when the home directory should contain only the chosen configuration links: zdot plan --root "$HOME/dotfiles" --target "$HOME" \ --state-dir "$HOME/.local/state/zdot/desktop" --backup --json zdot apply --root "$HOME/dotfiles" --target "$HOME" \ --state-dir "$HOME/.local/state/zdot/desktop" --backup zdot status --root "$HOME/dotfiles" --target "$HOME" \ --state-dir "$HOME/.local/state/zdot/desktop" zdot remove --root "$HOME/dotfiles" --target "$HOME" \ --state-dir "$HOME/.local/state/zdot/desktop" Pass the same --state-dir on every command. plan and status never create it. apply creates missing directories with mode 0700; recovery metadata and original files stay there. This mode adds no .zdot-state or .zdot.lock to the target's top level. The JSON plan reports the selected state_dir. The state directory must be absolute, private, and outside the source repository and every managed source or destination. Existing directory components must be real directories. Original files move without copying, so --backup requires the state directory and those originals to share a filesystem. A failed move rolls back earlier changes. Omitting --state-dir keeps the original layout. Sync Initialize your repository and choose its remote using normal Git commands. zdot init creates the file layout; it does not run Git or configure an account. git -C "$HOME/dotfiles" init git -C "$HOME/dotfiles" add profile.zdot files git -C "$HOME/dotfiles" commit -m "Add chosen dotfiles" git -C "$HOME/dotfiles" remote add origin YOUR_REMOTE zdot sync --root "$HOME/dotfiles" status zdot sync --root "$HOME/dotfiles" pull zdot sync --root "$HOME/dotfiles" push Sync uses the installed Git at /usr/bin/git or /bin/git. Pull only fast-forwards. Commit creation, remote selection, merge resolution and credentials stay with Git. A pull does not automatically deploy a changed profile. No shell is used to construct Git arguments. Boundaries Up to 128 mappings and 64 KiB per profile; limits fail before deployment. Parent symlinks, source symlinks, traversal, overlapping destinations and source/destination containment are rejected. Change a profile by removing its previous deployment, editing it, then applying it again. Keep the repository at its original path until removal. Metadata defaults to the target's .zdot-state directory; --state-dir selects an explicit recovery store. A target directory lock serializes new zdot processes. Default mode also retains the legacy .zdot.lock contract. State is never uploaded by zdot. Ordinary apply failures roll back newly created links and moved originals. An interrupted deployment retains its journal for remove recovery. Concurrent edits by other programs are outside this transaction model. Linux 4.11 or later and mounted /proc are required. Design and recovery · Performance measurements · Contributing · oh-my-ztty MIT.

title: Design and recovery
body: 预览、应用、备份与恢复 dotfiles 部署。 Design and recovery A profile is a set of links The repository owns source files. The target directory owns links to their absolute paths. A tab-separated profile makes the mapping explicit and permits spaces without a shell parser. Configuration content is never read by the planner; it checks source types, destination types and link identity. The reusable library borrows the manifest buffer and validates all mappings. It rejects traversal, ambiguous components and overlapping destinations. The executable opens parent directories with openat and O_NOFOLLOW. This prevents a pre-existing symlink parent from redirecting an operation. Deployment The planner inspects every source and destination before any deployment writes. A conflict stops the operation unless --backup was requested. The process then takes a nonblocking, target-wide flock, checks the destinations again, and creates a journal. A journal namespace includes the canonical repository path and profile path. A separate owner record verifies both values, so a namespace hash collision does not grant ownership of another deployment. Explicit state stores also bind the canonical target path; another target cannot reuse the same journal. The saved profile remains available if the current profile changes or is deleted. Originals move into numbered backup slots using renameat2(RENAME_NOREPLACE). The state store and originals must therefore share a filesystem; a cross-device move fails without silently copying or deleting an original. A new symlink never overwrites a newly appearing destination. Successful file and directory mutations are synchronized to disk. When an ordinary system call fails, links created in that attempt are removed, originals are moved back, and new empty parent directories are cleaned up. Removal and recovery Removal preflights the entire saved deployment. A matching absolute symlink can be removed. A missing target can receive its preserved original. A replaced target causes removal to stop before changing other mappings. Incomplete journals also permit untouched originals to remain in place. If apply was interrupted, first inspect zdot plan and the destinations. Run zdot remove --root REPO --target TARGET --profile PROFILE to remove known links and restore recorded originals, then apply again. If a destination has been replaced, move that replacement to a chosen safe location before retrying removal; zdot does not choose which version to discard. The repository path and selected profile name identify the journal. Keep that repository directory available for removal. Changing the profile content does not lose the saved deployment; moving the repository requires removing and redeploying its links. Default mode retains an empty .zdot-state and the small .zdot.lock after removal. An explicit --state-dir retains only its selected empty store. New versions lock the target directory itself, so different state directories do not create independent locks for the same target. Default mode also takes the legacy lock; explicit mode honors it if it already exists. No process remains running. The explicit state path is opened one component at a time with O_NOFOLLOW. Its final directory, journals and backup directories must be owned by the current effective user and inaccessible to group and other users. Parent directories are created with mode 0700 only during apply. The state path cannot contain the target or overlap the repository or any mapping. Plan and status check those conditions without creating directories. Removal validates the saved profile against the same state boundaries. A stable state path is part of a deployment's identity. Changing this argument does not migrate existing journals. Remove the old deployment with its original state path before choosing a new one. All clients of an explicit store must support --state-dir; an old binary does not know that store's recovery data. Transaction boundary The lock coordinates zdot processes, not arbitrary editors or Git hooks. Other programs should not rename parent directories or replace metadata while an operation is running. The journal enables recovery after process interruption; it is not a claim of whole-filesystem atomicity under every power failure. A corrupt or foreign journal causes a refusal. Source repositories are trusted configuration. Installing a directory link does not recursively audit its contents or sandbox programs that use those contents. Git hooks and credential helpers run under the user's Git configuration only when the user explicitly calls sync. Runtime budget The production dependency tree is zdot → zclap with zclap's default features disabled. Core parsing uses no allocator. The Linux executable defines its entry point and a small syscall boundary, and links neither Rust std nor libc. Build scripts, unit tests and Python developer tools may use their normal standard libraries; they are not part of the installed binary. Buffers have explicit limits: 64 KiB for a profile, 128 mappings, 4096 bytes per path and 64 components per relative path. Invalid or oversized inputs are rejected, rather than growing memory usage without a bound. Evidence and review Claim Evidence Preview does not write Default and nested external-store tests compare paths before and after plan/status Reapplication is idempotent Two applications report 1 then 0 changes per new mapping Conflicts preserve user data File, directory, broken-link and replaced-target tests Symlink parents cannot redirect deployment Source and destination parent fixtures Rollback works for an ordinary filesystem failure A read-only destination forces failure after earlier links and backups Recovery uses saved state Missing current profile and interrupted-backup tests for both layouts External state cannot target another deployment Target owner, path containment, private-mode and symlink tests External state does not create home metadata Roundtrip checks absence of top-level .zdot-state and .zdot.lock Different stores cooperate on one target Directory flock and legacy-lock tests Cross-filesystem backups fail without data loss Two-filesystem fixture verifies rollback after a failed move Git synchronization is real Temporary local bare remote, push, pull and divergence rejection No dynamic runtime library is linked scripts/check_binary.py inspects ELF headers and Cargo features Review questions: Is the purpose narrow enough to verify? Does each command have one meaning? Are failure tests representative? Are limits stated where users need them? Does recovery preserve existing data? These are checked by make check and the cases above. Performance claims remain measurements with a stated workload; this project does not claim a universal speed ranking.

title: Performance
body: 预览、应用、备份与恢复 dotfiles 部署。 Performance The latest x86_64 measurement used Rust 1.100.0 and the release build of zdot 0.2.0 on 2026-11-20 (UTC+08). Other development jobs were active on the host. Raw inputs, timing scope and binary/source hashes are in linux-x86_64-0.2.0.json. The 0.1.1 sample remains available; these separate runs do not isolate version overhead from changing host load. Measurement Result Scope Measured executable 58,344 bytes (56.98 KiB) Stripped static ELF; no libc or dynamic loader Version command, median 0.275 ms 50 warm runs including Python parent spawn and wait Version command, p95 0.357 ms Same 50-run sample Default JSON plan, median 7.472 ms 128 valid mappings with long names; 50 warm runs Default JSON plan, p95 12.220 ms Same plan workload External-state JSON plan, median 6.725 ms Same mappings; nested state path absent External-state JSON plan, p95 11.441 ms Same external-state workload Sampled RSS 236 KiB 128-entry plan blocked on its output pipe, 3 samples Sampled PSS 232 KiB Same sample; shared pages apportioned The output pipe is reduced to 4096 bytes so the process stays alive at a known point during the memory read. The measurement reads /proc/PID/smaps_rollup; it is a live resident-page sample, not a whole-run maximum. The larger buffers used during apply and rollback can produce a different peak. There is no idle zdot service. Each command exits, so no dotfile synchronization daemon adds background memory. The sync command replaces zdot with the installed Git; Git's memory and network behavior are outside the figures above. These numbers describe one machine, one compiler and three workloads. They do not establish a ranking against other dotfile managers. Reproduce the measurement with make benchmark; its JSON output includes the complete measurement scope and checksum of the measured binary.

title: 概览
body: 解析与编码 DNS 消息，向调用方返回报文和记录视图。 zdwire DNS wire parsing and encoding with zero dependencies, zero heap allocation, and safe Rust. The library is always #![no_std] and uses only core. Stable Rust 1.74 is the minimum supported version. zdwire handles the bytes of a DNS message. Transport, resolvers, caches, DNSSEC verification, and a command-line application are outside its scope. The output buffer, optional compression table, and input lifetime belong to the caller. Encode a query use zdwire::{Class, Header, MessageBuilder, Name, Type}; let name = Name::from_wire(b"\x03www\x07example\x03com\0")?; let mut output = [0u8; 512]; let mut message = MessageBuilder::new(&mut output, Header::new(0x1234, Header::RD))?; message.add_question(name, Type::A, Class::IN)?; let packet = message.finish(); // Only the initialized prefix; 33 bytes here. # Ok::<(), zdwire::Error>(()) For text input, encode_name("www.example.com.", &mut name_buffer) returns the used length. Name::from_wire(&name_buffer[..len]) then borrows it. Text conversion understands escaped dots/backslashes and three-digit decimal octets; it does not perform IDNA conversion. Wire labels may contain arbitrary bytes. Parse without allocation use zdwire::{MessageView, Rdata}; # let packet = [0u8; 12]; let message = MessageView::parse(&packet)?; let header = message.header(); let mut questions = message.questions(); for question in questions.by_ref() { let question = question?; for label in question.name.labels() { // `label` is a borrowed &[u8]; the terminating root is omitted. let _ = label; } } // Reuse the cursor: consumed questions are not scanned again. for record in questions.into_records()? { let record = record?; match record.data()? { Rdata::A(address) => { let _ = address; } Rdata::Txt(text) => { for string in text.iter() { let _ = string; } } _ => {} } } # Ok::<(), zdwire::Error>(()) MessageView::parse checks the 12-byte header and message-size limit. Question and record iterators validate the fields they visit; Record::data validates the requested typed RDATA. Unknown types retain their original bytes. MessageView::parse_strict or message.validate() checks the complete packet, including typed RDATA, EDNS placement and uniqueness, and trailing bytes. Choose strict validation at a boundary that requires a complete valid packet; choose streaming access when the application consumes and handles each result. records() traverses all three RR sections in one pass. answers(), authorities(), and additionals() locate an individual section by scanning the preceding sections; repeated calls repeat that scan. All fallible iterators stop permanently after their first error. Encode a compressed response use zdwire::{Class, CompressionEntry, Header, MessageBuilder, Name, RecordData, Section, Type}; let name = Name::from_wire(b"\x07example\x03com\0")?; let mut output = [0u8; 512]; let mut table = [CompressionEntry::EMPTY; 64]; let mut message = MessageBuilder::with_compression( &mut output, Header::new(0x1234, Header::QR | Header::AA), &mut table, )?; message.add_question(name, Type::A, Class::IN)?; message.add_record(Section::Answer, name, Class::IN, 300, RecordData::A([192, 0, 2, 1]))?; message.add_opt(1232, 0, 0, 0x8000, &[])?; let packet = message.finish(); # Ok::<(), zdwire::Error>(()) Append questions, answers, authorities, then additionals. Empty sections can be skipped. The builder owns section counts and starts them at zero, preserving the supplied header's ID and flags. add_opt places the sole OPT in Additional. Unknown EDNS versions, flags, and option payloads remain accessible as wire data. Each append validates input and computes its size before changing the output. On BufferTooSmall { needed }, needed is the exact total buffer length needed for that append with the current dictionary. Earlier bytes, counts, section position, and dictionary remain unchanged. len() and finish().len() give the actual used length. The builder does not resize or allocate memory; a caller that changes buffers rebuilds the packet in its new buffer. The compression table is a bounded direct-mapped dictionary. Collisions can reduce compression but cannot change name bytes. Pointers use only earlier, uncompressed label boundaries below offset 16,384. Generated names therefore have at most one pointer hop. Label case is preserved. An empty table disables compression. A 256-entry table occupies 2 KiB on common 32/64-bit targets. Wire coverage Data Representation Header All ID, flags, opcode, response code, and count bits retained Questions Borrowed name, numeric type and class Answer / Authority / Additional Sequential or section-specific iterators A / AAAA Borrowed address bytes on decode; fixed arrays on encode CNAME / NS / PTR Validated names with RFC 1035 compression MX / SOA Numeric fields and packet-relative compressed names TXT Separate length-prefixed byte strings, including empty strings SRV Priority, weight, port, uncompressed target CAA Flags, 1–255 ASCII alphanumeric tag bytes, opaque value OPT UDP payload size, extended response code, version, flags, options Unknown RR Type code and exact raw RDATA Names compare using ASCII case folding. eq_case_sensitive compares original octets. write_uncompressed writes into caller memory; as_uncompressed borrows a contiguous expanded representation when the packet already contains one. Display uses escaped DNS presentation notation without allocating inside the library. Opaque RDATA is not interpreted or rewritten. RFC 3597-compatible unknown data can be copied as-is; legacy unknown formats containing compression pointers need type-specific relocation by the caller. RecordData::Unknown rejects types that already have a typed encoder so they cannot bypass its checks. Error and work limits Error { kind, offset } gives a specific category and an absolute message-byte offset. A truncated field reports its first missing byte. Text-name errors refer to input text; encoding capacity errors refer to the output. The core contains no unsafe, recursion, mutable globals, allocation, or input-sized stack arrays. Limit Policy Message At most 65,535 bytes, excluding transport framing Label At most 63 bytes Expanded name At most 255 bytes, including length bytes and root Compression At most 32 hops per name; backward pointers only Pointer cycles Self-reference and repeated pointer positions rejected Unsupported label types Extended/reserved label encodings rejected RDATA boundary Inline fields stay inside RDLENGTH; pointers use the packet EDNS One OPT, literal root owner, Additional section only The 32-hop cap deliberately rejects some otherwise valid, unusually deep compression chains. This is an explicit resource policy, reported as PointerLimit. See SECURITY.md for the threat model. Performance and reproducibility The isolated comparison/ project pins NLnet Labs domain 0.12.3 with default features disabled. It checks semantic equality before timing, then measures raw-record traversal, typed traversal, and encoding into caller buffers. The root crate has no normal, build, dev, optional, or target-specific dependencies; the comparison dependencies never enter its package. cargo test --locked cargo test --locked --manifest-path comparison/Cargo.toml ZD_BENCH_MS=50 ZD_BENCH_SAMPLES=11 cargo run --release --locked --manifest-path comparison/Cargo.toml Read docs/benchmark.md for complete commands, compiler/CPU details, timings, equivalence boundaries, and scenarios where either library is faster. Performance claims apply to those measured paths and fixtures. Verification cargo +1.74.0 test --locked --all-targets cargo fmt --all --check cargo clippy --locked --all-targets -- -D warnings cargo test --locked --doc cargo doc --locked --no-deps cargo check --locked --lib --target wasm32-unknown-unknown cargo check --locked --lib --target thumbv7em-none-eabi cargo +nightly miri test --locked --test security cargo run --release --locked --manifest-path fuzz/Cargo.toml -- --iterations 200000 --seed 4277009102 python3 scripts/check-package.py python3 -m unittest discover -s scripts -p 'test_*.py' -v cargo package --locked cargo publish --locked --dry-run The tests include the RFC 1035 compression example, every supported RR, round trips, exact error offsets, bounded malicious pointers, truncated data, binary names, random malformed packets, and transactional output failures. The independent fuzz driver uses deterministic mutations and an optional input corpus; CI also runs it under AddressSanitizer. This is mutation fuzzing, not a claim of exhaustive verification or coverage-guided fuzzing. CI and release CI runs MSRV and stable tests on Linux, Windows, and macOS; it also checks formatting, Clippy, documentation, WASM, embedded no_std, package contents, publish dry-run, differential tests, Miri, and sanitizer fuzzing. Configure the repository secret CARGO_REGISTRY_TOKEN with permission to publish this crate. In Actions → Release → Run workflow, select the default branch and patch, minor, or major. current publishes the existing version or resumes an interrupted initial release without another version increment. The workflow updates the package version and all relevant lockfiles, pushes the version commit, validates its exact SHA through the complete CI workflow, then creates a version tag, publishes to crates.io, and creates a GitHub Release. Published versions are detected and never uploaded again. A release-event run also checks tag/version agreement and that the tag commit belongs to the default branch. All publishing steps stay in the same run, so GITHUB_TOKEN event suppression cannot break the publication chain. Credentials remain environment variables and are never printed by the release scripts. Standards RFC 1035: message layout, labels, compression, and original RR formats. RFC 3596: AAAA wire data. RFC 2782: SRV and its uncompressed target. RFC 6891: EDNS OPT fields and option framing. RFC 8659: CAA wire syntax. RFC 3597: handling unknown RR types. MIT licensed. See LICENSE.

title: 概览
body: 读取 Linux 系统与启动链信息，输出终端摘要或 JSON。 zfetch A small native Linux system summary with a restrained terminal view and stable JSON for scripts. The executable uses Rust no_std, fixed buffers and direct Linux system calls: no Cargo dependencies, allocator, libc, external commands, network requests or background service. Default output omits user names, host names, IP addresses and serial numbers. Releases · Measurements · Design · oh-my-ztty Use zfetch zfetch --no-color zfetch --json | jq '.memory_used_bytes' zfetch --format=json The terminal view groups system, hardware and session fields with whitespace, one blue accent and the terminal's default text color. It wraps values to the actual window width and puts labels above values in narrow terminals. No patched font is required. --no-color, NO_COLOR (even when empty), TERM=dumb, and redirected stdout disable ANSI styling. For scripts, --json, --format json, and --format=json emit the same zfetch.system.v1 object. All eleven fields remain present, unavailable values are null, and byte/second counters are integers. Quotes, backslashes and Unicode are escaped as JSON requires. There is no heading, color, progress text or success diagnostic. The field contract and limits describe each key. --format=text explicitly selects text. Redirected default text keeps its compact, uncolored layout for existing consumers. If format options are repeated, the last one wins. Invalid options and failed writes report errors on stderr and return a nonzero status. Install With Rust 1.100 or newer on Linux x86_64 or aarch64, Cargo builds and installs the same native command: cargo install zfetch --version 0.1.1 --locked On Arch Linux, install zfetch-project-z-bin for the official binary, or zfetch-project-z to build from source: yay -S zfetch-project-z-bin zfetch Both packages install the command zfetch. AUR already has an unrelated older project named zfetch; the package names distinguish Project Z and declare a conflict so one installation cannot overwrite the other. Download the archive for Linux x86_64 or aarch64 and SHA256SUMS from Releases, verify the checksum, then extract it. Install the executable to a user-owned command directory: sha256sum --check --ignore-missing SHA256SUMS tar -xzf zfetch-0.1.1-linux-x86_64.tar.gz install -Dm755 zfetch-0.1.1-linux-x86_64/bin/zfetch "$HOME/.local/bin/zfetch" The archive also includes a manual, zsh completion and license. To build from source with Rust 1.100 or newer: git clone https://github.com/LIghtJUNction/zfetch.git cd zfetch make check make install PREFIX="$HOME/.local" make uninstall PREFIX="$HOME/.local" removes the files installed by that target. zfetch has no state, cache, daemon or login-shell hook to remove. Performance with its scope The official v0.1.1 x86_64 executable is 28,648 bytes; the aarch64 executable is 66,168 bytes. Archive hashes, native release jobs, registry installation and AUR checks are recorded in release evidence. Locally compiled executables can differ with the build environment. The following measurements are from v0.1.0; they are not new measurements of the terminal layout added later. In 100 interleaved warm runs on one x86_64 developer machine, plain output took 0.429 ms median and JSON took 0.385 ms median, including Python process creation and waiting. fastfetch 2.71.0's same core module group took 2.503 ms median in JSON. Their fields are not identical: fastfetch offers more probes and a wider feature set. The JSON memory sample was 60 KiB RSS while blocked on its output pipe, compared with 4,996 KiB RSS for the fastfetch core-module command. These are resident samples at a known point, not peak memory guarantees. The separate stock-default fastfetch result, commands, p95 values and raw records are in Performance. Boundaries Linux x86_64 and aarch64 are supported. Shell means the SHELL environment variable's basename; terminal means TERM_PROGRAM, falling back to TERM. CPU model information is bounded to the first 4 KiB of /proc/cpuinfo. Memory used is MemTotal - MemAvailable. The summary intentionally does not enumerate packages, disks, GPUs, displays, sensors or desktop themes. This is part of Project Z. It can be bundled as a pinned Git submodule and used without starting an agent or opening a connection. MIT. Boot-to-desktop report Current source builds can inspect the local boot structure on demand: zfetch --boot zfetch --boot --json The report covers firmware, boot loader, kernel, initramfs, systemd, its default target, login manager, user session and desktop. Each stage lists its evidence, related service or target names, and configuration paths. Runtime evidence is marked observed; installed configuration is marked configured. Inaccessible paths have null presence in JSON. The schema is zfetch.boot.v1. EFI loader identity and the current logind session take precedence over installed boot-loader and display-manager configuration. Desktop names provided only by the environment remain configuration evidence. Hyprland Lua configuration and SDDM drop-in files are included when present. The report reads bounded local files, starts no process, and displays home-relative paths with $HOME. The stages describe the boot structure; systemd starts services in parallel. Unit activation state and elapsed timings are outside this report. See the systemd boot overview for the ordering and roles of the named targets.

title: Design
body: 读取 Linux 系统与启动链信息，输出终端摘要或 JSON。 Design zfetch gathers a small set of local values and formats one bounded output buffer. It does not discover every installed program or launch command-line helpers. This keeps the work per invocation small and makes unavailable data visible rather than triggering another subsystem. Field Source Interpretation OS /etc/os-release, then /usr/lib/os-release PRETTY_NAME, NAME or ID; quoted values are decoded without shell evaluation Kernel and architecture uname syscall Release and machine fields only; host name is not copied CPU First 4096 bytes of /proc/cpuinfo First model name, Hardware or Processor field; absent data remains unknown Logical CPUs /sys/devices/system/cpu/online Count of validated, nonoverlapping online ranges Memory /proc/meminfo Total bytes and total minus available bytes Uptime /proc/uptime Whole seconds, with no floating-point arithmetic Shell SHELL Configured shell's basename Terminal TERM_PROGRAM or TERM Declared program name or terminal type Fixed runtime The collector reuses an 8 KiB read buffer. Individual text fields have explicit byte caps, and truncation keeps complete UTF-8 characters. Control characters are replaced before terminal display; JSON has its own escaping. No parser allocates, no background work remains, and the process writes its summary once. The executable uses architecture-specific Linux startup and syscall conventions. Rust core provides parsing and formatting. The binary has no Cargo dependencies and links neither Rust std nor libc. Build scripts, developer tests, package tools and the compiler use their ordinary standard libraries; they are not installed as runtime dependencies. Output contracts Interactive text uses the terminal's window width. At 40 columns or more, labels and values share aligned rows; narrower terminals put labels above values. System, hardware and session rows are separated by whitespace. The title has one blue accent, labels are dimmed, and values use the terminal's own foreground color. NO_COLOR (including an empty value), --no-color, TERM=dumb, and redirected stdout disable ANSI styling. Wrapping keeps complete UTF-8 characters and reserves two cells for each non-ASCII scalar. Combining characters and some narrow Unicode text may wrap earlier than strictly necessary. A wide scalar in a one-column terminal is displayed as ?. The collector's bounded values remain unchanged in JSON. If the terminal reports no width, interactive text uses 80 columns. Redirected default text retains its existing compact, uncolored field layout. It does not gain terminal line wrapping. Scripts should select --json, --format json, or --format=json; --format=text explicitly selects text. The last format option wins. JSON is one object followed by a newline, including on a narrow terminal, with no color, heading, progress text, or stderr output on success. The zfetch.system.v1 object always contains all eleven keys: Key Type Meaning schema string Exactly zfetch.system.v1 os string or null Decoded OS name kernel string or null Kernel release architecture string or null Machine architecture cpu string or null Bounded CPU model logical_cpus integer or null Online logical CPU count memory_total_bytes integer or null Physical memory total, in bytes memory_used_bytes integer or null Total minus available memory, in bytes uptime_seconds integer or null Whole seconds since boot shell string or null Configured shell basename terminal string or null Terminal program or type Missing values stay null; they are never omitted or replaced by a human-readable placeholder in JSON. Strings use JSON escaping after the same bounded control-character sanitization used by the text collector. Invalid options produce only a stderr diagnostic and status 2. Write failures, including help and version output directed to /dev/full, produce a stderr diagnostic and status 1. Closing a pipe early retains the normal Unix SIGPIPE behavior (often status 141 in a shell); if SIGPIPE was inherited as ignored, the write failure follows the status-1 path instead. Checks and limits Claim Evidence Numeric parsing does not wrap Overflow, invalid digit, CPU range and unit tests Output does not inject terminal escapes Unicode/control fixture and hostile environment CLI test Kernel values are actually read Live total-memory, CPU-count, kernel and uptime checks Colors respect output context PTY color, NO_COLOR, --no-color, TERM=dumb and redirected-output tests Narrow terminals stay bounded Real PTY widths 1, 12, 24, 39, 40 and 80, including CJK input and a conflicting COLUMNS value JSON is a stable pipe interface Exact keys/types, explicit formats, quotes/backslashes/UTF-8, null fields and narrow-PTY JSON tests Output failures are observable /dev/full for all output paths, and closed pipes with default and ignored SIGPIPE No private identity fields are emitted Exact JSON-key contract No dynamic runtime is required ELF program-header, dynamic-table and undefined-symbol checks No child or network operation occurs Scoped strace evidence Linux ARM64 ABI works Cross build and QEMU execution; official release also builds/tests on a native ARM64 runner The 4 KiB CPU cap can omit model labels that appear late in unusual cpuinfo files. CPU count comes from the separate online list, so it does not count truncated cpuinfo blocks. Mutable system values are a sequence of reads, not a globally atomic snapshot. Permissions or missing virtual files produce unavailable values. Review: the purpose is a bounded system summary with an explicit script interface; each field has a documented source; parser and live-system tests support the claims; size and latency are measured within stated workloads; syscall-only collection keeps the runtime mechanism direct. No claim covers all fastfetch modules or every Linux system.

title: Performance
body: 读取 Linux 系统与启动链信息，输出终端摘要或 JSON。 Performance This record compares zfetch 0.1.0 with fastfetch 2.71.0 on one x86_64 developer machine on 2026-11-20 (UTC+08). Other development work was active. Each command ran 100 times after three warmups, with round-robin ordering to reduce drift. Command Median wall time p95 wall time Sampled RSS Sampled PSS zfetch plain 0.429 ms 1.062 ms 64 KiB 60 KiB zfetch JSON 0.385 ms 0.997 ms 60 KiB 56 KiB fastfetch core JSON 2.503 ms 5.340 ms 4,996 KiB 1,915 KiB fastfetch stock default 15.184 ms 26.604 ms 12,508 KiB 7,035 KiB Wall time includes Python's process creation, the executable and waiting. RSS/PSS come from three smaps_rollup samples after wchan confirms that the process is blocked on a prefilled output pipe. This is a reproducible resident sample after collection, not a whole-run peak or an idle-service measurement. Comparable scope The core command asks fastfetch for OS:Kernel:CPU:Memory:Uptime:Shell:Terminal, disables its logo and user configuration, and emits JSON. zfetch's corresponding data additionally names architecture and online CPU count explicitly. The programs do not expose identical fields or use identical definitions for shell and terminal. The separate stock-default result runs fastfetch --config none with its broader default modules. It is not an equal-feature comparison. The user configuration is disabled in both fastfetch workloads to avoid measuring unrelated commands or private customization. Size and build Executable Size Build zfetch x86_64 23,288 bytes Rust 1.100.0, opt-level z, fat LTO, stripped static ELF zfetch aarch64 66,168 bytes Cross build, default 64 KiB-compatible ELF layout; QEMU smoke tested Installed fastfetch x86_64 2,000,920 bytes Existing distribution executable; dynamic libraries excluded from this file size The production Cargo graph contains only zfetch. ELF checks reject a dynamic loader, undefined runtime symbols or shared-library dependencies. A process and network syscall trace recorded one entry execve, zero child processes and zero network calls for zfetch JSON. Raw timings and memory samples include commands and the measured binary's SHA-256. Syscall evidence states the trace scope. These measurements do not establish a universal ranking across hardware or other fetch tools. Reproduce with make benchmark. Pass --runs and --output directly to scripts/benchmark.py to select sample count and destination. Official release artifacts The official v0.1.0 binaries are 22,808 bytes on x86_64 and 66,168 bytes on aarch64. The x86_64 benchmark above used a locally linked 23,288-byte build of the same source; linker and platform differences affect ELF layout. The measurement record identifies that exact local binary and does not silently substitute the release file. Both official architecture jobs passed native tests, and both downloaded archives passed their published SHA-256 checks before AUR packaging. See release evidence.

title: 概览
body: 场景与布局核心，可选原生 GPU 与 CPU 窗口后端。 zgpui A portable UI core with optional native GPU and CPU windows for Project Z. zgpui turns bounded scenes into layout and renderer calls. Default builds use no_std + alloc, have zero Cargo dependencies, and forbid unsafe code. The optional native module supplies windows and immediate widgets through platform libraries; linux-software selects a CPU renderer instead of OpenGL on Linux. Applications own their state and event loop. Core Typed Rust scenes with atomic validation through State::replace_scene. Rows, columns, text, progress indicators, buttons and image references. Shared pixel layout, clipping bounds and revision-aware button hit testing. A Renderer contract with begin, draw, end and abort. Bounded JSON updates and a compatible ZUI/1 terminal transport adapter. Native hosts can use the typed API without parsing JSON or using a terminal. Use From a checkout: cargo add zgpui --git https://github.com/LIghtJUNction/zgpui.git cargo run --example host use zgpui::{Kind, Node, Scene, State}; let mut state = State::new(); state.replace_scene(Scene { surface: 1, revision: 1, root: 1, events: true, nodes: vec![Node { id: 1, kind: Kind::Button { label: "Run".into(), action: "run".into(), enabled: true, }, }], }).expect("valid scene"); Build a layout::Layout from the accepted scene, a pixel rectangle and host metrics. Layout::paint sends the visible nodes to your renderer. The host example shows the complete scene, rendering and button-action path. Host boundary The same core supports Linux, macOS, Windows, WebAssembly and bare-metal Rust targets. A host supplies an allocator and implements rendering and input. Desktop hosts can opt into zgpui::native for window creation and immediate widgets, or keep their own backend. Drivers and application policy stay outside the scene core. Native text rendering has its own platform limitations. ztty uses zgpui for its scene state and layout, with its own X11/GPU rendering and PTY input routing. Other hosts can use software rendering, native controls or a GPU backend through the same contract. See platform integration. Native windows Enable native for the platform OpenGL backend, or linux-software for Linux CPU rendering. Import windows and widgets from zgpui::native. The portable scene API and its default features remain unchanged. Native integration and migration covers features, system libraries, examples and the move from the former native UI package. Linux font fallback also supports fixed-size bitmap strikes, scaled to the requested text size. Color bitmap fonts such as Noto Color Emoji render as grayscale coverage through the shared native and headless font implementation. Strike selection and scaling follow the FreeType sizing contract; the FreeType glyph loading contract provides the grayscale bitmap when color output is not requested. Materials and folding layers Native hosts can opt into cached in-window materials: frosted glass, progressive blur, mica style, liquid glass, paper and custom GLSL fragment functions. Captured layers can include text and use a perspective fold. Source revisions, quality, texture budgets and redraw timing remain under application control; the API reports actual capabilities and flat fallbacks. cargo run --locked --release --features native --example materials The gallery provides strength, quality and openness controls, two sampling modes for folding, live cache counters and a cancellable 1.2-second animation. It waits for events when idle. These are application-window effects, not native Windows DWM Mica or Apple compositor materials. Materials and measurement explains the cache contract, shader extension point, GPU/fallback distinction and reproducible cached-versus-invalidated experiment. Headless pixels The source-only zgpui-raster companion in the repository's raster/ directory draws bounded premultiplied ARGB pixels into caller-owned buffers and reuses the Linux system font implementation without linking X11 or OpenGL. It is consumed from a pinned repository checkout and is not independently published. The root crate remains the default workspace member; applications opt into the companion separately. Terminal adapter The existing ZUI/1 wire prefix and revision rules are preserved. Terminal applications can probe capabilities, replace or update a scene, and receive opted-in action events. Images are references resolved by the host. The complete format, examples and limits are in the protocol guide. Validate and measure cargo test --locked --lib cargo test --locked --doc cargo run --locked --example host cargo bench --bench protocol The validation workflow runs the core tests on Linux, macOS and Windows, and checks WebAssembly and bare-metal targets. It can run manually or as part of a release. Benchmarks emit timing and allocation records for named workloads. Record the toolchain, machine and repeated samples when comparing runs; allocation totals are distinct from peak live memory and process RSS. Manual version bump and publishing describes the CARGO_REGISTRY_TOKEN release workflow. MIT © LIghtJUNction

title: ZUI/1 terminal adapter
body: 场景与布局核心，可选原生 GPU 与 CPU 窗口后端。 ZUI/1 terminal adapter ZUI/1 is the terminal wire adapter provided by zgpui. Native applications can use the typed scene and layout APIs directly; see platform integration. The library name is zgpui, while the existing ZUI/1 wire prefix stays compatible. The adapter carries bounded scene data. The host renders known components and owns input routing, session permissions, images and geometry. Frames do not run scripts, open network connections or execute shell commands. The wire bytes are 0x1B 0x5F, ASCII ZUI;1;, UTF-8 JSON, then 0x1B 0x5C. Each complete frame is one transaction. Invalid, cancelled, unsupported, or oversized frames preserve the previous scene. Ordinary terminal data and Kitty graphics keep their own paths. Messages capabilities has v:1 and op:"capabilities". Its response reports last_rev, the component catalog and limits. Read this before starting a new application. Generic zterm consumers default to supported:false and ignore scene mutations. An attached native frontend must call Terminal::set_ui_host_enabled(true) before pumping the PTY. Only that frontend advertises supported:true. Applications use text fallback on an unsupported response or probe timeout. Detaching the renderer clears the scene and cancels an incomplete frame. replace requires v, op, nonzero numeric surface, rev, root, and nodes. events defaults to false. Nodes have stable nonzero numeric id and a type. The complete tree must have one root, no missing children, sharing, cycles or unreachable nodes. Nodes are stored by ID; children supplies display order. update requires surface, base_rev, a newer rev, and set, a nonempty list of existing node IDs with changed properties. Types and IDs cannot change. All updates are validated together before any are committed. Use replace to add or remove nodes, change types or renegotiate events. clear requires surface, base_rev and a newer rev. Revisions are unsigned 64-bit integers and strictly increase across the terminal lifetime, including clear, RIS and primary/alternate screen switches. Replayed revisions are rejected. Screen switches and RIS dismiss the scene without resetting the revision floor. Trusted catalog Type Properties column, row children: node ID array text text, optional style: body, heading, muted, code progress integer value from 0 to 10000, optional label button label, action, optional enabled (default true) image nonzero image_id, optional generation, alt, cols, rows In ztty, images reference the current terminal's existing KGP image store. No pixels are stored here. Omitted generation follows that image ID's current content; a supplied generation pins exactly those contents. Missing images use alt/placeholder. The host controls fonts, theme, clipping and panel geometry. v1 does not reserve terminal rows or insert components into scrollback. Bounds and actions Maximum JSON frame: 65536 bytes; nodes: 256; tree depth: 8 (root is depth 1); aggregate scene text: 32768 UTF-8 bytes; individual string: 4096 bytes; action: 64 ASCII letters, digits or ._:-; image extents: 1..1024 cells. Progress uses integer basis points. Unknown fields and duplicate keys are errors. Text rejects control characters except newline and tab. The receiver does not execute escapes. Only events:true scenes can yield actions. The host passes the surface/revision captured from the displayed hit to State::action and additionally verifies live session ownership, current layout, and a complete press/release gesture. Actions are intents returned to the host, not automatically written to a PTY. An opted-in application can receive the same APC framing with JSON fields v:1, type:"action", surface, rev, node, action, event_id. Event IDs never wrap. This is a native ztty protocol, not a claim of MCP Apps HTML/iframe compatibility or complete A2UI/OpenUI conformance. Protocol tests and the named benchmark scenarios accompany the implementation; no performance ranking is implied. Layouts and actions belong to the same State and host that created them. Surface/revision checks are local freshness checks; the host retains its own session identity, ownership and generation checks. Complete exchange After a supported capability response with last_rev:0, wrap each JSON object below in the APC prefix and ST terminator described above. For an existing terminal, substitute the reported revision plus one. {"v":1,"op":"replace","surface":7,"rev":1,"root":1,"events":true,"nodes":[{"id":1,"type":"column","children":[2,3,4]},{"id":2,"type":"progress","value":2500,"label":"Building"},{"id":3,"type":"image","image_id":42,"alt":"Preview"},{"id":4,"type":"button","label":"Retry","action":"build.retry"}]} {"v":1,"op":"update","surface":7,"base_rev":1,"rev":2,"set":[{"id":2,"value":10000,"label":"Complete"}]} The image bytes must already have been uploaded through KGP; image_id:42 is only a reference. A click on the displayed button can yield this opted-in reply: {"v":1,"type":"action","surface":7,"rev":2,"node":4,"action":"build.retry","event_id":1} A mismatched base_rev, stale click, invalid graph or invalid property does not partially apply. The old scene remains usable. Mutation and event counters fail closed at unsigned 64-bit exhaustion instead of wrapping or reusing identities. Measuring the core Run cargo bench -p zgpui --bench protocol. The benchmark emits JSON lines for 256-node creation, single-node progress updates in a 256-node tree, capability parsing, oversized-frame rejection, image-reference creation, and byte-fragmented frame collection. Fixtures are constructed before measurement. Allocation hooks exist only in the benchmark executable; production code forbids unsafe code. The output reports allocations, reallocations and requested allocation bytes, not peak live memory or RSS. Timings include the allocator instrumentation. A batch whose set entries contain only id and integer value fields in 0..=10000 can update progress values in place. It verifies the surface and revision, each target's ID and type, and duplicate IDs before any mutation. Existing labels, tree structure and retained text stay unchanged, so this path reuses their earlier validation. Updates with other node properties retain the general staging and validation path. The parser still allocates its entries vector, even for a single numeric update. Record the commit, toolchain, CPU and repeated samples before comparing results. The existing zterm benchmark separately checks ordinary VT throughput.

title: Platform integration
body: 场景与布局核心，可选原生 GPU 与 CPU 窗口后端。 Platform integration zgpui owns scene validation, scene revisions, layout and action identity. A host chooses its operating-system integration and decides when a completed frame becomes visible. The optional native module provides the shared window and immediate-widget backend documented in native integration. Responsibilities zgpui Host Typed Scene and bounded JSON updates Window or surface creation Graph, text and property validation Allocator and event loop Row/column layout in pixels Fonts, shaping, theme and clipping Scene/revision-aware hit testing Pointer and keyboard events Action intents Permission checks and application commands Image identifiers and extents Image decoding, storage and rendering The core has no Cargo dependencies or platform FFI. It uses alloc for variable storage. A final no_std executable supplies an allocator and its platform's startup and panic handling. Layout Accept a scene through State::replace_scene, then construct Layout::new(scene, bounds, metrics). Rect expresses pixel position and dimensions. Metrics sets line height, row/column gaps and control padding. Columns stack their children; rows share available width. The layout retains visible leaf rectangles and the scene identity. natural_height reports the content height before host clipping. Keep each layout with the same State and host that created it. Matching checks only surface and revision; host/session identity, ownership and generation checks remain the caller's responsibility. Rebuild layout when the scene or viewport changes. The host may apply its own outer panel, scrolling or window chrome. Fonts, DPI conversion and image resolution stay in the host. Renderer contract pub trait Renderer { type Error; fn begin(&mut self, bounds: Rect) -> Result<(), Self::Error>; fn draw(&mut self, node: &Node, rect: Rect) -> Result<(), Self::Error>; fn end(&mut self) -> Result<(), Self::Error>; fn abort(&mut self); } Layout::paint checks the scene identity, calls begin, draws the visible leaves in order and calls end. An error from any rendering phase calls abort and returns PaintError::Renderer. A stale layout returns PaintError::Stale. Implement end to commit a prepared frame and abort to discard it. The host is responsible for preventing partially drawn content from reaching the display. The trait is suitable for software, GPU, native and test renderers. Input Use Layout::button_at(scene, x, y) for an enabled button in the displayed layout. Pass the returned node together with that layout's surface and revision to State::action. Only scenes with events: true yield actions. The host checks the complete input gesture and the application's current authority before executing an action. The library returns an intent; it does not write to a PTY, execute a command or open a URL. Platform scope Target Core validation configured in CI Host integration Linux Native unit tests, doctests and the host example ztty supplies X11/GPU rendering macOS Native unit tests, doctests and the host example Supply an AppKit or other native host Windows Native unit tests, doctests and the host example Supply a Win32 or other native host wasm32-unknown-unknown Library compilation Supply a WebAssembly host and allocator x86_64-unknown-none Library compilation Supply an embedded or bare-metal host This matrix describes the default core. Optional native builds additionally validate Linux OpenGL and CPU backends, Windows WGL and macOS NSOpenGLContext. Release jobs run the backend checks on their actual platform; configured jobs are not a claim that a particular source revision passed. ztty can keep its own window renderer and its native Wayland host independently of these features. Examples and compatibility examples/host.rs implements a small renderer and routes an action through the typed API. The ZUI/1 adapter supports terminal applications that already send bounded JSON scenes.

title: Native materials
body: 场景与布局核心，可选原生 GPU 与 CPU 窗口后端。 Native materials The optional native renderer can capture a region of its own window, reuse that image, and draw it through a material or a perspective fold. Applications control the cache identity, quality, texture budget, custom shader parameters and redraw schedule. The portable scene core still builds without native effects. These are in-window effects. The mica-style preset does not request Windows DWM Mica or read the desktop wallpaper. Liquid glass does not call an Apple compositor material API. A material samples content already drawn by the application inside its window; it does not capture other applications. Run the gallery Use the platform libraries listed in native integration, then run: cargo run --locked --release --features native --example materials The gallery offers frosted glass, progressive blur, mica style, liquid glass, paper, a spatial fold and an application-defined shader. Drag the strength and openness sliders, select a quality level, or change the backdrop. The footer shows the actual renderer, capabilities and material resource counters. A fallback is identified explicitly in the status text. The fold has two distinct sampling modes. Backdrop locked to screen keeps the background in window coordinates while the pane tilts. Captured content follows fold rotates a captured card, including its text, as one plane. The hinge stays at the same target position. This is a perspective transform of a flat layer, not a general 3D scene graph or a physically based optical model. The interface requires at least 1020 × 700 pixels. Keyboard shortcuts are 1–7 to select a material, left/right arrows to adjust openness, -/+ to adjust strength, A to animate one fold, Escape to cancel and Q to close. The animation lasts 1.2 seconds and has no automatic repeat. Pointer movement outside changed widget targets does not trigger a new frame. When no animation or relevant input is pending, the loop waits for events and does not redraw. For a bounded screenshot or idle observation: cargo run --locked --release --features native --example materials -- \ --sample fold --openness 0.6 --duration 5 cargo run --locked --release --features native --example materials -- \ --sample fold --openness 0.6 --local-content --duration 5 The process prints its actual frame count and resource counters when it exits. Initial expose/resize events and user input can add frames; the timer itself does not request frames. The duration check runs after bounded event waits, so exit can lag the requested duration by up to approximately one second. Enable effects explicitly The descriptions live in zgpui::effects. Construction and validation of these values perform no GPU work. The native window methods are implemented in zgpui::native. use zgpui::effects::{CacheKey, EffectBudget, Fold, Material, Quality}; use zgpui::native::{Rect, Window}; let mut window = Window::new("Material", 960, 640)?; window.set_effects(Quality::Balanced, EffectBudget::default())?; let capabilities = window.effect_capabilities()?; { let mut canvas = window.begin(0xf8f9fbff); canvas.rect(Rect::new(80., 80., 340., 260.), 30., 0x9dc6efff); let outcome = canvas.material( Rect::new(180., 140., 420., 280.), CacheKey::new(1, 1), &Material::frosted(), &Fold::default(), )?; // Inspect outcome: Rendered and Fallback are different results. let submitted = canvas.effect_stats()?; } window.present(); # Ok::<(), String>(()) Quality::Off requests the flat fallback. Low, Balanced and High select the backend's quality settings. The gallery starts at Balanced; applications choose their own policy. A quality label is not proof of hardware acceleration: an OpenGL implementation such as Mesa llvmpipe may execute shaders on a CPU. Keep the reported driver string alongside measurements. EffectCapabilities reports capture, blur, progressive blur, custom shader and projective-fold availability for the current renderer. Its limits describe supported texture dimensions, cache entries and shader registrations. Check the returned EffectOutcome as well: a supported effect can still fall back when its current configuration or allocation cannot be served. Runtime path Meaning Shader/FBO capabilities available Materials can use the OpenGL effect pipeline. The driver string identifies the implementation; this alone does not establish physical GPU execution. Legacy OpenGL without required capabilities The renderer reports the unavailable features and uses a flat fallback where supported. Linux software feature The CPU window renderer remains available; callers must inspect its capabilities and fallback result instead of assuming GPU effects. Explicit cached-layer operation without capture support The operation cannot create or use the required captured layer; callers handle the returned error. The benchmark records this scenario as skipped. Keep source identity separate from appearance A CacheKey contains a nonzero application-owned ID and a content revision. Keep the key stable while the captured pixels are unchanged. Increase its revision when the backdrop or captured content changes. A source rectangle change also changes the capture identity. Reusing a revision after changing pixels intentionally asks the renderer to reuse the old image. Target position, fold angle and material parameters are separate from source identity. They can change without recapturing the backdrop. A blur configuration change may require new derived blur work even when the source capture is reused; the capture and blur-pass counters expose those different operations. Canvas::material captures and renders at the same rectangle. Canvas::material_at accepts separate source and target rectangles, with screen-space backdrop sampling. Window::invalidate_effect(id) removes a specific captured identity. Window::clear_effects() releases cached capture and blur textures while keeping registered custom shaders alive. For a complete folding layer, capture its text and surface first, clear/repaint the window, then draw the saved layer with cached_material: # use zgpui::effects::{CacheKey, EffectBudget, Fold, FoldAxis, Material, Quality}; # use zgpui::native::{Rect, Window}; # let mut window = Window::new("Layer", 960, 640)?; # window.set_effects(Quality::Balanced, EffectBudget::default())?; let source = Rect::new(160., 140., 420., 260.); let key = CacheKey::new(7, 1); { let mut canvas = window.begin(0xf8f9fbff); canvas.rect(source, 20., 0xfafcffff); canvas.text("The text folds too", 190., 190., 24, true, 0x20252dff); canvas.capture_effect(source, key)?; } { let mut canvas = window.begin(0xf8f9fbff); let mut image = Material::blur(); image.blur_radius = 0.; let fold = Fold { axis: FoldAxis::Vertical, angle_degrees: 35., anchor: 0., ..Fold::default() }; canvas.cached_material(source, key, &image, &fold)?; } window.present(); # Ok::<(), String>(()) cached_material is cache-only and attaches texture coordinates to the folded layer. It never silently captures a replacement. Use a material with transparent tint, such as the zero-radius Material::blur() above, when preserving the captured text. An opaque paper tint would cover that image. Recapture after a resize or an explicit cache clear before drawing the layer again. Customize the material and shader The built-in constructors produce editable Material values. Fields include tint, tint mix, opacity, corner and blur radii, saturation, grain, refraction, highlight, border width and progressive blur. Colors are literal 0xRRGGBBAA values and do not pass through the widget theme palette. Validation rejects nonfinite and out-of-range parameters before native renderer state changes. A custom shader is a GLSL 1.20 fragment function. The renderer supplies main, rounded clipping, opacity and the projective vertex transform. The input base_color is the sampled material color; local_uv belongs to the surface, and screen_uv refers to the screen sampling convention. Eight explicit floats are exposed as u_params. There is no implicit time uniform. vec4 effect(vec2 local_uv, vec2 screen_uv, vec4 base_color) { float stripe = 0.5 + 0.5 * sin(local_uv.y * 48.0 + u_params[1]); vec3 ink = mix(base_color.rgb, vec3(0.42, 0.51, 0.88), stripe * u_params[0] * 0.32); return vec4(ink, base_color.a); } Register source once with Window::register_shader, construct Material::custom(handle), and update material.parameters when application state changes. Registration is synchronous and returns compilation diagnostics; it belongs in preparation or an explicit editor action, not an ordinary frame. unregister_shader releases the registration. Removed handles and handles from another window are rejected rather than treated as raw native program IDs. Shader source is application code. Source length, registration count and parameter bounds are enforced; these checks do not establish a shader's execution time. Measure the custom workload on its intended driver. The gallery's ribbon shader is included as source and has no downloaded images, models or other binary assets. Resource limits and counters The default effect budget is 32 MiB of owned effect textures, 16 cache entries and 8 custom shader slots. The hard cache ceiling is 256 MiB and shader source is bounded to 16 KiB per registration. Applications can select smaller budgets with EffectBudget; the renderer evicts cached textures to respect those limits. A cached-content caller must be ready to recapture an evicted layer. EffectStats separates current texture bytes, lifetime peak texture bytes, capture count, cache hits/misses, blur passes, effect draws, evictions, shader compilations and fallback draws. Canvas::effect_stats reads those counters without forcing GPU completion, so a gallery can display this frame's submitted operations without adding a redraw loop or a synchronization stall. Texture bytes cover this effect cache's owned texture storage. They are not process RSS, total GPU memory, driver overhead, font-cache memory, backbuffer storage or compositor memory. Peak bytes are cumulative for the window, not a fresh per-scenario memory measurement. Cache hits also do not imply zero draw cost: the saved texture still has to be shaded and composited. Reproduce cached and invalidated workloads Build the example once, then pass the resulting executable to the repetition runner. Set an absolute target directory so generated files stay outside source history. On a shared Project Z development machine, use its prescribed target directory and outer Cargo lock instead. export CARGO_TARGET_DIR=/tmp/zgpui-materials-build cargo build --locked --release --features native --example materials python3 scripts/bench_materials.py \ --binary "$CARGO_TARGET_DIR/release/examples/materials" \ --output /tmp/zgpui-materials-balanced \ --quality balanced --iterations 120 --warmup 12 --repeats 3 \ --label "Record the GPU, driver, display and power mode here" Windows executables have an .exe suffix. Native Linux runs need a usable X11 display. xvfb-run can provide a display for automated checks, but its OpenGL driver may be software-backed; record that outcome rather than calling it a hardware-GPU measurement. A separate build with --features linux-software tests the CPU fallback path. Use a distinct output directory for each quality, renderer or build. The fixed-size probe renders a 960 × 640 window with a 460 × 280 material region. Each scenario uses strength 0.75 and a fixed geometric backdrop. The spatial and captured-content folds use openness 0.6. Cached iterations retain the same source key; invalidated iterations change its revision each frame. The captured-content case includes repainting the layer when its revision changes. Unsupported custom-shader or captured-layer scenarios are listed under skipped, rather than being relabelled as successful effect measurements. With --warmup 0, the first cached iteration includes its initial capture; use a nonzero warmup for a steady-state cache comparison. Each measured iteration records CPU submission time from begin through effect drawing, then calls Window::finish_effects() and records synchronized frame wall time. On the OpenGL backend this explicitly finishes submitted GL work; the CPU fallback is already synchronous. The second interval includes CPU work, driver overhead and waiting for GPU completion; it is not a GPU timestamp-query duration. Presentation is outside both intervals to avoid directly timing a swap/VSync wait. Warmup frames are excluded. The example does not call this synchronization method during normal interactive drawing. The runner preserves every raw JSON result and stderr log, the executable SHA-256, machine annotation and command line. It checks scenario identity, capability consistency and finite nonnegative measurements before reporting the median of each repetition's median and p95 values. A median of per-run p95s is not a pooled-sample percentile. Capture/pass/fallback counter deltas remain available per repetition instead of being averaged away. Use the evidence to answer separate questions: Question Relevant evidence Did a stable source avoid recapture? Cached stats_delta.captures, alongside actual capabilities and fallback count. Did invalidation request fresh source work? Invalidated capture and blur-pass deltas for the same material, size and driver. How much texture storage remained live? texture_bytes; compare with the configured budget and lifetime peak_texture_bytes. How expensive was submitting the frame? submit_median_us and submit_p95_us. How long until the submitted frame completed? completed_median_us and completed_p95_us, with the synchronization definition above. Did the renderer produce the requested effect? Capabilities, returned fallback/error state, and visual capture on that backend. Timing alone cannot establish visual correctness. Validation scope The example and measurement runner define reproducible workloads; they do not establish a universal performance advantage over another UI framework or an operating-system material. Publish comparisons only with matched dimensions, quality, driver, build, power state and visible output. Include software-driver runs as their own category. Interactive visual appearance, GPU timing and real memory behavior require a native run. Rust parameter tests can establish input validation, and CPU tests can establish fallback behavior, but neither substitutes for a real shader/FBO run. Cross-platform compile success also does not establish visual parity. Keep actual platform screenshots and raw measurement artifacts outside Git; record the tested commit and remaining untested platforms with the results. When a fold is active, positive progressive blur increases with distance from the selected hinge, along its fold axis; negative values reverse that gradient. Fold dimming also increases away from the hinge. A surface without a fold retains the vertical blur gradient and uniform dimming.

title: Native windows and migration
body: 场景与布局核心，可选原生 GPU 与 CPU 窗口后端。 Native windows and migration zgpui provides the native window and widget implementation formerly shipped as zui-native. The implementation now lives in this package under zgpui::native; there is no dependency on an old package or a compatibility import alias. Choose a backend Cargo features Platform code Rendering Default features, or default-features = false None Host-provided scene renderer std None The same scene core with the Rust standard library available native Linux X11, Windows Win32, macOS AppKit OpenGL through the platform API linux-software Linux X11 A CPU framebuffer presented through XPutImage native enables std; linux-software enables native. On other desktop platforms linux-software keeps their existing native renderer. Features are additive, so a Linux build with all features selects the CPU backend. Validate native separately when the application ships the OpenGL backend. The default scene core remains no_std + alloc, with zero Cargo dependencies. Native builds use a C bridge and system libraries; unsafe FFI is confined to the native module. Enabling a native window does not change the ZUI/1 scene protocol or implement an application event loop. Update a consumer Replace the old dependency key, package selection and vendor gitlink together: [dependencies] zgpui = { path = "vendor/zgpui", version = "=0.1.5", default-features = false, features = ["native"] } Use the linux-software feature for a Linux application that explicitly chooses CPU rendering. An optional application GUI should name dep:zgpui in its own feature declaration and mark this dependency optional = true. # fn main() -> Result<(), String> { # #[cfg(feature = "native")] { use zgpui::native::{Window, colors}; let mut window = Window::new("example", 640, 400)?; { let mut canvas = window.begin(colors::SURFACE); canvas.text("Hello", 20., 20., 18, false, colors::TEXT); } window.present(); # } # Ok(()) # } The public native types are Window, Canvas, Event, Rect, Theme, Palette, Ui, ButtonStyle and colors. Window stays on its creating thread and the backend allows one live window per process. native::Rect belongs to immediate drawing; layout::Rect belongs to the portable scene layout. A host implements a layout::Renderer adapter when it wants to paint scene nodes in a native window. Update .gitmodules to https://github.com/LIghtJUNction/zgpui.git, move the source directory to vendor/zgpui, pin the tested commit and regenerate the consumer lockfile. Rust calls use zgpui::native; do not retain a zui alias. Outer source bundles and installer repositories must update their own pins. Optional window colors and fonts Version 0.1.3 adds a window-local palette and preferred font family. Existing applications that do not call these setters retain their original theme and font selection. The default no_std scene core and its dependency list are unchanged. # fn main() -> Result<(), String> { # #[cfg(feature = "native")] { use zgpui::native::{Palette, Theme, Window}; let mut window = Window::new("example", 640, 400)?; window.set_theme(Theme::Dark); let mut ink = Palette::for_theme(Theme::Dark); ink.background = 0x161412ff; ink.surface = 0x201c18ff; ink.text = 0xe8ded2ff; ink.accent = 0xd4a373ff; ink.on_accent = 0x161412ff; window.set_palette(ink); window.set_font_family("JetBrains Mono")?; # } # Ok(()) # } Palette fields use 0xRRGGBBAA. The sixteen roles cover background, surface, text, muted text, lines, accent, hovered accent, soft accent, hovered surface, success and its soft surface, danger and its soft surface, disabled surface, disabled text, and text on an accent. Canvas primitives and the existing button and input widgets resolve canonical color tokens through the same palette. The token's alpha multiplies the selected role's alpha. Other RGB values pass through unchanged. Use on_accent for primary-button text; it is already resolved and is not interpreted again as a surface token. An explicit palette stays active when set_theme changes the built-in theme. Call clear_palette to return to that theme. Palette::for_theme initializes semantic roles from an existing theme; it groups legacy color aliases into their corresponding role. Leaving the palette unset preserves the original individual aliases exactly. set_font_family("monospace") selects the platform's fixed-width family. A missing named family falls back to that selection, and platform glyph fallback remains available for characters outside the chosen font.
