Linux honors installed Fontconfig aliases and language settings, Windows uses its installed family or Consolas/Courier New fallback, and macOS uses the requested family or its system monospaced font. The setter does not install fonts or change system preferences. Names may contain at most 255 UTF-8 bytes and no control characters. Surrounding whitespace is removed. An empty name resets the original default; repeating the same normalized request does no native work. Native preparation finishes before the old family is replaced. Failure returns an error and preserves the previous font and text cache. Success invalidates only text masks or textures, leaving geometry caches, framebuffer storage and the graphics context intact. Redraw the complete frame after a font change. Window access remains confined to its creating thread. The native bridge still allows only one live window per process; these setters do not introduce concurrent multiwindow support. Closing a window releases its font selection, so a later window starts with the original defaults. Fontconfig matching uses private temporary configurations and does not replace a host's process-wide configuration. Native build requirements Linux needs a C compiler, pkg-config, X11, FreeType and fontconfig development files. The native backend also needs OpenGL development files; the linux-software backend neither creates a GLX context nor links OpenGL. XWayland is required in Wayland sessions. Windows uses MSVC, Win32, WGL and GDI; macOS uses the Xcode tools, AppKit, NSOpenGLContext and CoreText. The CPU renderer owns one four-byte-per-pixel framebuffer and a bounded text mask cache. X11 server storage, fonts and the process runtime consume additional memory. This does not establish a whole-application memory limit. The renderer requires a compatible RGB X11 visual and bounds its framebuffer allocation. Linux releases temporary Fontconfig matching state after opening the required FreeType faces. Matching retains system and user aliases and default-language settings. Fonts added only to a host's in-memory Fontconfig configuration are not inherited by the private matching configuration. OpenGL mask storage The native GPU renderer uploads text and rounded-corner alpha masks with power-of-two storage dimensions, including on legacy OpenGL 1.1 drivers. This follows the platform's texture size contract. Texture coordinates select only the populated mask. The renderer reads GL_MAX_TEXTURE_SIZE and divides larger text masks into bounded tiles; adjacent tiles include neighbour pixels so linear filtering at fractional positions does not introduce a seam. Text advance and the original rasterization limits remain unchanged. The text cache allows at most 96 entries and 2 MiB of uploaded alpha texels, counting padding and tile borders. This is an accounting bound on those uploads, not a bound on total driver memory, fonts or the application. Rounded masks use a separate fixed cache. A failed upload releases all tiles created for that entry and does not cache an invalid texture. Closing the window releases both texture caches and resets the remembered device limit. CPU frame lifetime The Linux CPU backend keeps its framebuffer in a dedicated private anonymous mapping. After ordinary XPutImage copies the frame and XFlush drains the Xlib output, it releases the mapping's resident pages with MADV_DONTNEED. The virtual address remains reserved. This path does not use XShm, a server-side renderer or an additional process. See the Xlib image-transfer contract and Linux discard semantics. A successful Window::begin clears every pixel before drawing. CPU present consumes that frame; another present before a new begin is a no-op. Redraw the complete frame after Event::Resize, which also represents an X11 Expose event. The text-mask cache survives presentation. Drawing cannot write discarded frame contents before the next successful begin. Resize allocates a replacement mapping before releasing the old one. An allocation failure preserves the previous storage and dimensions; a failed begin does not expose a stale frame for presentation. Failure to discard pages retains memory without changing rendering correctness. If XImage metadata allocation fails, presentation retains the prepared frame for a later attempt. Drawing still requires the full four-byte-per-pixel surface. At 1120x760 this is 3,404,800 bytes, rounded to complete pages by the mapping. Report drawing peaks separately from idle residency; discarding this surface does not establish a whole-application memory limit. Checks cargo test --locked --lib cargo test --locked --lib --features native cargo test --locked --lib --features linux-software cargo clippy --locked --all-targets --features native -- -D warnings cargo clippy --locked --all-targets --features linux-software -- -D warnings python3 scripts/test_software.py python3 scripts/test_fonts.py -v cargo build --release --locked --example window_probe --features linux-software xvfb-run -a -s "-screen 0 1280x900x24 -nolisten tcp" python3 scripts/check_x11.py Private X11 checks inspect the actual title, WM_CLASS, minimum size and client geometry. Software rasterizer tests exercise clipping, alpha blending, text cache lifecycle, discarded-page residency and allocation failures under AddressSanitizer and UBSan. Font tests use installed Latin/CJK fonts to check locale matching, face reuse, raster stability across sizes and configuration ownership under the same sanitizers. Linux window checks also present multilingual regular and bold text, reject an empty frame, preserve a PNG and require a clean exit. The font checks require scalable Latin and CJK fonts, such as Liberation Sans and Noto Sans CJK. The Linux window checks require Xvfb, xauth, xdotool, x11-utils and ImageMagick in addition to the native development libraries. These are validation requirements, separate from application runtime libraries. Native window checks under Xvfb do not measure hardware GPU performance or establish a whole-application memory limit. The native release gate also runs style_probe on Linux, Windows and macOS. It records the actual OpenGL version, renderer, extensions and maximum texture size for GPU builds. Pixel checks require glyph foreground and background and transparent rounded corners, so a solid text rectangle cannot pass as text. It also reads actual pixels for primary-button text, disabled controls, input focus and selection, alpha and custom colors. It changes font families, checks fixed-width advances, rejects invalid names without changing the active font, restores the original frame, and closes/reopens a window to check default isolation. PPM frames accompany the result. The Linux sanitizer fixture also forces font preparation to fail, verifies that cached text and framebuffer storage survive, and repeatedly changes fonts while retaining host Fontconfig ownership. These checks exercise rendering and resource lifetimes rather than only comparing palette constants. The Linux GPU gate additionally exercises a real GL 1.1 context with the NPOT extension disabled. A separate fixture constrains texture limits to 256 and 64, compares the same complete viewport at fractional text positions and scaling, verifies the actual padded-upload budget, and injects an upload failure after the first tile to check cleanup and recovery. These cases use a private software GL context; they do not establish hardware GPU performance. The frozen native import and original file hashes are recorded in native-import.json. Historical source names in that receipt identify provenance; current dependency and import names are zgpui. The formal native entry point is scripts/check_native.py. It accepts --features native or --features linux-software; --window --package adds native-window and packaged-source checks. Release jobs use those options. Local validation evidence records the frozen runtime source, core and native checks, four real X11 cases per backend, and CPU driver dependency inspection. It reports no hardware benchmark or whole-application memory target. The Linux CPU release gate also compares real window pixels with the pre-discard implementation. Its source checkout must contain the frozen baseline commit. This test covers repeated presentation, resize/Expose redraw, allocation-failure rollback and an antialiased text/geometry scene under AddressSanitizer and UBSan: xvfb-run -a -s "-screen 0 1600x1000x24 -nolisten tcp" \ python3 scripts/test_software_x11.py \ --baseline cb50f2fe554622fdc984ae7fec9bcd844f175d67 \ --output /var/tmp/zgpui-framebuffer-x11

title: 概览
body: 处理 Kitty / Sixel 图像协议，向宿主提供图像与放置数据。 zgraphics Bounded Kitty Graphics Protocol and DEC Sixel processing for no_std terminals. The library uses alloc, performs no operating-system calls, and does not select a window system or renderer. All production Rust dependencies disable default features. It accepts direct (t=d) RGB, RGBA and PNG image data, including zlib compression, base64 transfers, capability queries, image IDs/numbers, source cropping, placements, placement IDs, scaling, z-order and deletion. PNG decoding uses zune-png; the container is checked before decoding and nonessential metadata is removed. Kitty animation frames, frame composition and playback use a monotonic clock supplied by the host; the library starts no timer. APNG remains unsupported. File, temporary-file and shared-memory transfers use an optional host-supplied ExternalReader. The host owns object validation, bounded reads and unlink policy. Without that callback, external transfers are unavailable. Unicode placeholders and relative placements resolve through the same scene: the host supplies decoded Placeholder cells, and draws_with_placeholders returns the corresponding draws. use zgraphics::{Context, Graphics}; let mut images = Graphics::default(); let context = Context { col: 0, row: 0, cols: 80, rows: 24, cell_width: 8, cell_height: 16, }; let mut replies = Vec::new(); images.command(b"Ga=T,i=1,f=24,s=1,v=1,C=1;/wAA", context, &mut replies); let draw = images.draws(0).next().unwrap(); assert_eq!(draw.image.pixels.as_slice(), [255, 0, 0, 255]); assert_eq!(replies, b"\x1b_Gi=1;OK\x1b\\"); Graphics::command accepts one protocol-sized APC body starting with G, without the surrounding ESC _ and ESC \\. For a byte stream, use CommandStream: it retains at most a 512-byte header and 4096 encoded bytes, decoding larger bodies incrementally into the bounded transfer. This also accepts existing clients such as kitten icat which can emit an entire image in one APC. Both padded and unpadded final base64 are accepted; an explicit nonfinal m=1 chunk must still be a multiple of four without padding. The host owns ESC/ST framing and passes cursor/grid context. Images become visible only when finish receives ST. Graphics::draws returns sorted, borrowed straight-alpha RGBA images and source and destination rectangles. The renderer honors Draw::clip while preserving the full source-to-destination transform, additionally clips to its viewport, and implements the documented z-order around text and explicit backgrounds. Pixel buffers use Arc<Vec<u8>>; a native renderer can retain a buffer until its graphics API has finished reading it. Renderers must release their retained references and converted-image caches when no longer needed. The dependency on Arc requires targets with pointer-width atomics. Default limits per scene are 8192 pixels per dimension, 32 MiB per decoded image, 32 MiB total decoded storage, 16 MiB per pending transfer, 128 stored images and 512 placements. Limits are configurable. PNG decoding has additional temporary buffers bounded by validated dimensions and compressed input; the decoded-store quota is not a claim about peak process RSS. A terminal normally keeps independent scenes for primary and alternate screens. No image storage is allocated while idle. The decoded-storage accounting includes vector capacity, not only populated pixels. scroll, trim_history, and set_viewport let the host keep placements attached to terminal content. revision changes on scene mutations; Image::generation distinguishes replacement pixel data under an existing ID for renderer caches. Generation values are local to a scene; clear renderer caches when changing to a different scene. Full-screen upward scrolls can retain images in history, while partial-region scrolls move only placements whose anchors lie inside the region. Protocol reference: https://sw.kovidgoyal.net/kitty/graphics-protocol/. Sixel begin_sixel, sixel_put, finish_sixel, and abort_sixel decode a DCS body incrementally into the same image scene used by Kitty images. The decoder handles repeat counts, raster extents, integer pixel aspect ratios, graphics carriage return/newline, 256 color registers, RGB percentages, DEC HLS colors, and opaque or transparent backgrounds. Raster extents are minimum dimensions, so following pixel data may extend them. Redefining a register recolors earlier pixels within the image. The initial 16 registers use VT340 colors; remaining registers start black. The host can retain the returned palette for shared-register mode. The decoder creates no image storage before its first pixel or declared raster. It counts encoded input against max_transfer_bytes, decoded RGBA capacity against max_image_bytes, and expanded painting/copying work against eight times max_image_bytes pixel operations. Dimensions include the vertical aspect scale; aspect ratios are rounded to an integer of at least one and bounded at 64. Malformed parameters or a quota violation immediately release the partial decoder. A host must call finish_sixel only for ST; CAN, SUB, replacement escape sequences and a truncated stream must cancel it. Invalid input cannot replace a completed image or move the text cursor. During decoding the indexed canvas uses at most half the decoded-image quota. Final conversion can briefly hold that canvas and one RGBA buffer together (48 MiB with the default 32 MiB image quota). Completed images remain subject to the existing 32 MiB scene quota; renderer-owned uploads are separate. Palette changes in a later image do not recolor already completed RGBA images. The zterm host implements default scrolling, display mode (DECSDM 80), the right-of-image cursor option (8452), and private/shared color registers (1070). It accepts ESC P introducers and either ESC \\ or the 8-bit ST byte as the terminator. It preserves framing across arbitrary PTY read boundaries. Sixel protocol and raster/color definitions: https://vt100.net/docs/vt3xx-gp/chapter14.html. Modern DECSDM polarity and cursor extensions: https://invisible-island.net/xterm/ctlseqs/ctlseqs.html. The DEC manual's DECSDM set/reset prose conflicts with modern xterm behavior; this implementation follows xterm: mode 80 set disables scrolling and uses the top-left origin, while reset enables scrolling at the text cursor. The host-level Sixel reference test compares fixture pixels, libsixel's sixel2png, and the zterm parser at five input chunk sizes. It remains in the host repository. This crate's tests exercise protocol and pixel behavior; they do not establish native GUI presentation. Standalone crate and validation This repository contains the independent zgraphics 0.2.0 workspace. It was extracted from ztty at f2db31d7; the extraction record records the original file blobs. Public types remain under zgraphics::, and the module split changes neither their paths nor the method bodies. Module Responsibility lib.rs Public data, scene storage, quotas and content lifecycle kitty.rs Kitty command execution, transfer completion and replies sixel_scene.rs Sixel stream lifetime, scene commit and cell erasure sixel.rs, decode.rs Bounded raster and image decoding placement.rs Relative anchors and Unicode placeholder draw geometry animation.rs Frame storage, composition and host-clock advancement protocol.rs, stream.rs, transport.rs Command parsing, APC streaming and host I/O callback Run the library checks from this directory with Rust 1.100 or newer: cargo test --locked --lib cargo test --locked --doc cargo fmt --all -- --check cargo clippy --locked --all-targets -- -D warnings python3 tools/check_package.py cargo package --locked rustup target add wasm32-unknown-unknown x86_64-unknown-none cargo check --locked --lib --target wasm32-unknown-unknown cargo check --locked --lib --target x86_64-unknown-none The manually invoked candidate workflow checks one fixed commit on Linux, macOS and Windows, plus WebAssembly and bare-metal compilation, formatting, Clippy and the crate archive. It has read-only repository permissions and does not publish a crate or create a release. Compilation on a target does not establish renderer, filesystem callback or GUI behavior on that platform. The separate release workflow is also manual. It prepares an optional version bump or resumes an exact existing candidate, runs the full candidate workflow, then verifies the package's embedded Git identity and crates.io checksum before pushing the matching tag and completing the GitHub Release. Repeating an interrupted release requires matching package bytes and the same tag commit. Publication credentials are supplied only when the repository owner invokes that workflow.

title: 概览
body: 工具执行前的策略、能力与审批检查，提供有界审计接口。 zguard Lightweight Security Guardrails for AI Agents. zguard makes an explicit decision before an AI tool or command is executed. It matches host-owned policies, checks capability and input limits, consumes exact request approvals, and records a bounded audit event before reserving a call. The library is no_std, uses no allocator, has no Cargo dependencies, and forbids unsafe Rust. Use [dependencies] zguard = "=0.1.0" use zguard::{ActionKind, Context, Decision, Guard, Limits, NoAudit, Policy, Request, Rule}; let rules = [ Rule::new(1, ActionKind::Tool, "files.read", Decision::Allow).requiring(1), Rule::new(2, ActionKind::Tool, "files.write", Decision::RequireApproval).requiring(2), Rule::new(3, ActionKind::Tool, "shell.run", Decision::Deny), ]; let policy = Policy::new(7, &rules)?; let mut guard = Guard::new( policy, Context { session: 42, capabilities: 3 }, Limits { max_calls: 20, max_payload_bytes: 4096 }, ); let request = Request::tool("call-1", "files.read", br#"{"path":"notes.txt"}"#); let verdict = guard.authorize(request, 100, None, &mut NoAudit); assert!(verdict.is_allowed()); // Invoke the trusted executor now, with this exact request. // For production audit, replace NoAudit with your Audit implementation. # Ok::<(), zguard::PolicyError>(()) The host owns the executor, identity, session epoch, policy, monotonic clock and approval channel. Construct capability masks from authenticated host state. Model arguments and remote tool annotations are request data and grant no rights. MCP documents this trust boundary for tool annotations. Decisions and limits Names match exactly and case-sensitively. Tool and command namespaces are separate. Unknown names and an empty policy are denied. When several rules match, explicit deny wins, then approval, then allow; the smallest relevant rule ID makes audit results deterministic. All matching capability requirements combine. RequireApproval stops execution. After its external approval process, the host calls Guard::approve(request, expires_at) and passes the returned object to authorize. Approval binds the complete immutable policy and context, call ID, kind, name and raw tool bytes or structured command argv/cwd. A mismatched, expired or consumed object grants nothing. Expiry is exclusive: now >= expires_at is expired. Clock values may stay equal and must never decrease. The approval object is not cloneable and is consumed on every authorization attempt, including rejected attempts. The trusted host can issue a new object. Use a fresh session epoch when recreating a guard; equal policy/context values deliberately describe the same authorization domain. Tokens are process-local Rust values, not signed credentials or persistent replay protection. Limits cap authorized attempts and each request's payload bytes. Tool bytes are counted verbatim. Command bytes sum argv and cwd UTF-8 lengths; argv boundaries remain separate for approval matching. An allowed call reserves one quota unit after audit succeeds and before execution. Failed executors do not refund it. The host must count any retry as another authorization attempt. Audit and execution boundary Audit::record receives numeric session/policy/sequence IDs, action kind, payload length and a verdict. It receives no arguments, command lines, names, call IDs or outputs. A sink error changes the returned verdict to Deny / AuditFailed and does not reserve a call. The sequence still advances, identifying the attempted decision. The sink controls durability, transport and access to records. Only authorize(...).is_allowed() permits an effect. evaluate is a pure preview. Place authorization immediately before the executor and use the same request without mutation or substitution. zharness integrates this boundary through its native guarded execution APIs. Direct application executors remain trusted code. Scope zguard evaluates deterministic host policy. The host provides JSON validation, argument/resource policy, OS isolation, canonical paths, network controls and execution timeouts. Authorizing a general shell or plugin grants the capabilities that its adapter exposes. Use narrow tools and OS isolation where required. Natural-language prompt-injection detection is outside this core. Validate python3 scripts/check.py cargo bench --locked --bench policy cargo check --locked --lib --target x86_64-unknown-none The final command requires that Rust target to be installed. See SECURITY.md for trust and approval contracts and docs/VALIDATION.md for claim-to-evidence mapping. The first local validation and optimized measurements are recorded in docs/VALIDATION-2026-11-20.md. Release instructions describe immutable tags and verified registry/GitHub recovery.

title: 概览
body:
复用上下文、工具循环、hook 与协作执行原语。 zharness Caller-buffered primitives for developer-owned AI harnesses: context windows, model/tool turns, hooks, output transforms and multi-agent coordination. The core is no_std, forbids handwritten unsafe Rust and directly depends on zcall = "=0.4.0", zplugin = "=0.3.1" and zguard = "=0.1.0" with default features disabled. zplugin's official macro generates the native interface and introduces compilation-only parser dependencies. Native library loading is shared through zsys = "=0.1.1", a transitive dependency of zplugin. The default/native runtime graph stays within Project Z crates; the explicit wasm feature adds zplugin's Wasmi sandbox. The dependency audit checks exact Z versions, registry sources and a single resolved package for each name. The protocol layer consumes zconv 0.4.0 through zcall and retains trusted native and untrusted Wasm plugins with named operations, mixed-backend routing, explicit disabling/replacement and existing authorization hooks. It retains skills, typed lifecycle channels, provider-bound tool signatures and conversation/model/request/response primitives. The library does not start an HTTP client or agent runtime. Development uses Rust 1.100.0; MSRV remains 1.99.1, edition 2024. To use the published package: [dependencies] zharness = "=0.6.0" Default features enable filesystem skill discovery and native path loading. Set default-features = false to use the no_std core. Add features = ["wasm"] for sandboxed plugins. This feature needs an allocator but does not imply std; native plugin loading continues to require trusted code. Response lifecycle hooks distinguish raw reasoning from summaries and preserve provider-owned Anthropic blocks, citation deltas and usage metadata as separate actions. Those server tool blocks never enter the local execution queue. The re-exported zharness::zcall contract also exposes structured tool results, continuous usage configuration and the api resource codecs. Boundary The library maintains bounded state and returns actions. Your application owns I/O, model selection, authorization, scheduling and persistence. No HTTP client, background worker, retry engine, tokenizer, summarizing model or database is started implicitly. MCP is developed independently in zmcpio; this repository contains no MCP integration directory or cross-repository build dependency. Module Atomic capability context Grouped history, budgets, pinned retention, eviction, explicit summaries, forks and zcall request construction turn Model/tool actions, real ToolReady retention, bounded rounds/calls and out-of-order completion hooks Existing native before/completion/error callbacks for tools, commands, results and coordination lifecycle New independent typed Gate/Observer/Interceptor channels, correlation and paired operations conversation, settings New gated message acceptance and committed model/reasoning/configuration changes request, response New actual-send boundary and replay-aware real zcall event consumption/final reply acceptance execution, command Hooked user executors, preserved IDs/status and bounded output checks; no OS runtime guard Native zguard execution policy, single-use approvals, quotas and audit-before-effect boundaries output Caller-buffered text reduction and validated JSON minification cluster Capability matching, task dependencies, leases, handoff, joins and bounded mailboxes skills Borrowed SKILL.md metadata, caller-buffered summaries, ordered directories and on-demand loading plugin Trusted native loading, explicit mixed-plugin routes, checked outputs and an Executor bridge plugin::wasm Optional untrusted Wasm loading, named operation allowlists, execution limits and safe replacement tools, validation, bridge Tool definitions, argument policy and public zcall result APIs Native security guardrails Use Prepared::execute_guarded and Command::execute_guarded to apply zguard at the actual execution boundary. Policies deny unmatched calls, separate tool and command permissions, require host-issued approvals where configured, and check call/input limits. A failed audit write blocks execution. Models cannot grant themselves permission through argument fields. Authorization and the executor adapters are single-attempt values. Reuse the session Guard to preserve quotas, and construct a new Authorization with current host time for each call. Existing low-level execution APIs retain their explicit host-authorization contract. See GUARDRAILS.md for request binding, plugin routing, privacy and the complete compiled example. cargo run --locked --example guarded_execution Native extensions plugin::Plugin exposes zplugin's actual native loader. Load an explicitly chosen trusted library, create ExtensionApi's typed proxy, then call operations with borrowed input and caller-owned output buffers. The same proxy implements Executor, so it works with the existing tool registry and execution hooks. The v1 extension interface has one operation: call(operation, input, output). The library checks returned lengths and can validate UTF-8; the application owns operation semantics, payload schemas, scheduling, permissions and recovery. There is no automatic plugin scan, tool registration, execution or reload loop. See PLUGINS.md for loading, plugin authoring, lifecycle and examples. Untrusted Wasm and mixed plugin tools Enable wasm, then use plugin::wasm::WasmExtension::load with an explicit interface ID/version, resource limits and a host-owned name-to-operation map. The safe loader accepts zplugin's import-free Wasm32 protocol. It denies WASI, filesystem/network/host imports, checks memory ranges and meters execution fuel. The adapter implements the same Executor used by native extension proxies. plugin::Router borrows explicit Route and Slot arrays. A public tool name selects a slot and backend operation; set_enabled denies a slot without invoking it, and replace switches a previously validated executor at a call boundary. Execute through Prepared::execute_with_hooks to authorize the public tool name before routing. Unknown or disabled tools fail closed, with no fallback or retry. rustup target add wasm32-unknown-unknown python3 scripts/wasm.py This builds a real allocator-free guest and runs both a sandbox-only host and a host routing tools to native and Wasm plugins. WasmExtension::reload validates a fresh same-interface instance before replacement; failure retains the current state. Runtime failures preserve detailed diagnostics through last_error(). Wasm is a separate synchronous byte-buffer ABI. Native tasks, pointers, resources and callbacks are not forwarded into it. Isolation depends on the Wasm engine; guest-memory limits do not cap process RSS, and fuel does not time module compilation. Use additional process isolation for stricter resource/threat models. See the complete contracts and examples. The Wasm adapter measurements compare matched zplugin, Executor and Router calls with raw samples and allocation counts. They distinguish warmed calls from loading and do not claim process RSS limits or end-to-end agent latency. Native skills SkillPaths::from_env(project) combines project and global skills with any directories in SKILLS_PATH. Earlier valid names win, while unrelated global skills remain available. The environment follows the host PATH syntax and precedes the defaults. Use prepend or push for software-specific directories, or SkillPaths::new(roots) for an exact search plan. export SKILLS_PATH="$PWD/.agents/skills:$HOME/.claude/skills:/opt/editor/skills" cargo run --locked --example skills Discovery retains each skill's name, description and location. Summary generation writes escaped XML into your buffer; selected bodies and resources load on demand. The default std feature enables the filesystem adapter. Disabling default features retains the borrowed parser and summary writer with no alloc or I/O. See SKILLS.md for Rust examples, precedence, diagnostics and limits. Grouped lifecycle hooks (0.2.3) Use a small typed event rather than a hundred methods in one Hooks trait. The families are conversation, model, prompt, request, response, tool, context, agent, persistence and runtime. Gates decide; interceptors change copied candidates; observers record facts. Observers get payload metadata by default, with explicit content opt-in. Tuples compose statically; there is no global mutable registry. Lifecycle::run wraps an actual operation. begin/finish supports application- owned async work and out-of-order completion without an async runtime. Native adapters already cover user acceptance, message edits/deletes, model and reasoning changes, request building/sending, stream consumption and assistant finalization. Storage, routing, rate limits and other application-owned work use explicit wrappers, not fictitious automatic interception. See LIFECYCLE.md for the full 97-action matrix, compiled examples, privacy and failure/replay contracts. An accepted send is not provider receipt. A model turn ending in WaitingTools is not a final assistant reply. A paused stream event must be replayed before it is counted as accepted. ModelSettings records intent for future requests; provider capability checks and wire mappings still belong to the application and zcall. Context without an owned conversation heap use zharness::context::{Budget, Context, Group, Message, Overflow}; use zharness::zcall::v1::{Content, Role}; let instructions = [Content::text("Use only approved tools.")]; let question = [Content::text("Review this change.")]; let system = [Message::new(Role::System, &instructions)]; let user = [Message::new(Role::User, &question)]; let mut slots = [None; 8]; let mut context = Context::new( &mut slots, Budget { limit: 4096, reserved: 1024 }, )?; // Caller estimates for illustration; use the target model's tokenizer in production. context.push(Group::new(0, &system, 16).pinned(), Overflow::Reject)?; context.push(Group::new(1, &user, 20), Overflow::EvictOldest)?; assert_eq!(context.tokens(), 36); # Ok::<(), zharness::Error>(()) Keep related calls/results in one Group. Eviction/compaction never splits a group. Forks copy descriptors, not borrowed content; explicit summaries come from the application. Context::build delegates protocol representation and checked tool results to zcall instead of creating another provider adapter. Drive a loop without surrendering control use zharness::{ToolLoop, hooks::NoHooks, turn::{Action, CallSlot, LoopLimits}}; let mut slots = [const { CallSlot::<1024>::new() }; 4]; let mut flow = ToolLoop::new(7, &mut slots, LoopLimits::default()); let mut hooks = NoHooks; assert_eq!(flow.next(&mut hooks)?, Action::CallModel { run: 7, round: 1 }); // The application has not sent a model request yet. assert_eq!(flow.next(&mut hooks)?, Action::Pending); # Ok::<(), zharness::Error>(()) Feed genuine zcall events to observe, then execute only approved Execute tickets. ToolReady is retained until WaitingTools is confirmed. Several tickets can finish out of order. Retain history/results, acknowledge the Session and commit each result explicitly before another model action is issued. No hidden loop performs network requests or retries side effects. Execution and output processing Prepared::execute_with_hooks and Command::execute_with_hooks gate actual user executors, distinct from scheduling or history commitment. Pause/deny does not invoke an adapter. Nonzero command exits and business tool errors retain their status; invalid output or adapter failures remain errors. The core does not spawn processes, interpret shell strings or enforce adapter timeouts. use zharness::{bridge::Completion, hooks::{HookResult, NoHooks}}; use zharness::output::{Chain, DedupAdjacentLines, Truncate}; let original = Completion { call_id: "real-call-id", text: "error: missing config
error: missing config
", is_error: true, }; let mut scratch = [0; 1024]; let mut output = [0; 256]; let mut pipeline = Chain::new( DedupAdjacentLines, Truncate::new(256, "
...[truncated]")?, &mut scratch, ); let HookResult::Applied(reduced) = original.transform_with_hooks( "build", &mut pipeline, &mut output, &mut NoHooks, )? else { unreachable!("NoHooks never pauses"); }; assert_eq!(reduced.text, "error: missing config
"); assert_eq!(reduced.call_id, original.call_id); assert!(reduced.is_error); # Ok::<(), zharness::Error>(()) Reduction preserves identity/status. Retry failed output processing with retained raw input, not by rerunning the tool. JsonMinify validates through zcall; text truncation is explicitly lossy and does not promise valid truncated JSON or exact token savings. Custom semantic summaries remain an application decision. Run from the source checkout cargo test --locked --all-targets cargo test --locked --doc python scripts/examples.py cargo run --locked --example conversation_hooks cargo run --locked --example tool_loop cargo run --locked --example command_hooks cargo bench --locked --benches The conversation example covers user approval, settings changes, real zcall request encoding, an in-memory send, recorded response parsing and explicit final persistence. Tool-loop tests cover real interleaved calls. Command hooks run controlled child processes on the host. No live provider credentials are required; these examples do not claim real network/model/database integration. All proportional core storage is caller-owned. Generic callback code and adapters can independently allocate or cause side effects. Hooks are not a sandbox, IDs are not authentication, and leases do not provide external exactly-once execution. Read architecture, typed lifecycle, hook boundaries, context, loop, commands, output, agents, skills, plugins, security, and performance.

title: Command execution hooks
body: 复用上下文、工具循环、hook 与协作执行原语。 Command execution hooks Command hooks surround an explicitly supplied command adapter, not every process in the host application. The core remains no_std and does not spawn a process, interpret a shell string, create threads, wait on I/O or allocate capture buffers. Use the hooked entry point to obtain its guarantees; direct OS calls bypass it. Minimal complete example This memory adapter demonstrates the contract without starting an OS process. The actual process adapter is in examples/command_hooks.rs. use zharness::command::{Command, CommandError, CommandExecutor, CommandOutput, ExitStatus}; use zharness::hooks::{Decision, HookResult, Hooks}; struct Approval { approved: bool } impl Hooks for Approval { fn before_command(&mut self, command: Command<'_>) -> Decision { if command.program != "approved-program" { return Decision::Deny; } if self.approved { Decision::Allow } else { Decision::Pause } } } struct MemoryAdapter { calls: usize } impl CommandExecutor for MemoryAdapter { fn execute(&mut self, _: Command<'_>, _: &mut [u8], _: &mut [u8]) -> Result<CommandOutput, CommandError> { self.calls += 1; Ok(CommandOutput { status: ExitStatus::Exited(0), stdout_len: 0, stderr_len: 0 }) } } let command = Command::new("command-1", "approved-program", &["--literal-argument"]); let mut adapter = MemoryAdapter { calls: 0 }; let mut approval = Approval { approved: false }; assert!(matches!(command.execute_with_hooks(&mut adapter, &mut [], &mut [], &mut approval)?, HookResult::Paused)); assert_eq!(adapter.calls, 0); approval.approved = true; let HookResult::Applied(result) = command.execute_with_hooks(&mut adapter, &mut [], &mut [], &mut approval)? else { unreachable!("approval was supplied"); }; assert!(result.status.success()); assert_eq!(adapter.calls, 1); # Ok::<(), CommandError>(()) Event contract Command::execute_with_hooks validates nonempty identities/executables and rejects NULs in executable/arguments/cwd. These are structural checks, not executable resolution or permission checks. Invalid descriptors never reach the hooks or adapter. Empty literal arguments are allowed; an explicitly empty cwd is not. before_command sees the exact command ID, program, argument slice and optional working directory. Tuple chains evaluate left-to-right. Pause returns HookResult::Paused; Deny returns CommandError::Denied. Both prevent the adapter call and leave stdout/stderr buffers untouched. No after/error callback describes these as attempted process executions. After Allow, the adapter is invoked once. A normal completed result first passes capture-length checks, then after_command receives the original description, exit status and borrowed stdout/stderr bytes. Nonzero exit codes and termination without a code remain completed results with success() == false. They are not silently normalized to success or automatically retried. Adapter errors call command_error and return that same bounded error. Categories include Spawn, Io, TimedOut, Cancelled, Capacity and adapter-defined codes. Invalid capture lengths produce InvalidOutput before after_command can observe invalid slices. Error observers cannot suppress failure or replace it with success. Output may be binary: UTF-8 checking belongs to an explicit text conversion. There is one completion OR error observation per attempted adapter call on normal return. Hook/adapter panics, process crashes and externally abandoned work are not caught or guaranteed to generate a final callback. A later explicit invocation is a new attempt, not an idempotent replay protected by command ID. Actual tool execution versus commands Prepared::execute_with_hooks brackets the actual generic Executor invocation using before_execute, after_execute and execute_error. It retains the real model call ID, validated arguments and failure flag. Business is_error=true results invoke after_execute; executor errors, oversized lengths and invalid UTF-8 invoke execute_error. Pause/deny does not execute or modify output. These boundaries differ from ToolLoop's Before::Tool ticket issuance and After::ToolFinished result commitment. A command inside a tool can use its own command hooks. A typical composition is: ToolLoop ticket gate -> before_execute -> application Executor -> before_command -> application OS adapter -> after_command / command_error -> after_execute / execute_error -> before_result -> optional output transforms -> after_result -> explicit history and Session acceptance -> ToolLoop result commitment No inner event is fabricated: a tool that does not execute commands emits no command hooks, and no result processing happens unless requested explicitly. Execution hooks see raw output, so apply appropriate secrecy policy to observers. Output transforms remain the separate redaction/reduction layer from OUTPUT.md. Adapter responsibilities Pass argv elements literally; never concatenate them into an implicit shell. An explicit shell program (sh -c, cmd /C, etc.) is still a shell and requires its own authorization. A string allowlist does not defeat PATH replacement, symlinks, working-directory races or executable substitution. Resolve and enforce identities and privileges at the actual OS boundary when those risks matter. The descriptor intentionally omits OS-specific environment, stdin, file handles, resource limits and sandbox policy. Configure those in a trusted adapter and make them available to application policy out of band. Do not treat the descriptor as a full audit record of unrepresented OS settings. UTF-8 descriptors do not encode all possible native OS paths; use a platform-specific application boundary for non-UTF-8 requirements rather than lossy conversion. The example clears inherited environment, disables stdin, uses an absolute path to its own controlled child executable, and drains stdout/stderr concurrently into bounded buffers. It waits/reaps the child even after capture exceeds capacity. It tests success, exit code 7, and both pipes exceeding capacity without retry. It deliberately has no timeout implementation; TimedOut/Cancelled are adapter reports, not library timers or cancellation mechanisms. An error after execution may follow real side effects. Do not rerun a command just to enlarge a capture buffer. Retain available results and apply explicit idempotency or recovery policy. Parallel commands need separate buffers and hook state or application synchronization. The library does not schedule workers. Run cargo run --locked --example command_hooks. The example uses std and application threads; those allocations and OS calls are outside the no_std core.

title: Architecture
body: 复用上下文、工具循环、hook 与协作执行原语。 Architecture The application owns external work. zharness supplies bounded state transitions; zcall owns model protocols, IR, streaming aggregation and lifecycle. All zcall integration uses public v1 APIs. No provider-specific fields or MCP source are parsed by the harness components. The guarded tool path preserves application-owned I/O and result retention: flowchart TD C["Conversation and context"] --> R["Request and host sender"] R --> S["zcall session"] S --> T["ToolLoop tickets"] S --> F["Final response acceptance"] T --> G["Hooks and zguard authorization"] G --> E["Host executor"] E --> O["Retained tool result"] O --> C Context retains borrowed message groups, caller token costs and explicit summaries. Whole-group eviction preserves correctly grouped tool exchanges. Forks copy only descriptors. Token estimates, semantic summaries and payload lifetime remain caller contracts; the core does not create a tokenizer, storage system or summarizer. ToolLoop separates stream observation from execution. Genuine ToolReady events are retained in fixed slots, and the terminal WaitingTools outcome permits dispatch. The application owns concurrent work and retains results/history before clearing per-turn storage. Original call IDs and run/round tickets reject mismatched or stale completions without a hidden cross-system transaction. Existing Hooks methods gate/observe native operations without changing their semantics. Typed lifecycle channels extend coverage independently rather than appending dozens of methods to that trait. Gate controls proposals; Interceptor edits a copy before validation/gating; Observer records metadata by default. The non-cloneable Span receipt supports explicitly bracketed async work without requiring Futures, threads or a runtime in the core. All identities and retained receipt storage are supplied/owned by the caller. Conversation and ModelSettings make their local state changes only on accepted operations. These do not globally observe UI changes or reconfigure in-flight model calls. Sender acceptance is adapter-defined, not proof of server receipt. ResponseStream receives original zcall events and honors event rejection/replay; first visible output, terminal outcome and final message acceptance remain separate. WaitingTools and failures cannot be finalized as successful replies. TaskBoard stores descriptors, not agent workers. Topological dependencies, one active lease per agent, attempt/epoch fencing and explicit expiry give a bounded coordination layer. Leases do not revoke already-started external effects or provide distributed consensus/exactly-once delivery. Mailboxes need caller-owned synchronization and transport when used across threads or machines. Lifecycle::run can surround prompt construction, database writes, checkpoints, policy checks, retries and worker operations. A label/notification alone performs none of those tasks. Native wrappers and explicitly application-wrapped boundaries are enumerated separately in LIFECYCLE.md. Error propagation never implies rollback of external effects or permission for a blind retry. Panics are not caught. The direct runtime dependencies are zcall 0.4.0, zplugin 0.3.1 and zguard 0.1.0. zcall uses zconv 0.4.0; zplugin shares native loading through zsys 0.1.1. zguard has no Cargo dependencies. zplugin-macros and its parser dependencies run during compilation. The optional Wasm feature adds its separately audited engine; there is no MCP repository dependency. The guard owns per-session authorization state. Prepared and Command guarded methods retain exact request identity and feed it to zguard before invoking user code. Default denial, one-use host approvals, limits and metadata audit are part of that boundary. Existing low-level adapter methods keep their explicit host permission contract. See GUARDRAILS.md for the complete integration path. Native extensions use zplugin's real loader and generated v1 interface. The interface passes an operation name, input bytes and caller output storage, with no prescribed payload format. ExtensionProxy checks output sizes and optionally UTF-8; its Executor implementation passes validated tool arguments unchanged. Prepared's guarded execution methods check policy and audit before the actual native call; existing hooks retain their independent callbacks. The proxy borrows its library, so object destruction precedes unloading. Trust decisions, operation meaning, tool registration, scheduling and reload policy are explicit host responsibilities. The core contains no handwritten FFI or unsafe block. Skills have a separate metadata and filesystem boundary. SkillMetadata borrows frontmatter and summary writers use caller buffers without alloc or I/O. The optional std SkillPaths adapter reads explicitly configured directories and keeps only metadata in a SkillCatalog. An ordered root list determines name precedence; an index accelerates lookup without duplicating owned names. A chosen skill loads its instructions and resources on demand. The application decides prompt placement, activation and tool permissions; discovery never starts a process or model call.

title: Native and Wasm plugin primitives
body: 复用上下文、工具循环、hook 与协作执行原语。 Native and Wasm plugin primitives The plugin module connects zharness to zplugin 0.3.0. Trusted native libraries use the frozen Extension v1 interface; optional untrusted Wasm modules use a separate bounded byte-buffer protocol. Both adapt to the existing Executor boundary and caller-owned routes. A plugin implements its operations; the host chooses files, interface versions, operation maps, tool metadata and permissions. The module is available in the no_std core. The default std feature forwards to zplugin/std for native path handling and plugin-side panic containment. Loading trusted native code remains an explicit unsafe host operation. Binding and normal calls then use zplugin's generated safe proxy. Load, bind and call This example loads a library whose echo operation returns its input. The filename is chosen by the host; zharness does not scan plugin directories. # #[cfg(feature = "std")] # fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> { use zharness::plugin::{ExtensionApi, Plugin, UnloadPolicy}; // SAFETY: the selected file and its dependencies are trusted native code // implementing zplugin ABI v1 and the Extension contract below. let library = unsafe { Plugin::load_path("./libnative_plugin.so", UnloadPolicy::Pinned)? }; let mut extension = ExtensionApi::create(&library)?; let mut output = [0; 256]; let bytes = extension.call_bytes("echo", b"hello", &mut output)?; assert_eq!(bytes, b"hello"); let text = extension.call_text("echo", b"hello", &mut output)?; assert_eq!(text, "hello"); # Ok(()) # } # #[cfg(not(feature = "std"))] # fn main() {} Plugin and UnloadPolicy are the actual zplugin types re-exported by zharness. load_path uses the platform's native path representation, including Unicode Windows paths. Use .so on Linux, .dylib on macOS and .dll on Windows. Without std, unsafe Plugin::load(&CStr) uses the platform loader and pins the image. Windows also provides the allocator-free UTF-16 load_wide entry point. ExtensionApi::create checks the interface ID, version and complete method signature before creating an instance. The returned ExtensionProxy borrows the library. Bind once and reuse it for steady calls; do not load a library or look up a symbol for every operation. The interface contract The v1 contract has ID dev.project-z.zharness.extension and one method: use zharness::plugin::Extension; struct Echo; impl Extension for Echo { fn call( &mut self, operation: &str, input: &[u8], output: &mut [u8], ) -> Result<u64, zplugin::Error> { if operation != "echo" { return Err(zplugin::Error::Unsupported); } if output.len() < input.len() { return Err(zplugin::Error::BufferTooSmall); } output[..input.len()].copy_from_slice(input); Ok(input.len() as u64) } } operation and input are borrowed for one call. output is writable only for that call. The success value is the number of output bytes initialized by the plugin. The operation namespace and byte encoding belong to the application; the crate adds no JSON envelope, tool-discovery protocol, permission convention or result-status bit packing. The zplugin macro generates ExtensionApi, ExtensionBinding, ExtensionProxy and ExtensionExport<T>. ExtensionApi::SPEC exposes the fixed interface specification. The interface version must change if its method name, order, receiver or boundary types change. Plugin package versions, application payload versions and this interface version are separate contracts. ExtensionProxy::call is the generated low-level typed call and returns u64. Use call_bytes to validate that the returned count fits usize and the output buffer, then borrow exactly those bytes. call_text additionally validates UTF-8. Neither helper allocates, copies the completed output or retries the plugin. Export a Rust plugin The plugin is a separate cdylib. Depend on zharness for the shared interface and on the same zplugin version for its export macro. Cargo unifies the zplugin dependency; this does not create a second runtime copy inside one crate graph. [lib] crate-type = ["cdylib"] [dependencies] zharness = "=0.4.0" zplugin = { version = "=0.3.0", default-features = false, features = ["std", "macros"] } The following complete export uses the pinned lifetime policy: # #[cfg(feature = "std")] # mod plugin_example { use zharness::plugin::{Extension, ExtensionExport}; struct Echo; impl Extension for Echo { fn call( &mut self, operation: &str, input: &[u8], output: &mut [u8], ) -> Result<u64, zplugin::Error> { if operation != "echo" { return Err(zplugin::Error::Unsupported); } if output.len() < input.len() { return Err(zplugin::Error::BufferTooSmall); } output[..input.len()].copy_from_slice(input); Ok(input.len() as u64) } } fn create() -> zplugin::Result<Echo> { Ok(Echo) } zplugin::export!(ExtensionExport<Echo>, constructor = create, version = (1, 0, 0), unload = pinned); # } # fn main() {} The repository's native_plugin example supplies echo and uppercase, and plugin_host loads it through the same public interface. The example's operation implementations are sample application logic, not behavior hidden in zharness. cargo build --locked --example native_plugin cargo run --locked --example plugin_host -- target/debug/examples/libnative_plugin.so On macOS use libnative_plugin.dylib; on Windows use native_plugin.dll. python scripts/examples.py locates Cargo's actual platform artifact and runs the host with that path, alongside the other standalone examples. Use the existing tool boundary ExtensionProxy implements Executor. A validated tool name becomes the operation name, and the existing JSON argument bytes become the input. A valid UTF-8 success result becomes ToolOutput::success. A nonzero native status stays an execution error; application-specific business failures and their is_error mapping remain the host's policy. # #[cfg(feature = "std")] # fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> { use zharness::{Invocation, Tool, ToolSet}; use zharness::hooks::{HookResult, NoHooks}; use zharness::plugin::{ExtensionApi, Plugin, UnloadPolicy}; use zharness::validation::ArgumentLimits; use zharness::zcall::v1::TokenStorage; // SAFETY: this is the host-approved plugin and implements the expected ABI. let library = unsafe { Plugin::load_path("./libnative_plugin.so", UnloadPolicy::Pinned)? }; let mut extension = ExtensionApi::create(&library)?; let tools = [Tool::new("echo", "Echo input", r#"{"type":"object"}"#)]; let registry = ToolSet::new(&tools)?; let invocation = Invocation { signature: None, call_id: "call-1", name: "echo", arguments: br#"{"message":"hello"}"#, }; let mut tokens = TokenStorage::<16>::new(); let prepared = invocation.prepare(&registry, &mut tokens, ArgumentLimits::default())?; let mut output = [0; 256]; let HookResult::Applied(completion) = prepared.execute_with_hooks( &mut extension, &mut output, &mut NoHooks, )? else { unreachable!("NoHooks always allows"); }; assert_eq!(completion.call_id, "call-1"); assert_eq!(completion.text, r#"{"message":"hello"}"#); # Ok(()) # } # #[cfg(not(feature = "std"))] # fn main() {} The host supplies ToolSet and hooks. Existing pause/deny decisions happen before the plugin's actual call; completion/error observers keep their current timing. Calling call_bytes directly intentionally bypasses that tool boundary, so the host must place any desired policy or lifecycle wrapper around the direct call. Nothing automatically registers plugin operations as model-visible tools. Load untrusted Wasm operations Enable the explicit wasm feature. It forwards to zplugin/wasm, implies an allocator and does not enable std. WasmExtension owns one sandbox and borrows a host-approved operation map. The map translates names used by Executor to the numeric operation codes defined by the plugin interface; application arguments remain the original bytes, with no additional serialization envelope. # #[cfg(feature = "wasm")] fn load(module: &[u8]) -> Result<zharness::plugin::wasm::WasmExtension<'static>, zharness::plugin::wasm::LoadError> { use zharness::plugin::wasm::{Interface, Limits, Operation, WasmExtension}; static OPERATIONS: [Operation<'static>; 2] = [ Operation::new("echo", 0), Operation::new("uppercase", 1), ]; WasmExtension::load( module, Interface { id: 0x7a6861726e657373, version: 1 }, &OPERATIONS, Limits::default(), ) } Names obey the same bounded ASCII rules as tool names. Duplicate names fail before module parsing; numeric aliases are permitted explicitly. Unknown names return UnknownTool without executing guest code. The map is an allowlist of callable entry points, not a grant of host capabilities or proof of module identity. Model-visible tool metadata still comes from the caller's Registry. call_bytes returns a checked prefix of caller storage. call_text and Executor also validate UTF-8. Engine errors leave host output unchanged; invalid UTF-8 is a host text-contract error after a successful byte copy, so discard that output. Business errors preserve their guest status and do not automatically poison the instance. Traps, fuel exhaustion and invalid success lengths invalidate it. zharness::Error remains Copy. Execution hooks receive Error::Wasm(Fault) with a bounded classification and status/length details. last_error() borrows the original zplugin diagnostic, including trap text; it is cleared before each call attempt and after successful replacement. Constructor LoadError preserves the full validation/interface error, separate from invalid host configuration. reload(module, limits) constructs a new instance with the same interface before replacing the active one. A failed load keeps the old instance and diagnostic; success resets guest state and drops the old sandbox without running guest destructors. For business-specific initialization or state migration, load and test a separate candidate first, then replace its Router slot. No retry, state migration, background task or unbounded old-generation list is created. The guest uses the core SDK re-exported by zharness, const state and fixed scratch buffers. It is independently compiled for wasm32-unknown-unknown, with panic=abort and no allocator. Its operations are examples, not built-in harness tools. The sandbox host bounds file reads before loading. Run it and the mixed-backend host with: rustup target add wasm32-unknown-unknown python3 scripts/wasm.py Compose, disable and replace plugin executors Route::new(public_name, slot_index, backend_operation) and Slot::new(executor) describe caller-owned routing. Router::new(&routes, &mut slots) validates all names, duplicate public names and target indices before construction. The Router borrows existing native proxies, Wasm instances or application executors, so their resources outlive routed calls. It does not load files or infer trust from suffixes. set_enabled(index, false) makes all routes to that slot return Denied without touching output or invoking the plugin. replace(index, candidate) returns the old executor borrow and preserves the slot's enabled state. Invalid indices do not change an existing slot. Configure aliases by adding routes to the same slot; there is no catch-all route, automatic fallback or retry after failure. Execution hooks observe and authorize the public tool name before mapping, while the target receives its backend operation name. Original arguments, call IDs, business-result flags and errors retain the existing Executor contract. A direct Router::execute call is an application-level call and bypasses Prepared hooks. The mixed host exercises both plugin backends, explicit disabling and request-boundary routing. Wasm trust and resource policy The sandbox accepts zplugin's core Wasm32 v1 protocol and rejects all imports, start sections, shared/memory64/multiple memories and incompatible interfaces. No WASI, filesystem, network, environment, clock, process or host callback API is linked. Default limits are 4 MiB module bytes, 16 MiB guest linear memory, 4,096 table elements, 1 MiB input/output capacities, 10 million fuel per call, 64 KiB interpreter value stack and 128 call depth. Hosts can choose tighter limits. Limits cover guest resources, not total process RSS or compilation wall time. The engine, parser, allocator and application remain trusted components. Add OS process/container limits for stronger multi-tenant isolation. Bound file reads, compilation rate and resident instance counts. Instances retain prior inputs; use separate instances for distinct tenants or confidential sessions. Dropping an instance releases allocations without secure-erasure guarantees. Wasm calls are synchronous. zplugin's native async tasks, callbacks and owned resources remain available through the re-exported native APIs, but do not cross this sandbox protocol. Arbitrary WASI programs, JavaScript-importing wasm-bindgen modules and Component Model binaries are not accepted. Both native proxies and Wasm adapters use exclusive calls and remain !Send + !Sync. Errors, ownership and unloading Boundary Result Native file loading or interface binding fails Original zplugin::Error Native call fails zharness::Error::Plugin(original_error) Returned count overflows usize or exceeds output capacity zharness::Error::InvalidOutput call_text or executor receives invalid UTF-8 zharness::Error::InvalidOutput Existing execution hook pauses or denies Plugin is not called Invalid Wasm operation map plugin::wasm::LoadError::Configuration Wasm loading/compatibility failure Original error in LoadError::Sandbox Wasm call fails Copy Error::Wasm(Fault) plus original last_error() Unknown route or disabled slot UnknownTool or Denied, with no backend call An error can follow partial output writes or external side effects. Discard the output for that failed call and decide recovery in the application. Increasing capacity and blindly replaying an operation can repeat its effects; the adapter never retries automatically. Library, instance and proxy lifetimes remain zplugin-owned. Proxies are neither Send nor Sync; calls require mutable access. The borrow prevents dropping a library while its proxy remains usable: use zharness::plugin::{ExtensionApi, Plugin}; fn invalid_order(library: Plugin) { let mut extension = ExtensionApi::create(&library).unwrap(); drop(library); let mut output = [0; 16]; extension.call_bytes("echo", b"hello", &mut output).unwrap(); } Pinned loading keeps the native image resident until process exit. Cooperative unloading requires a plugin that explicitly implements zplugin's UnloadSafe contract and a host that chooses UnloadPolicy::Cooperative. Drop all proxies first, then call Plugin::try_close. A busy result returns ownership of the library so the host can retain it and retry closing later. zharness adds no forced unload, timer, reload watcher or migration policy. Native code runs with the host's privileges. Metadata and length checks do not sandbox a malicious library. Under zplugin std with an unwind-enabled plugin, generated adapters contain Rust panics and poison the instance; panic=abort, native faults and foreign exceptions retain their process-level behavior. Dependencies and performance scope The direct runtime dependencies are the pinned Project Z crates zcall and zplugin; zcall pins zconv 0.3.0. zplugin's official interface macro adds zplugin-macros, syn, quote, proc-macro2 and unicode-ident to the compilation dependency graph. These macro dependencies are not additional runtime libraries. The handwritten zharness crate keeps #![forbid(unsafe_code)]; the generated FFI and zplugin's loader contain their own unsafe implementation, and the host explicitly accepts native loading. With wasm, the runtime graph additionally contains Wasmi 2.0.0, wasmi_core, wasmi_ir, wasmi_collections, wasmparser 0.228.0, spin 0.9.9, libm 0.2.16 and bitflags 2.13.2. Default/native and optional Wasm graphs are audited separately. The lockfile uses the latest compatible versions: newer incompatible syn, wasmparser and spin release lines are not forced through upstream requirements. The native call path uses a cached function table and caller storage. Host-side output checking and UTF-8 validation do not allocate. Plugin initialization, a plugin's own operation implementation and the platform loader may allocate independently. cargo bench --locked --bench plugins ZHARNESS_BENCH_SMOKE=1 cargo bench --locked --bench plugins The benchmark builds and loads an actual native plugin before timing. For 64 B, 1 KiB and 4 KiB payloads it measures the generated call, checked byte view, prepared executor and executor with two hooks. Fixture construction, library loading, interface creation, JSON argument preparation and buffers are outside timing; the plugin's echo operation and output copy remain inside it. Each measured case asserts zero host alloc, alloc_zeroed and realloc calls. A separately linked dynamic library has its own allocator; this counter does not measure arbitrary plugin allocations. proxy_state_bytes is the Rust proxy value's size, excluding its plugin object, library image, loader state and caller buffer. Percentiles include per-operation clock overhead, while mean_ns is a batch average. The benchmark does not measure loading latency, process RSS or model inference, and does not promise a fixed latency on every platform. The separate Wasm adapter report compares the same guest through direct zplugin, named byte calls, checked text calls, Executor and Router. It measures load/drop separately and records allocator requests, not RSS. Every warmed batch asserts zero allocations. Its percentiles describe batch averages, unlike the native benchmark's instrumented individual calls, so the two reports must not be divided into a cross-backend speed ratio. References zplugin 0.3.0 public API zplugin ABI and ownership contract zplugin Wasm protocol and limits Runnable native plugin example Runnable host example

title: Context management
body: 复用上下文、工具循环、hook 与协作执行原语。 Context management A Context stores caller-owned Group descriptors. Each group borrows a slice of Message values, and each message borrows zcall Content blocks or a retained Completion. This preserves rich zcall content instead of converting everything to strings. Message::ToolResult uses zcall's checked append_tool_result API. Budget and retention Budget::available is limit minus reserved, checked for underflow. Reserve space for model output, tool schemas and non-history prompt overhead. Group.tokens must come from the application's tokenizer or a clearly labelled estimate. Costs can change with the target model or serialization; recompute/rebuild the context when changing that accounting contract. No hard token-fit promise is made for incorrect caller counts. push rejects duplicate group IDs, empty message groups, insufficient capacity or insufficient token budget. Overflow::Reject preserves all prior groups. Overflow::EvictOldest removes the oldest unpinned groups until both storage and budget permit insertion. It never removes part of a group. All checks occur before mutation; failure leaves ordering, descriptors and accounting unchanged. Pinned groups survive eviction and cannot be replaced by compact. Pinning is a retention rule, not authorization: an application can still create a new Context with different instructions. Never combine independent security principals in one context merely because their content fits the same buffer. Tool history and compaction Put an assistant message containing all parallel tool calls and every matching tool result in one group. The library does not automatically infer conversation boundaries or repair unrelated groups. Context::build delegates call/result ID checks to zcall. Unknown and duplicate tool results fail rather than receiving invented IDs. A build error exposes no partially constructed Request. compact(range, summary) replaces a nonempty range of complete, unpinned groups with one caller-supplied Group. The summary must fit the same budget and must not reuse an ID outside the replaced range. The library does not call a model or assert that the supplied summary preserves every original fact. The caller chooses role, content and cost, then can gate the change with a hook. Fork and lifetime fork_into copies descriptors into another supplied buffer. Later eviction or compaction on either branch does not alter the other's descriptors. Borrowed message data remains shared and immutable; this is not a deep payload clone. Keep every borrowed string/content/result alive while a Context or built Request uses it. Reuse output buffers only after those borrows end. push_with_hooks and compact_with_hooks emit Before::Context, then After::ContextChanged only after an accepted mutation. Pause and Deny preserve context state. Unhooked methods are explicit opt-outs, not hidden policy checks. Run cargo run --locked --example context_window. Accounting, failure atomicity, pinned groups, fork isolation and tool-result construction are tested in tests/context.rs; seeded randomized operations are in tests/recovery.rs.

title: Native security guardrails
body: 复用上下文、工具循环、hook 与协作执行原语。 Native security guardrails zharness directly depends on zguard and exposes it as zharness::zguard. The guard module connects deterministic host policy to actual tool and command execution. Each accepted call passes policy, approval, quota and audit checks before the adapter receives it. Execution boundary Use Prepared::execute_guarded or Command::execute_guarded with an Authorization containing a persistent session guard, an audit sink and the current host clock value. The _with_hooks variants preserve existing hooks. A hook can reject or pause first; the guard then checks immediately before the underlying adapter runs. flowchart TD P["Prepared tool or command"] --> H["Host hooks"] H --> G["zguard policy and approval"] G --> A["Audit sink"] A -->|Recorded and allowed| E["Invoke adapter once"] A -->|Recorded denial or pending approval| R["Return structured rejection"] A -->|Failed| R Only Decision::Allow reaches the adapter. Deny and RequireApproval return Error::Guard(Verdict) for tools or CommandError::Guard(Verdict) for commands. The bounded verdict contains a decision, a reason and an optional rule ID; it does not contain arguments or outputs. Hooks observe guard rejections through the existing execution-error callback. Output buffers remain untouched when the guard rejects. The call is checked and executed with the same data. For a prepared tool, the request uses its actual call ID, name and Arguments::as_bytes(). These are the validated JSON object bytes delivered to the executor; the JSON parser removes whitespace surrounding the object. Commands retain the exact call ID, program, argv element boundaries and optional working directory. No concatenation or hash approximates the approved command. Host-owned policy and approvals Create rules from trusted application configuration. Rules match exact names within either the Tool or Command namespace. Empty policies and unmatched calls are denied. Explicit denial wins over approval requirements and allow rules. Capabilities come from the host context; argument fields such as approved: true, tool descriptions, skill instructions and MCP annotations do not alter that context. A trusted host issues an approval with Guard::approve after reviewing an exact request. The approval borrows that request, the complete immutable policy and the session context. It is neither Copy nor Clone and is consumed by one authorization attempt. A changed call ID, argument byte, argv boundary, cwd, policy or session fails the binding check. Expired approvals and clock regressions fail closed. The host supplies monotonic clock values in one consistent unit and a fresh session epoch when recreating the guard. Authorization and the two executor wrappers are single-attempt values. A wrapper consumes its authorization on entry, including an invalid command. Calling it again returns InvalidState without rechecking, spending another budget unit or reusing an old clock value. Construct a new authorization for another attempt while retaining the same Guard. Hook pauses consume the supplied authorization value without reserving an execution quota; the host decides whether its external approval evidence still applies when it prepares a retry. Integration choices The native methods provide the shortest path for a prepared call: let result = prepared.execute_guarded( &mut executor, &mut output, Authorization::new(&mut guard, &mut audit, now), )?; The complete, compiled guarded_execution example uses an in-memory adapter. It demonstrates a model-supplied approval field being rejected, an explicit host-issued approval and a single accepted execution: cargo run --locked --example guarded_execution GuardedExecutor and GuardedCommandExecutor also implement the existing executor traits. Use them when an existing caller already dispatches through those traits. A direct GuardedExecutor user supplies the actual call ID. Choose the native method or an explicit wrapper for one boundary; the native method already wraps its adapter. Explicitly nesting different guards evaluates each host policy separately. A plugin Router implements Executor, so passing the router to Prepared::execute_guarded checks the public tool name before resolving a backend operation. The same path applies to native proxies, Wasm extensions and a host-supplied MCP Executor. zharness supplies no MCP transport. Native plugin loading and direct call_bytes/call_text remain trusted host operations. Existing Prepared::execute, execute_with_hooks and raw adapter methods retain their explicit host-authorization contract; select the guarded boundary to enforce zguard policy. Quotas, audit and adapter failures A persistent Guard caps authorized attempts and each request's input bytes. Quota reservation precedes the adapter, so an adapter error, nonzero command exit or invalid result never refunds the attempt or replays the approval. Retry decisions, external idempotency and recovery remain application-owned. The audit sink receives only numeric session/policy/sequence identifiers, action kind, payload byte count and the verdict. Names, call IDs, raw arguments and outputs are absent. A sink error prevents invocation. Durability, access control and log retention belong to that sink. NoAudit is an explicit opt-out chosen by the host; the library writes no files or telemetry. The guard controls entry to an adapter. An allowed shell or program can exercise its complete privileges unless the host also applies argument/resource policy and operating-system isolation. Native-library initializers run during loading, before guarded operation dispatch. Use the existing Wasm backend or an OS sandbox for untrusted code. Verification tests/guard.rs exercises real preparation, wrappers and plugin routing with side-effect counters and untouched-buffer assertions. It covers: Contract Evidence Rejections precede adapter calls Empty policy, approval requirement, expiry and audit-failure cases Approval follows the actual request Real call ID, exact executed JSON, program, argv boundaries and cwd changes Model data grants no permission Forged approved/capabilities fields Quotas survive adapter failure Failed executor followed by an exhausted-budget rejection Native methods check once One accepted call, one audit event and one reserved call Single-attempt values cannot replay Tool wrapper reuse and invalid command followed by wrapper reuse Plugin policy uses the public identity Real Router dispatch test Existing result behavior is preserved Business tool error and nonzero command exit tests Run the focused integration checks and dependency audit: cargo test --locked --test guard cargo check --locked --no-default-features --target wasm32-unknown-unknown python3 scripts/audit.py The dependency audit includes zguard in the Project Z runtime closure. zguard adds no Cargo dependencies, allocator or operating-system runtime. The verification above covers policy enforcement in these explicit library entry points; each consuming application's actual dispatch path needs its own acceptance check.

title: Model/tool loop primitives
body: 复用上下文、工具循环、hook 与协作执行原语。 Model/tool loop primitives ToolLoop is an application-driven state machine. Calling next issues one action; it does not call a model, run a tool, sleep or create a task. Drive it from a sync loop, a future, an event loop or a distributed coordinator chosen by the caller. Ready -> CallModel -> Receiving | real zcall events +-- terminal Completed -> Stopped +-- terminal failure -> Stopped +-- terminal WaitingTools -> Tools | Execute tickets (possibly several concurrently) | retained results + commit_result for each ticket | next -> CallModel, or Stopped at the round limit Observation and dispatch Create a distinct application run ID and caller-owned CallSlot array. N is bytes per retained call: the real call ID, name and complete argument object share that storage. LoopLimits bounds model rounds and total tool calls. The controller retains genuine zcall EventData::ToolReady; it never fabricates a provider event or executes partial argument deltas. Pass events from Session::step to observe. Return Control::Continue only after observe succeeds. An event that cannot fit accepts no partial invocation. For recoverable slot-count exhaustion, return Pause, replace_slots with larger caller storage and resume the same Session with only its unconsumed input suffix. The recovery integration test exercises this actual replay path. Per-call byte size N is a fixed configuration; a limit/policy failure should abort or cancel unless the application has a safe recovery strategy. ToolReady alone does not authorize execution. The controller waits for zcall's WaitingTools terminal outcome. next then issues Execute tickets after the Before::Tool hook allows them. Issue several tickets to run concurrently, or finish one before asking for another. Prepared arguments and authorization remain mandatory at the application's execution boundary. Completion and persistence An invocation returned by invocation(ticket) borrows controller storage. Copy it into application transcript storage when it must outlive the next mutable controller operation. The example keeps history InvocationStorage buffers and result arrays separate from per-turn CallSlot storage. Retain the tool result, accept it into application history, acknowledge it through Completion::submit to the zcall Session, and call ToolLoop::commit_result. These are explicit boundaries, not an atomic transaction across memory, external I/O and persistent storage. commit_result checks the original call ID and rejects stale or duplicate completion tickets. It does not perform the history/session operations implicitly. Failures use a retained Completion with is_error=true. Once all results are committed, next can issue the following CallModel action. It clears per-turn retention only after the before-model hook allows that action. Durable history must already exist elsewhere. Context::build constructs the next Request from that history via zcall, without loss of real tool-call IDs. Pause, stop and cancellation Pending means model input or dispatched work is still outstanding. Paused means a before hook deferred a proposal without dispatching it. Deny is Error::Denied and leaves the proposal uncommitted; the application chooses whether to cancel, revise policy or produce an explicit error result. No implicit retry occurs. cancel marks the controller stopped and rejects late commits. It cannot stop an already-running process, revoke a network request or undo a side effect. Model failure, explicit cancellation and round-limit exhaustion are distinct stop reasons. Use fresh run IDs after recreation; tickets are not authentication tokens. examples/tool_loop.rs composes Context, Hooks, a real zcall Session and the tool executor for two recorded model rounds. tests/turn.rs, tests/recovery.rs and tests/native_example.rs execute normal, denied, incomplete, cancelled, replay and out-of-order paths without live provider credentials.

title: Hook systems and boundaries
