body: 复用上下文、工具循环、hook 与协作执行原语。 Hook systems and boundaries zharness has two complementary interfaces. Existing Hooks callbacks remain source-compatible and directly cover native tool-loop scheduling, context changes, agent assignments, actual tool/command execution and output processing. Since 0.2.3, the lifecycle module supplies typed, independent channels for wider conversation, configuration, transport, reply and application-storage boundaries. No global callback registry or runtime is added by either interface. Existing native callbacks (unchanged) Boundary Gate Completion Attempt failure Model/tool scheduling and context/agent state before(Before) after(After) Returned error Actual validated Executor before_execute after_execute execute_error Command adapter before_command after_command command_error Result reduction before_result after_result Returned transform error; no after_result Before::Tool issues a ticket; it is not actual execution. After::ToolFinished is loop-result commitment; it is not just an Executor return. Paused/denied execution never invokes the adapter or modifies output. Business-error tool results and nonzero command exits remain completed unsuccessful results, distinct from an adapter error. Output reduction remains an explicit step before history commitment. Existing tuple/reference forwarding and default callback methods are unchanged. Grouped lifecycle channels (new source API) Use Gate<E>, Observer<E> and Interceptor<E> independently for typed event E. The ten families are conversation, model, prompt, request, response, tool, context, agent, persistence and runtime. They cover 97 action labels without expanding the legacy Hooks trait. Gate controls proposals; Observer records facts; Interceptor edits a copied candidate before validation/gating. See LIFECYCLE.md for every action, exact native entry points, compiled examples and manual-integration boundaries. Lifecycle::run surrounds a real caller operation. begin/finish lets an app schedule/await work itself and later finish the correlated receipt. notify is only for already-observed facts. None of these methods creates a UI, model call, checkpoint store, rate limiter or remote worker by declaring an event name. Native entry points include Conversation message acceptance/edit/delete/start/ close, ModelSettings model/reasoning/route/options changes, a complete-message Sender wrapper, Context request/budget/fork/compaction wrappers and ResponseStream for real zcall events. Final assistant acceptance is distinct from a model turn's WaitingTools terminal outcome. Legacy and grouped channels are not automatically duplicated; applications choose which explicit boundaries to compose. Shared operational rules Gates short-circuit left-to-right with Allow, Pause or Deny. Before callbacks can repeat and must not perform the proposed action. Observers cannot veto already committed effects or turn a failure into success. Processing errors do not grant permission to replay side-effecting tools. Panics/crashes are outside normal-return observation guarantees, and external I/O may have partial effects before an error. Use separate state/buffers for concurrent operations or caller synchronization. Give each Lifecycle coordinator a unique epoch and keep event borrows alive while its receipts are outstanding. New observers default to payload metadata only; Visibility::Content opts in to content access. This does not change the original raw-data contract of legacy command/tool Hooks. Never log secrets indiscriminately. Direct unhooked Context/Prepared operations, external OS calls and arbitrary UI changes remain explicit opt-outs. Hooks are policy boundaries, not authentication, process isolation or universal interception. Adapters own their actual network, OS, storage, cancellation and environment guarantees.

title: Typed Harness Lifecycle API
body: 复用上下文、工具循环、hook 与协作执行原语。 Typed Harness Lifecycle API Version 0.2.3 publishes the typed lifecycle APIs that were developed after v0.2.2. Use the published zharness 0.2.3 crate or its matching source tag. No integration with an MCP repository is needed; no runtime, database or transport dependency has been added. Three independent primitives Gate<E> decides whether a typed proposal is allowed, paused or denied. Observer<E> records started, completed, failed, deferred or externally observed facts. Interceptor<E> edits a copied candidate before validation and gating. The callback interfaces are generic over a small domain event, not a giant trait with a method per every conceivable lifecycle location. A Lifecycle<G, O> owns callback state and monotonically numbered proposals. There is no global registry, hidden thread, lock or heap-backed event bus. Tuples compose gates/interceptors/observers in order. Gates stop at the first non-Allow; interceptors stop on error; all normal-return observers run in order. NoGate, NoObserver and NoInterceptor opt out explicitly. The old Hooks trait and its methods/Before/After variants remain unchanged and continue to work independently. Coverage: ten typed families Each action has the same before/started/finished-or-failed contract when used with run or begin/finish. These are 97 action labels, not 97 automatically installed callbacks. notify reports a fact that has already happened; it cannot veto it. Family Actions conversation Start, Close, AcceptUser, AppendMessage, EditMessage, DeleteMessage, Fork, Restore model Select, Switch, ReasoningChange, OptionsChange, RouteSelect, Fallback, Unavailable prompt Build, SystemInstructions, InjectContext, ToolDefinitions, Compact, BudgetExceeded request Build, Encode, Send, Retry, Receive, Headers, Timeout, Cancel response TurnStart, IdentityUpdated, BlockStart, TextDelta, ReasoningDelta, ToolArgumentsDelta, RefusalDelta, Signature, BlockEnd, ToolReady, Usage, ChoiceEnd, Snapshot, BlockIncomplete, Loss, TurnEnd, FinalizeAssistant, CommitMessage, Cancel tool Register, Unregister, ParseArguments, Validate, Authorize, Dispatch, Execute, TransformResult, CommitResult, Cancel context Load, Save, Append, Merge, Fork, Evict, Compact, BudgetChange, BudgetWarning, BudgetExceeded agent Start, Stop, Assign, Handoff, Join, Complete, Fail, Timeout, Recover, LeaseExpire, SendMessage, ReceiveMessage persistence SaveConversation, LoadConversation, RestoreHistory, Checkpoint, Snapshot, DeleteSnapshot runtime BudgetConsume, BudgetExceeded, RateLimit, RateLimitExceeded, Retry, Cancel, Timeout, Error, Interrupt, Resume, Shutdown The enum variants are non-exhaustive to allow later action additions. Amount and revision fields are caller metadata, with units defined for each application operation. Correlation records conversation/run/request/message/agent IDs and the application retry attempt separately from the library proposal serial. Native integration versus explicit wrapping Native wrappers already connect the important boundaries to real operations: Entry point What it actually gates/observes Conversation::start/close The supplied create/close operation and local state transition Conversation::user_message, append_message, edit_message, delete_message Actual supplied history/storage operation; revision advances only on success Conversation::user_message_intercepted Final filtered payload acceptance; identity/action/revision cannot be rewritten by the filter ModelSettings::select/switch_model/set_reasoning/set_route/set_options/configure Committed local configuration, with actual previous and proposed values Context::build_with_lifecycle Real zcall request building, including returned capacity/ID errors Context::set_budget_with_lifecycle, fork_with_lifecycle, compact_with_lifecycle Native checked context operations request::send_with_hooks One actual Sender invocation, with complete-message length verification ResponseStream::accept/finalize/cancel Acceptance of genuine zcall events, final assistant commit and logical cancellation Prompt assembly, retry policy, checkpoint databases, remote workers, limits and other application-owned boundaries use Lifecycle::run around the actual operation. Declaring an action or calling notify alone does not implement those systems. Existing tool/command/output hooks remain native to their established entry points; they are not silently duplicated into the new channels. Model and reasoning settings use zharness::hooks::HookResult; use zharness::lifecycle::{Correlation, Fault, Lifecycle, NoGate, NoObserver}; use zharness::lifecycle::domains::model::{Configuration, Reasoning}; use zharness::settings::ModelSettings; let mut hooks = Lifecycle::new(100, NoGate, NoObserver); let HookResult::Applied(mut settings) = ModelSettings::select( Correlation::default(), Configuration::new("model-a"), &mut hooks, )? else { unreachable!("NoGate does not pause"); }; let _ = settings.switch_model("model-b", &mut hooks)?; let _ = settings.set_reasoning(Reasoning::Level("high"), &mut hooks)?; assert_eq!(settings.current().model, "model-b"); assert_eq!(settings.revision(), 2); # Ok::<(), Fault>(()) A real model Gate validates allowed models, provider capabilities and budget. Reasoning::Level preserves application intent without inventing a universal provider vocabulary. Settings do not modify an already-built Request or an in-flight Session. The application snapshots current settings and maps them through zcall's supported options for its next request. Recompute model-specific context costs after a model change; changing a label cannot guarantee compatibility. Bracket a real operation use zharness::hooks::HookResult; use zharness::lifecycle::{Correlation, Fault, Lifecycle, NoGate, NoObserver}; use zharness::lifecycle::domains::persistence; let mut hooks = Lifecycle::new(101, NoGate, NoObserver); let mut stored = false; let result = hooks.run( Correlation::default(), persistence::Event::new(persistence::Action::Checkpoint), |_| { stored = true; Ok(()) }, )?; assert_eq!(result, HookResult::Applied(())); assert!(stored); # Ok::<(), Fault>(()) Replace the example's memory mutation with the real storage call. The closure runs at most once per run invocation, only after an allowed valid proposal. Errors are observed and returned without replacement or automatic retry. A failed operation may already have changed external state; the hook layer is not a transaction manager. It never claims that a request was saved merely because an application sent a SaveConversation event. Async boundaries and completion pairing use zharness::hooks::HookResult; use zharness::lifecycle::{Correlation, Fault, Lifecycle, NoGate, NoObserver, Outcome}; use zharness::lifecycle::domains::request; let mut hooks = Lifecycle::new(102, NoGate, NoObserver); let HookResult::Applied(mut pending) = hooks.begin( Correlation::default(), request::Event::new(request::Action::Send), )? else { unreachable!(); }; // The application performs/awaits its actual operation outside the hook layer. // This example reports abandonment without pretending a network send happened. hooks.finish(&mut pending, Outcome::Abandoned)?; assert!(pending.is_finished()); assert!(hooks.finish(&mut pending, Outcome::Succeeded).is_err()); # Ok::<(), Fault>(()) Span is private-field, non-Clone and must-use. Several receipts can be outstanding and finish out of order. Duplicate completion and different-epoch dispatch are rejected without emitting another terminal notice. A rejected finish preserves the receipt so routing can be corrected. Dropping a pending receipt does not cancel external work or manufacture an observation: explicitly finish, fail, cancel, defer or abandon it. Give every Lifecycle coordinator instance a distinct epoch, including after restart/recreation. Reusing the same epoch across instances defeats cross-instance receipt detection. Epochs/IDs are application correlation, not security tokens. There is no global allocator of identities. Keep borrowed event data alive until finish, and serialize access to each coordinator. Panics/crashes are not caught; normal-return pairing is not an exactly-once external execution guarantee. Sending, streaming and final replies are different boundaries Sender acceptance means exactly what the supplied adapter documents: for example, queued locally or fully written. A send completion does not prove provider receipt, model generation, response delivery or persistence. A partial-length receipt is an InvalidOutput failure, even though bytes may already have left the process. The wrapper never retries on its own; the application owns idempotency/recovery. ResponseStream maps only public zcall EventData, not provider-specific JSON. TurnStart means a real normalized response start. first_visible identifies the first accepted nonempty text/refusal delta, separately from reasoning or tool arguments. ReasoningDelta exposes only what the provider returned; it does not reveal hidden internal reasoning. The application consumer still receives the original EventData, preserving metadata not repeated in the hook view. TurnEnd retains the exact TurnOutcome. Successfully accepting a failed terminal event means the observation was consumed, not that the model call succeeded. WaitingTools is not finalization. finalize runs a separate caller operation only after TurnOutcome::Completed; it prevents duplicate finalization and rejects waiting-tools, failed, incomplete or cancelled turns. It does not infer that the whole agent task is done or persist/render text without a caller operation. A gate Pause does not invoke the stream consumer. A consumer Pause produces a Deferred observation and leaves accepted counters/state unchanged. The same event must be replayed through zcall with only the unconsumed byte suffix. The consumer must not commit side effects then return Pause. Errors, including Deny, return to the driver; it must explicitly stop/cancel or safely resume the Session. Logical ResponseStream cancellation does not stop network reads by itself. Privacy and interception Payload Debug prints only byte counts and whether content was supplied. New observers receive redacted payloads by default: body pointers are removed, not merely hidden in formatting. Visibility::Content explicitly permits access to supplied content. Gates can inspect supplied content when making policy decisions. Model names, routing labels, numeric amounts and IDs remain metadata; do not put secrets in those fields. Custom Event implementations must correctly implement redacted. Legacy Hooks keep their original raw-data contracts; this default does not retroactively change command/tool callbacks. Interceptors edit copied candidates; original immutable data is unchanged. The final candidate is validated and gated before it reaches the operation. Failure never falls back to raw input. Native user-message/configuration filters can change only content/proposed settings, not correlation, prior settings or revision. Generic custom event transforms are trusted application code and must preserve their declared semantics. Text reduction still uses the separate caller-buffered ToolResultTransform primitives where appropriate. Reproduction cargo run --locked --example conversation_hooks executes a complete local flow: message approval and history acceptance, settings changes, actual zcall request construction/encoding, memory-send acceptance, a captured model response parsed by zcall, assistant finalization and a memory persistence operation. It makes no live provider request and requires no credentials. Model-reasoning intent is changed and reset explicitly rather than falsely claiming provider mapping. The lifecycle, lifecycle_adapters, lifecycle_policy and lifecycle_replay tests cover domains, pairing, ordering, privacy, final-candidate checks, send failures, state mutation, real stream replay and finalization boundaries. Every legacy test remains in CI. cargo bench --locked --bench lifecycle measures 13 local cases, including no-hook/paired-hook dispatch, split finish, settings changes, message acceptance, memory sending and normalized-event handling. It does not measure network/model/database latency, tokenizer accuracy or prove zero runtime cost.

title: Tool output processing
body:
复用上下文、工具循环、hook 与协作执行原语。 Tool output processing A tool result can be reduced before it enters model history. Completion::transform and transform_with_hooks accept a ToolResultTransform, immutable tool metadata and caller-owned output. They preserve the real call ID and original is_error flag. They never run the tool, append history, acknowledge a Session or complete a ToolLoop ticket on the application's behalf. validated/authorized tool execution -> retain original Completion -> Hooks::before_result (allow / pause / deny) -> ToolResultTransform (one stage or a caller-buffered Chain) -> validate output length and UTF-8 -> Hooks::after_result (observe the validated text) -> retain reduced history -> submit to zcall -> ToolLoop::commit_result Minimal use use zharness::{bridge::Completion, hooks::{HookResult, NoHooks}}; use zharness::output::{Chain, DedupAdjacentLines, Truncate}; let original = Completion { call_id: "real-call-id", text: "error: missing config
error: missing config
", is_error: true, }; let mut scratch = [0; 1024]; let mut output = [0; 256]; let mut pipeline = Chain::new( DedupAdjacentLines, Truncate::new(256, "
...[truncated]")?, &mut scratch, ); let HookResult::Applied(reduced) = original.transform_with_hooks( "build", &mut pipeline, &mut output, &mut NoHooks, )? else { unreachable!("NoHooks never pauses"); }; assert_eq!(reduced.text, "error: missing config
"); assert_eq!(reduced.call_id, original.call_id); assert!(reduced.is_error); # Ok::<(), zharness::Error>(()) Run cargo run --locked --example tool_output for a complete executor, custom DEBUG-line filter, result hooks, error-preserving context construction and JSON minification. tests/output_flow.rs also drives genuine interleaved zcall events, transforms two results, submits them out of order and advances the model turn. Processing primitives Identity returns Transform::Unchanged: no copy and no output capacity needed. Trim removes leading/trailing Unicode whitespace. DedupAdjacentLines removes only adjacent byte-identical lines, including identical line endings. These are opt-in text policies: repeated messages or surrounding whitespace can be meaningful. Truncate::new(max_bytes, marker) limits plain text by UTF-8 bytes, including a required nonempty truncation marker. It never splits a UTF-8 code point. It can still cut grapheme clusters or important facts. This is not a token budget and must not be used to produce a shortened-but-still-structured JSON document. JsonMinify::new(&mut tokens, limits) first validates complete JSON with zcall's public parser and caller-provided TokenStorage. It removes only insignificant JSON whitespace outside strings. String escapes, numeric spelling and key/array order remain unchanged. Malformed or resource-exceeding input fails; no unchecked fast path bypasses validation. Minification does not enforce a JSON Schema or remove fields. A schema-aware projector should be a custom transform that re-encodes valid JSON and checks the projected contract. Chain::new(first, second, scratch) validates intermediate output, runs stages in order and stops on the first failure. Nest chains for more stages. An unchanged second stage cannot return a borrow into temporary scratch: the chain copies that intermediate text into the final caller output. If every stage is unchanged, the original text is reused without copying. Stages may expand output; allocate scratch for the largest intermediate, not just the expected final summary. Hooks and custom transforms Implement ToolResultTransform::transform(meta, input, output) and return either Unchanged or Written(n). The library validates n and UTF-8 before creating a Completion or passing the text to the next stage. Metadata is read-only input; there is no return field that can silently substitute a call ID or change failure to success. Custom transforms remain trusted application code, not a sandbox. Hooks::before_result sees tool name, call ID, error status and original text. Pause returns HookResult::Paused without calling a transform or touching its output. Deny returns Error::Denied. after_result observes successful output and original byte length; it cannot veto. Tuple hooks short-circuit before and observe after in left-to-right order. Existing lifecycle enums are unchanged and new trait methods have defaults, preserving existing hook implementations. Result hooks do not replace Before::Tool or After::ToolFinished. The latter still means the tool-loop result was committed. A result observer can run again if the application explicitly repeats a successful transformation; do not count it as an exactly-once side effect or a history commit. Failure, async work and parallel execution Keep raw output until processing succeeds. On capacity/validation failure, discard partial target/scratch bytes and retry only the transform, with retained input and larger storage or a corrected policy. No automatic fallback exposes raw output when a redaction/filtering stage fails. Before/transform callbacks must not re-execute the original tool. A successful pipeline is not an atomic transaction with history persistence or external effects; the application commits each layer. For model-generated summaries or remote approval, pause and let the application schedule that work. Retain the original result and any required call data. When ready, supply an application transform using the saved summary, or construct an explicit replacement Completion with the same identity/status. There is no hidden model call, async runtime, network transport or allocation in these primitives. Concurrent tools use separate raw/output/scratch buffers and per-task callback state, or caller-managed synchronization. Return reduced results to one serialized coordinator for history, Session and ToolLoop commitment. Scoped-thread tests verify independent buffers and metadata; the library does not spawn those threads. Semantics and accounting Lossy reductions must preserve the facts needed for the next decision. Preserve error causes, warnings, IDs, required schema fields and source references under your tool-specific policy. Mark truncation/summarization; retain raw output or an application-owned retrieval reference when auditability requires it. Raw output must not be elevated into trusted instructions by a summarizer. Recompute the model-specific token cost after reduction before inserting the message Group. Bytes saved are not necessarily tokens saved. Result reduction and Context::compact_with_hooks solve different problems: the former transforms one completed tool output; the latter replaces caller-selected whole history groups with a supplied summary. Neither API silently summarizes or repairs a broken tool-call/result relationship.

title: Performance methodology
body: 复用上下文、工具循环、hook 与协作执行原语。 Performance methodology Run cargo bench --locked --benches on an otherwise idle machine. Record git revision, rustc -Vv, CPU, operating system and power policy. Native harness evidence retains source, environment, test logs and six raw benchmark CSV files. CI uses ZHARNESS_BENCH_SMOKE=1 for correctness checks only; the full evidence step unsets it. Fixture construction, sample vectors and printing are outside timing. Benchmark- only System allocator wrappers count alloc, alloc_zeroed and realloc and assert zero calls during measurement. Their unsafe forwarding is not linked into the unsafe-forbidden library. Arbitrary user hooks, payloads and adapters may allocate independently. Real OS process and transport costs are not disguised as core costs. mean_ns is a batch-amortized mean. p50/p95/p99 time individual operations including Instant overhead; they are not quantiles of batch means. Clock overhead is not subtracted. Workspace columns report configured state/buffers, not process RSS, borrowed payloads or all stack frames. No-hook controls still have explicit state validation/counter work; no universal zero-overhead claim is made. Existing suites The 43 dispatch cases cover linear/indexed registries, validated echo execution, context sliding/forks, task claim/complete/requeue, mailboxes, hooks and loop starts. The 25 output cases cover identity, marked UTF-8 truncation, adjacent-line dedup, a three-stage pipeline and validated JSON minification at 64 B through 64 KiB. The 12 execution cases compare local tool/command adapter wrappers with callback variants. They do not measure command process startup or external tool latency. Typed lifecycle suite (published in 0.2.3) Thirteen cases cover no-hook paired operations, two gates/observers, split receipt completion, committed model switching, and conversation acceptance, memory sending and normalized response-event handling at 64, 1024 and 4096 bytes. Gate/observer calls, validation, redaction, state transitions and required memory copies remain inside the measurement. Callback state, output slices and operation results are black-boxed to avoid removing the measured work. Fixtures are prepared beforehand. The response case consumes already normalized Started/Delta/Terminal events; it does not include JSON/SSE parsing or model inference. Real zcall parsing and paused event replay are separately integration-tested. Conversation cases accept a borrowed payload, not a database transaction. Model switching updates a local configuration, not a network route or provider session. Memory Sender is not HTTP latency. Table scans, context/mailer shifts and dependency failure propagation remain bounded but size-dependent costs. Transform pipelines can require multiple scans and caller scratch. Event payload length computation may decode escaped text. No framework speedup, tokenizer savings, cancellation timer or universal latency guarantee is asserted. Historical reports apply only to their recorded revision. Skill metadata and catalogs cargo bench --locked --bench skills measures borrowed parsing, normalized description rendering and complete escaped catalogs with 1, 16, 64 or 256 entries. Each parser fixture pairs a 256-byte header with the identical header followed by a 1 MiB body. Parsing stops at frontmatter; instruction size does not add a body scan. Catalog timing includes validation/capacity preflight and output. All measured operations assert zero allocator calls. Filesystem discovery and activation allocate separately and are excluded from these core measurements. See SKILLS.md for reproduction and functional boundaries. Native plugins cargo bench --locked --bench plugins builds and loads a real local dynamic library, then measures cached proxy calls, checked byte calls and the Executor bridge with and without execution hooks. Fixtures, compilation, loading, binding and object creation remain outside timing. The host allocator counter asserts zero measured host allocations; an independently linked plugin has its own allocator and is outside that counter. No startup-time or arbitrary plugin allocation claim is inferred from steady calls. The sample operation copies bytes; payload size and application work remain part of the measured call cost. See the 2026-11-12 measurement record and its raw CSV for a recorded run.

title: Skills
body:
复用上下文、工具循环、hook 与协作执行原语。 Skills zharness provides metadata parsing, ordered discovery, compact catalogs and on-demand loading for SKILL.md skills. The core borrows its input and writes into caller-owned buffers. The optional std adapter reads environment variables and local files, retaining metadata rather than every skill's instructions. A skill summary means its declared name, normalized description and source location. Generating it requires no model call and does not infer a semantic summary from the Markdown body. Applications decide which skill to activate, where to place its instructions, and which tools may execute them. Parse and summarize without I/O The skills core is available with default-features = false; it needs neither std nor alloc and adds no third-party dependency. Keep the source string alive while using its borrowed metadata. use zharness::skills::{SkillMetadata, SkillSummary, write_summaries}; # fn main() -> Result<(), zharness::skills::SkillError> { let source = "---
name: review
description: >-
 Review code changes.
 Use before a merge.
---
# Review
Read the diff first.
"; let metadata = SkillMetadata::parse(source)?; let mut description_buffer = [0; 1024]; let description = metadata.description().write_to(&mut description_buffer)?; assert_eq!(description, "Review code changes. Use before a merge."); let mut output = [0; 1024]; let summary = write_summaries( core::iter::once(SkillSummary { name: metadata.name(), description, location: "/project/.agents/skills/review/SKILL.md", }), &mut output, )?; assert!(summary.contains("<name>review</name>")); assert!(source[metadata.body_offset()..].starts_with("# Review")); # Ok(()) # } SkillMetadata::parse stops at the closing frontmatter delimiter. Its body_offset() points immediately after that delimiter's line; parsing does not walk the remaining instructions. Description::len() reports normalized UTF-8 bytes, and Display or write_to decodes the description without an intermediate owned string. Allocation by a destination such as format! remains the caller's choice. For a single entry, metadata.write_summary(location, output) avoids a separate description buffer. For a collection, use write_summaries and a repeatable, cloneable iterator of SkillSummary entries. summaries_len and metadata.summary_len(location) return the exact required buffer capacity. Summary rendering escapes XML text and returns a complete <available_skills> catalog. Invalid XML characters or insufficient capacity return an error; capacity errors report needed and preserve the output buffer. Discover project, global and custom skills The std feature is enabled by default. Its types are re-exported directly from zharness::skills, including SkillPaths, SkillCatalog and DiscoveryLimits. # #[cfg(feature = "std")] # fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> { use zharness::skills::SkillPaths; let mut paths = SkillPaths::from_env("/workspace/project"); paths.push("/opt/editor/skills"); let catalog = paths.discover(); for diagnostic in catalog.diagnostics() { eprintln!("{diagnostic:?}"); } let mut output = vec![0; catalog.summary_len()?]; let summary = catalog.write_summary(&mut output)?; // Supply `summary` to your model using your own prompt/context policy. println!("{summary}"); if let Some(entry) = catalog.get("review") { let loaded = entry.load(256 * 1024)?; println!("{}
{}", loaded.directory().display(), loaded.body()); // Read a resource only when the selected skill needs it: // let guide = entry.read_resource("references/review.md", 64 * 1024)?; } # Ok(()) # } # #[cfg(not(feature = "std"))] # fn main() {} SkillPaths::for_project(project, home) uses these roots, in priority order: Priority Root 1 <project>/.zharness/skills 2 <project>/.agents/skills 3 <home>/.zharness/skills 4 <home>/.agents/skills Pass None for home to omit global roots. The application supplies the project root; zharness does not search ancestors or infer a Git root. A typical skill is <root>/review/SKILL.md. A root may also point directly at a skill directory. Discovery combines distinct skill names across roots. For a duplicate name, the first valid definition wins and the later definition produces a Shadowed diagnostic containing the winner's path. Thus the default order lets a project replace a same-named global skill while retaining other global skills. The library selects one complete definition; it does not concatenate their bodies. prepend(root) gives a directory highest priority. push(root) gives it lowest priority. Both accept an application's own skills directory, including locations used by another client. Identical roots are deduplicated, and roots() exposes the final ordered search plan. Explicit relative roots use the process working directory. Control order with SKILLS_PATH SkillPaths::from_env(project) reads SKILLS_PATH once, prepends its entries in left-to-right order, then appends the four project/global defaults. It reads HOME on Unix and USERPROFILE on Windows for the global roots. Entries earlier in the resulting list win name collisions, including collisions with defaults. export SKILLS_PATH="$PWD/.agents/skills:$HOME/.claude/skills:/opt/editor/skills" On Unix the separator is :. On Windows it is ;, using the platform's PATH quoting rules. prepend_search_path(value, relative_to) applies the same parsing to an explicit OsStr, without reading the process environment. Relative environment entries are anchored at project; empty entries are ignored. An unset or empty SKILLS_PATH leaves defaults intact. No shell, tilde, environment-variable or glob expansion occurs inside the library. In the shell example above, the shell expands $PWD and $HOME before zharness receives the value. Prefer absolute paths for configuration shared between applications with different working directories. Use SkillPaths::new(roots) for an exact, ordered set of directories without defaults or environment reads. Use SkillPaths::default() for an empty plan. For example, SkillPaths::new(["/opt/editor/skills"]) discovers only that source. This keeps an application's explicit configuration independent of ambient SKILLS_PATH settings. Discovery and loading boundaries The filesystem adapter sorts child paths before scanning them and preserves discovery order in catalog.skills(). It recursively finds grouping directories but treats a directory containing SKILL.md as a leaf, including when that file's metadata is invalid. Hidden child directories and node_modules are skipped. Symlink targets are canonicalized to prevent cycles and duplicate file registration. An explicitly listed root receives its full depth budget even if an earlier, broader root already reached that directory with less depth left. Missing roots are skipped. Read errors, invalid metadata, non-UTF-8 skill paths, collisions and reached limits are available through catalog.diagnostics(). An invalid high-priority definition does not reserve its name: a valid definition in a later root can still load. Review diagnostics when showing an incomplete catalog to a user. discover_with_limits accepts DiscoveryLimits. Defaults are grouping depth 8, 4,096 skills, 65,536 inspected directory entries and 65,536 frontmatter bytes per file. The entry limit counts ignored files too. Reaching a limit produces a diagnostic instead of silently promising a complete search. Discovery reads bounded frontmatter and stores names, normalized descriptions and canonical source paths. It does not retain bodies or read bundled resources. The filesystem adapter allocates metadata and traversal storage; the core's allocation-free contract does not cover filesystem discovery. catalog.get(name) uses the retained metadata index without I/O. catalog.summary_len() reports the exact caller-buffer size for write_summary. entry.load(max_bytes) reads the selected UTF-8 file with an explicit size cap and returns its full source(), exact body() and base directory(). Body-only edits appear on the next load. If its name or normalized description changed, loading returns SkillLoadError::Changed; rediscover to update the catalog. entry.read_resource(relative, max_bytes) loads bytes relative to the selected skill directory. It rejects absolute paths, parent traversal and symlinks that resolve outside that directory. These checks are path guards for trusted local files, not an operating-system sandbox against concurrent hostile filesystem changes. Discovery, summary generation and loading do not execute scripts or grant tool permissions. Supported metadata syntax The parser implements the string forms needed for skill metadata, not a complete YAML processor. Required fields are top-level name and description between --- delimiter lines. UTF-8 BOM, LF and CRLF are accepted. Field or form Behavior name 1–64 lowercase ASCII letters, digits or single hyphens; no leading/trailing hyphen description 1–1,024 Unicode scalar values after whitespace normalization Plain text Supports indented continuations and whitespace-delimited comments Single-quoted text Decodes doubled single quotes Double-quoted text Decodes supported YAML character escapes, including Unicode escapes ` and>` block text Duplicate required keys Error; no ambiguous winner inside one file Aliases, tags and flow collections in required fields Unsupported; returns an error Other top-level keys Skipped with their indented contents Descriptions normalize whitespace to a single space regardless of scalar style; they are routing summaries, not a lossless YAML representation. Raw instructions remain available through the original source. Names use a portable ASCII subset, and quoted names cannot require escape decoding. The declared name is the lookup key; matching it to the containing directory remains advisable for interoperability, but zharness does not enforce that match. Fields such as allowed-tools, disable-model-invocation, hooks and client-specific metadata do not acquire execution or permission semantics merely by being present. Applications that use those extensions must implement their policy explicitly. Reproduce core measurements cargo bench --locked --bench skills ZHARNESS_BENCH_SMOKE=1 cargo bench --locked --bench skills cargo test --locked --no-default-features The benchmark covers plain and multiline 256-byte headers, the same headers with a 1 MiB body, description rendering, and catalogs of 1, 16, 64 and 256 skills. The paired inputs expose any body-length-dependent parsing cost. Catalog timing includes the capacity/validation pass and the write pass. Fixtures, output buffers and timing storage are allocated before measurement. Each case asserts zero allocations inside its measured operations. CSV bytes means input bytes for parsing and rendered bytes for output cases. mean_ns uses a batch; percentile samples include the clock's instrumentation overhead. Smoke mode checks execution and allocation assertions with fewer iterations; it is not a stable performance comparison. No filesystem, process startup or model latency is included, and no fixed latency is promised across machines. Design references Agent Skills specification: portable SKILL.md structure and metadata-first loading. Agent Skills integration guide: discovery, compact catalogs, diagnostics and activation. OpenCode skills: multiple sources and on-demand instructions; its registration order differs from zharness. Rust split_paths: platform PATH separators and Windows quoting. The Agent Skills format does not standardize search roots or SKILLS_PATH. zharness's first-valid-wins order and environment behavior are the contract described above, rather than an attempt to reproduce every client's precedence.

title: 概览
body: 在字节数据与十六进制文本之间转换，写入调用方缓冲区。 zhex Hexadecimal encoding and decoding into caller-owned buffers. The crate always uses #![no_std] and only core: no allocation, dependencies, build script, or external runtime. Stable Rust 1.70 or newer. let mut text = [0; 8]; assert_eq!(zhex::encode_lower(&[0, 18, 171, 255], &mut text), Ok(8)); assert_eq!(&text, b"0012abff"); let mut bytes = [0; 4]; assert_eq!(zhex::decode(b"0012aBfF", &mut bytes), Ok(4)); assert_eq!(bytes, [0, 18, 171, 255]); encode_upper produces uppercase text. encoded_len checks multiplication overflow; decoded_len rejects odd lengths. All functions return Result. An oversized output is accepted and its unused suffix stays unchanged. Decoding accepts only ASCII 0–9, a–f, and A–F. Empty input succeeds. Error precedence is odd length, insufficient capacity, then the first invalid byte. Error::InvalidByte { index, byte } uses the original input byte offset. Encoding checks overflow before capacity. Length and capacity errors leave all output unchanged. An invalid byte may leave an unspecified output prefix modified; decoding checks characters as it goes, without a full prescan. Backends and verification On x86/x86-64, encoding from 16 bytes and decoding from 32 text bytes use AVX2 after a cached core::arch CPUID/XGETBV check verifies CPU support and OS vector-state handling. A build explicitly targeting AVX2 omits that probe and requires that CPU/OS feature set to run. When the target guarantees SSE2, decoding from 16 text bytes uses SSE2 if the AVX2 path is not selected. AArch64 uses NEON when the target guarantees it. Smaller inputs, other targets, SGX, and unsupported CPUs use scalar code. --features force-scalar disables handwritten SIMD; the compiler may still vectorize ordinary Rust. No slice padding is required. cargo test --locked cargo test --locked --release --features force-scalar CI runs stable and MSRV tests on x86-64 and AArch64 hosts, forced supported SIMD, Miri on scalar code, bare-metal compilation, and package dependency checks. Shared-runner benchmark timings are smoke tests without performance thresholds. The standalone comparison project is excluded from the crate's workspace and published package. It pins checked, nonallocating competitor APIs and records every size, offset, failed goal, and raw sample. Its third-party dependencies never enter zhex's dependency tree. Measured performance On an Intel Xeon Platinum 8573C cloud host, Linux 6.18.57 and Rust 1.99.1, the second optimization pass measured the following geometric mean speed ratios. A value above 1 means zhex is faster; each operation uses preallocated buffers and checked decoding. Generic and target-cpu=native builds are separate. Comparison Generic Native Previous zhex / current, 0–64-byte payloads, lowercase encoding 1.278× 1.386× Previous zhex / current, 0–64-byte payloads, uppercase encoding 1.301× 1.360× Previous zhex / current, 0–64-byte payloads, decoding 1.305× 1.386× Previous zhex / current, fixed 96 primary cases 1.012× 1.055× Fastest external baseline / current, same 96 cases 0.783× 0.794× The 2× target was not met; no primary case reached 2× the fastest competitor. Primary cases span 16 bytes–8 MiB and four alignments. Compared with previous zhex, 39/96 generic and 40/96 native primary cases regressed, including some large encodes. These shared-host, hot-buffer timings are exploratory. The acceleration report records latency, payload throughput, scalar/SIMD and dispatch ablations, rejected experiments, every regression, raw samples and reproduction metadata. Publishing Run Bump and release on the default branch with patch, minor, major, or custom plus an explicit X.Y.Z. current publishes the manifest's version only if it has no release tag yet. For example: gh workflow run bump.yml -R LIghtJUNction/zhex -f bump=patch The workflow updates both manifests and lockfiles, commits the change, creates an immutable vX.Y.Z tag, and runs the complete release checks on that exact commit. Pushing a version tag directly or selecting an existing tag in the Release workflow is also supported. The tag must match Cargo.toml. Only the actual publish step receives the repository's CARGO_REGISTRY_TOKEN secret; a missing secret fails explicitly. Publication follows package and dry-run checks. A GitHub Release is created only after crates.io publication succeeds. Published versions cannot be overwritten, and active releases are serialized without cancellation. MIT licensed.

title: Second optimization pass: measured gains and limits
body: 在字节数据与十六进制文本之间转换，写入调用方缓冲区。 Second optimization pass: measured gains and limits On the measured Intel Xeon Platinum 8573C, this pass improves the geometric mean of all 0–64-byte cases against the preceding implementation by 1.278–1.305× in the generic build and 1.360–1.386× in the native build, depending on the operation. The unchanged 96-case primary target remains unmet: against the fastest eligible external library for each case, the scores are 0.783× generic and 0.794× native, with zero primary cases reaching 2×. Short-tail gains do not establish leadership over the strongest competitors. These conclusions use the four committed-source runs at f69459e8e58db7d761099a00bb161da34ef638ee. The historical self-comparison is frozen at 86f569aa72b945073187877323f4a20a6b4f12f6 and runs in the same executable. Only module import paths and its crate-level attribute were adapted; its codec logic and error semantics were preserved. Every slower case remains in the raw results. The independent audit checks coverage, timing arithmetic, medians, both scorecards, archived source and binary provenance. The first-pass report remains available separately. What changed and why Bounded overlapping tails. Encoding and decoding used to finish incomplete vector chunks with scalar work. The new path processes a final full vector ending exactly at the end of the slice. It rereads an already processed prefix, then handles the remaining bytes. Every read and write stays within the caller's slices; there is no padding assumption. Encoding writes identical values over its overlap. Decoding first validates the whole vector, and the overlapped prefix was already valid, so the first invalid index remains the original input position. No output from a failing vector is stored. A shorter encoding entry. On supported x86 CPUs, AVX2 encoding begins at 16 input bytes. A widening operation maps 16 input bytes into 32 nibble positions and one table shuffle emits their text. The earlier 32-byte main loop is retained for bulk input. An experiment using the widening path throughout the bulk loop did not produce a consistent gain and was rejected. SSE2 short decoding and two-table AVX2 decoding. Targets that guarantee SSE2 use its checked 16-character decoder for short input. AVX2 handles 64-character groups using a subtract-one hash and two delta tables. Subtracting one places 0, 1–9, A–F and a–f in four useful high-nibble buckets. One table marks invalid bytes; the other yields nibble values. The two vector check masks are combined before stores. On failure, the first vector mask is examined first, then the second, preserving source order without rescanning the whole input. The tables follow Daniel Lemire's public-domain base16 example and article. Its provenance is recorded in the source and LICENSE. The Rust slice boundaries, dispatch, group error handling and tails are implemented here. The scalar algorithms, public API, validation rules, MSRV and dependency policy are unchanged. Rust 1.70.0 release tests, stable generic/native release tests, rustfmt and Clippy passed after the final code change. The local logs are MSRV, stable, native and Clippy. These runs cover 14 reference-based integration tests, concurrent dispatch, unit checks and the documentation example; target-specific unit-test counts vary when native features make runtime detection unnecessary. Fixed workload and environment The protocol retains the original eight primary payload sizes (16, 32, 64, 256, 4,096, 65,536, 1,048,576 and 8,388,608 bytes), three successful operations and four input/output offsets: (0,0), (1,3), (7,15), (31,1). That is 96 primary cases. The full sweep still includes every size 0–64, all specified vector-boundary neighbors, large inputs and first/middle/last invalid bytes. No workload or validity requirement was removed to improve the score. Hardware and software are recorded in each metadata.json: Intel Xeon Platinum 8573C; Linux 6.18.57, glibc 2.41; x86-64; Rust 1.99.1 (LLVM 23.1.1); CPU affinity [0]. Both builds use optimization level 3, fat LTO, one codegen unit and abort on panic. Generic has empty RUSTFLAGS; native has -C target-cpu=native for all linked libraries. The published crate still supports Rust 1.70.0; comparison dependencies are built only in their separate workspace with the recorded newer toolchain. All adapters use checked, preallocated slice APIs. Input generation, allocation, output poisoning and reference checks happen outside timing. A fixed seed, at least 1 ms of warmup, calibrated 2 ms samples, seven unfiltered samples, rotating implementation order and black_box are used. CPU feature caches are warm; the first CPUID discovery is not timed. Buffers are reused and warm. const-hex's prefix extension is rejected by its adapter; libraries without an error position are scanned only after their checked decoder returns an error. The adapter suite independently checks all 65,536 two-character byte pairs. The official registry recheck at 2026-11-09 16:37:40 UTC confirms the same latest stable versions: hex 0.4.3, faster-hex 1.0.0, const-hex 1.19.3, hex-simd 0.8.0, better-hex 1.0.1, fashex 0.1.1 and hex-turbo 0.4.0. Registry provenance records their checksums, licenses and published VCS commits. The final comparison retains each library's normal dispatch on this CPU. hex lacks a nonallocating uppercase slice API; its 328 unsupported combinations are explicitly retained per full run. The unchanged primary score A speedup is baseline median ns / zhex median ns. A ratio below 1 is slower for zhex. The external score chooses the fastest eligible competitor separately for every case. The previous implementation and internal kernels are excluded. Build Fastest external GM External losses External cases ≥2× Previous-zhex GM Previous losses generic 0.783× 86/96 0/96 1.012× 39/96 native 0.794× 80/96 0/96 1.055× 40/96 The generic competitive range is 0.251–1.080×; native is 0.326–1.804×. Full case-by-case results are generic fastest, native fastest, generic previous and native previous. title: Performance evidence
body: 在字节数据与十六进制文本之间转换，写入调用方缓冲区。 Performance evidence The 2× performance target was not met. On the fixed 96 primary cases, zhex achieved a geometric mean of 0.744× the fastest eligible baseline in the generic build and 0.723× in the native build. No primary case reached 2×. zhex lost 89/96 generic cases and 92/96 native cases; all losing cases and raw samples are retained. A ratio below 1 means the competitor was faster. These are exploratory measurements on a shared cloud CPU, not a claim of leadership across machines. The measured source commit is 60d913d2501a858825cf774ac454efe25e509234. The five final runs contain 201,264 measured samples, plus 984 explicitly unsupported rows for hex’s absent uppercase slice API. The source was clean during every final capture. Source archives, compiler settings and executable hashes accompany each run. Fixed protocol and strongest baselines The protocol was written before the first timing run. Primary payloads are 16, 32, 64, 256, 4,096, 65,536, 1,048,576 and 8,388,608 bytes. Each has lower encoding, upper encoding and mixed-case decoding at four input/output offsets modulo 64: (0,0), (1,3), (7,15), (31,1). The full sweep covers 82 distinct lengths, including every length 0–64, vector boundaries, and the large inputs. Invalid bytes at first/middle/last positions are reported separately. All implementations use checked APIs and the same initialized, preallocated output slices. Allocation, seeded input generation, poisoning, guard checks and independent output verification occur outside timing. All 65,536 possible two-byte decoder inputs are checked for every adapter before measurement. Each valid output byte is poisoned to the complement of its expected value before per-codec validation. black_box surrounds function pointers, inputs, outputs and results; the timer includes the common function-pointer call overhead. Each measured combination has seven unfiltered samples after at least 1 ms warmup, calibrated toward 2 ms per sample. Implementations rotate order between samples. Results use sample medians, with min/max samples retained in CSV. Throughput is payload GiB/s: input bytes for encoding and decoded output bytes for decoding, divided by 2^30. A successful conversion reads and writes a total of three times the payload length. Invalid-input rows report latency without a throughput value. The adapters enforce the same length/capacity/error-index contract without allocating. const-hex’s 0x/0X acceptance is rejected. Libraries lacking an invalid-byte index get a position scan only after their checked decoder returns an error. No unchecked decoder or allocating String API is used. Transactional decoders keep their stronger write behavior; no validation is removed for speed. Versions were checked against the official crates.io sparse index on 2026-11-09. Each archive checksum, license and published VCS commit is recorded in registry.json; dependency resolution is fixed by Cargo.lock. The three additional baselines extend the required four with current reproducible implementations. Baseline Version Published license hex 0.4.3 MIT OR Apache-2.0 faster-hex 1.0.0 MIT const-hex 1.19.3 MIT OR Apache-2.0 hex-simd 0.8.0 MIT better-hex 1.0.1 MIT OR Apache-2.0 fashex 0.1.1 MIT OR Apache-2.0 hex-turbo 0.4.0 0BSD OR Apache-2.0 Hardware, toolchain and builds The host reports Intel Xeon Platinum 8573C, x86-64, AVX2 and AVX-512 features. Measurements were pinned to logical CPU 0, but the physical host and neighboring workloads were shared. The OS reports Linux 6.18.57 with glibc 2.41. The compiler was rustc 1.99.1 (58cf8f9c3, LLVM 23.1.1). Final captures started between 23:48 and 23:59 on 2026-11-09 in Asia/Taipei (UTC+8); exact UTC timestamps are stored in metadata. Every dependency uses the comparison workspace’s release profile: opt-level=3, lto="fat", codegen-units=1, panic="abort". Generic means empty RUSTFLAGS; native means -C target-cpu=native. The scalar run keeps generic flags and enables only zhex’s force-scalar feature. Competitors keep their default dispatch. Compiler auto-vectorization remains enabled in the scalar build, so “force-scalar” means no hand-written zhex SIMD, not an absence of SIMD machine instructions. Primary scorecard The score is the geometric mean of fastest competitor median ns / zhex median ns, with equal weight for every primary case. Each case picks its fastest eligible competitor. Each competitor value comes from its matching build and checked API. Build Operation zhex GiB/s Fastest baseline Baseline GiB/s zhex / baseline generic encode_lower 19.37 faster-hex 24.80 0.781× generic encode_upper 18.71 hex-simd 26.42 0.708× generic decode_mixed 7.50 hex-turbo 17.10 0.438× native encode_lower 20.47 hex-turbo 25.79 0.794× native encode_upper 20.91 better-hex 28.61 0.731× native decode_mixed 11.25 hex-turbo 22.21 0.507× Measured implementation choices Arithmetic, tables and SWAR The safe candidate sweep retained 5,400 combinations × seven samples in candidates-full, with its source snapshot and compiler metadata. Arithmetic encoding allows ordinary compiler vectorization; the alternatives use a 16-byte nibble table, 256 byte-pair entries per case, or four input bytes expanded through a u64 SWAR expression. The same checked adapter/preallocated output protocol applies. For payloads 16–64 bytes, the pair-table candidate’s geometric mean speed relative to the selected arithmetic production path was 0.873× lower / 0.964× upper; SWAR was 0.871× / 0.940×. Across measured payloads 256 B–8 MiB, pair-table ratios were 0.541× / 0.691× and SWAR ratios 0.528× / 0.631×. Arithmetic remains the production choice. Small-table gains below 16 bytes were mixed, so no additional short-table branch was added. These are local engineering experiments, not competitor rankings. Decoding uses a 256-entry nibble table with an invalid sentinel, preserving first-error order with a single combined validity test per pair. Range-match and LUT decoder prototypes are both retained in the candidate source and raw data. Earlier exploratory scalar results and their capture limitations are explicitly documented in EXPLORATORY.md. SIMD and the scalar fallback The final kernel ablations include the exact production sources with checked wrappers. The table reports geometric mean direct scalar latency / public zhex latency over the same 32 primary cases for each operation, across all offsets. Generic scalar still benefits from compiler auto-vectorization; native gives the compiler additional target instructions. Build Lower encode Upper encode Mixed decode generic 1.886× 1.784× 4.793× native 1.100× 1.063× 5.146× Evidence: generic full kernel sweep, native primary kernel sweep. Native reduces the incremental encoding benefit of hand-written SIMD, while decode keeps a substantial advantage over the LUT loop. These gains are against zhex’s own scalar path and do not satisfy the strongest-competitor 2× target. Short-input cutoff and warm dispatch On x86 the public path avoids AVX2 entry below 32 input bytes: encoding payloads below 32 bytes and decoding payloads below 16 bytes. The no-short wrapper performs the same safe preflight and CPU/OS check, then enters AVX2 even for tiny inputs. It therefore measures the combined effect of the cutoff, cached detection and kernel entry within one compilation. Operation Payload range Cases No-short latency / public latency, geometric mean Cases where public was slower encode_lower 0–31 B 128 1.056× 38 encode_upper 0–31 B 128 1.084× 21 decode_mixed 0–15 B 64 1.139× 7 The cutoff had a modest aggregate benefit with individual regressions; the table explicitly retains them. Native compilation folds feature detection away, but also changes ordinary code generation. No universal or isolated nanosecond saving is attributed to dispatch alone. Warmup performs initial detection before timing, so these results exclude cold CPUID/XGETBV initialization. AVX2 decode variants The kept 32-character decoder computes validated nibbles as (text & 15) + (is_letter & 9). The preceding implementation used separate digit/letter value selection. The controlled primary kernel runs measured a 1.381× geometric mean public decode improvement across all 32 size/offset cases: original and revised32, with exact source archives beside each. A 64-character packing variant was also implemented and tested, then rejected. The ratio revised32 latency / revised64 latency was 0.992× across the same primary decode cases; at offset zero, 32 B increased from 9.75 to 13.18 ns and 64 B from 11.13 to 16.90 ns. Some large cases improved and others regressed. All revised64 results, including its source archive, remain available. The simpler revised32 kernel is the delivered implementation. These sequential variant timings are exploratory shared-host evidence, not a precise hardware-wide guarantee. Fallbacks, rejected input and scope limits Production falls back to the arithmetic/LUT implementation when SIMD is disabled, on unsupported architectures, under Miri, on excluded x86 SGX targets, or when x86 CPU/OS state does not support AVX2. The x86 check verifies CPUID, XSAVE/OSXSAVE/AVX, XCR0 XMM/YMM state and AVX2; the cached successful state is used only after those checks. AArch64 NEON is selected only when the compilation target guarantees it. Its public cutoff is 16 input bytes for encode and 32 input bytes for decode. ARM correctness was exercised by CI; this report contains no ARM performance claim from benchmark smoke. Partial vector tails use the scalar path with bounded slices. The full 0–64 and boundary sweep retains their costs instead of truncating inputs to favorable vector lengths. Invalid-input first/middle/last timings remain in all full raw/summary files under group invalid. Different native library error policies, including transactional writes and full-input checks, affect those timings. They are not included in the valid-input performance target. Buffers are repeatedly warmed and reused. No cold-cache, multi-thread scaling, memory-controller counter or independent memory-copy ceiling experiment was performed. Therefore no failure to reach 2× is attributed to a proven memory-bandwidth limit. This is one shared x86 cloud environment. Scheduling variation and code layout affect small differences. Per-sample ranges are retained and no performance threshold is enforced on shared CI runners.
