Method and result support Feature Entry point Application responsibility Resources list, templates/list, read; legacy subscribe/unsubscribe URI authorization, content lookup, template/schema semantics and change delivery Prompts list/get Prompt lookup, argument rules and permission checks Completion completion/complete Generate values, limits and schema semantics Legacy logging logging/setLevel Configure host logging and deliver permitted notices Legacy callbacks roots/list, sampling/createMessage, elicitation/create Correlate callback IDs, obtain consent, run the model/UI and return a result Modern MRTR input_required, requestState, inputRequests/inputResponses Protect opaque state, authorize each requested input, explicitly continue with a new request ID Modern subscriptions subscriptions/listen and Subscription Own the long-lived stream, emit acknowledgments/notifications, bind it to authentication Modern Tasks extension task handle, tasks/get, tasks/update, tasks/cancel Durable task state, ownership, expiry, scheduler and lifecycle transitions Legacy 2025-11-25 Tasks nested task handle, tasks/get/result/list/cancel Legacy task storage and execution, negotiated task-augmented calls Generic result views preserve the full borrowed JSON rather than copying into a partial model. Required container shapes, discriminators, IDs, supported versions and capability gates are checked. This is not full JSON Schema validation of every nested resource, prompt, sampling or elicitation result. Request and server dispatch Enable server routes with Server::with_extensions(&[Method::...]). Client::request(method, params, output) validates the method's wire fields, reserves a bounded pending slot only after successful serialization and adds modern request-scoped metadata while preserving non-reserved application metadata. It rejects caller attempts to replace reserved protocol/capability/clientInfo keys. Server::handle returns Action::Extension { context, method }. The application authorizes and performs the operation, then calls Server::extension_result. Disabled/unknown methods remain method-not-found; enabling resources does not quietly enable filesystem access or callbacks. Client::receive returns a borrowed Event::ExtensionResult for the correlated request. Run the public-API example: cargo run --locked --example mcp_extensions It performs an in-memory resource exchange, returns a modern task handle, and explicitly polls a completed fixture. The fixture is not a task scheduler. Capabilities, callbacks and MRTR Client capabilities default to empty. Use with_client_capabilities with a retained parsed object to opt in. Sampling tools/context and elicitation form/URL sub-capabilities are checked independently. URL permission does not grant form permission; a toolChoice requires the sampling tools capability. Capability objects are type-checked rather than treating arbitrary truthy values as consent. Legacy callback_request encodes an authorized server-to-client request. The application owns the callback ID registry, deadlines and returned result validation. Modern callbacks instead appear inside MRTR input requests; they are not unsolicited nested JSON-RPC exchanges on the HTTP response stream. For modern tools/call, resources/read and prompts/get, Server::input_required can return opaque requestState and/or inputRequests. The client validates requested callbacks against its declared capabilities before releasing the pending slot. It does not execute them or automatically retry the operation. After explicit approval and input handling, use Client::request with inputResponses and the original opaque requestState; a new RPC ID is allocated. Keep state integrity, ownership, expiry and one-time continuation policy in the host. Modern Tasks Opt in with this client capability object: {"extensions":{"io.modelcontextprotocol/tasks":{}}} A server advertises modern Tasks when get, update and cancel handlers are all enabled. The host must create and authenticate-bind the task before calling Server::task_result. The result is a flat resultType: "task" handle, reported to the client as Event::TaskCreated; it is not a completed tool result. Poll using tasks/get, supply inputs using tasks/update and request cancellation using tasks/cancel. There is no modern tasks/list or tasks/result. Poll results carry detailed state: completed output, failure information or pending inputs. TaskView checks status-specific wire containers and nonnegative integer millisecond fields. The host enforces timestamp formatting, expiry and legal state transitions and checks the returned taskId against its retained task ID. No automatic polling, scheduling, state database, generated task ID, callback execution or task ownership policy is included. In particular, do not run tools/call again to “poll” a task. Legacy Tasks Legacy Tasks require the negotiated 2025-11-25 profile and the server's advertised tasks.requests.tools.call support. Use an explicit params.task for task-augmented tools/call. A successful creation contains a nested task object; later result retrieval uses tasks/result rather than the modern inline get result. Older legacy profiles reject these methods before allocating a pending slot. Task TTL and polling interval field names differ by era. The codec keeps those distinctions; it does not manufacture a modern task from a legacy response. Subscriptions Keep the request's filter and the acknowledgment input/token storage alive while using Subscription. Notifications must carry the matching subscriptionId. The acknowledgment must precede data and cannot broaden the requested filters; the final response must also carry the matching ID. Duplicate acknowledgments, unrequested notification classes and wrong IDs are rejected. Resource updates match exact URIs by default. Use observe_with_resource_match only with an explicit, authorized URI-aware subresource rule; naive string prefixes are not a safe resource policy. Task subscriptions require the Tasks capability and accept only requested task IDs with valid detailed task states. The host chooses stream lifetime, cancellation, delivery queues and notification authorization. The library does not open a background connection or retain an unbounded notification queue. Validation scope and evidence Capacity failures do not consume a pending request ID or slot. Malformed or uncorrelated replies do not complete outstanding work. Tests cover resource roundtrips, callback sub-capabilities, MRTR continuation with new IDs, task-era differences, task input validation, subscription acknowledgment order, filter subsets and final-response correlation. Results beyond checked wire fields remain application data. This crate neither claims to implement every future/vendor extension nor passes unrecognized requests through to an executor. JSON-RPC batches use a separate bounded API and are accepted only for 2025-03-26; they do not expand method availability. Sources checked 2026-11-11: https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28 https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-11-25 https://modelcontextprotocol.io/extensions/tasks/overview https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/ext-tasks/blob/main/schema/2026-07-28/schema.ts See tests/extensions.rs, tests/client.rs and examples/mcp_extensions.rs for executable contracts.

title: HTTP and SSE integration
body: MCP 客户端与服务端原语，连接工具调用和宿主传输。 HTTP and SSE integration The default crate handles protocol bytes without sockets, allocation or a runtime. Enable std for bounded blocking HTTP/1.1 framing over a caller-supplied BufRead/Write stream. A verified TLS stream can use the same interface; TLS, DNS, OAuth, connection pooling and async scheduling remain application choices. Choose the negotiated transport, not merely “SSE” Profile Requests and replies Session and stream lifetime 2026-07-28 Streamable HTTP POST; request returns JSON or SSE, accepted notification returns empty 202 Stateless binding; no legacy GET/DELETE, session header or Last-Event-ID behavior. Closing the response stream cancels that request. 2025-03-26, 2025-06-18, 2025-11-25 Streamable HTTP POST; request returns JSON or SSE, accepted notification/response returns empty 202; optional GET SSE and DELETE Optional server-issued sessions. GET with Last-Event-ID supports host-managed resumption. Disconnection alone does not cancel a request. 2024-11-05 HTTP+SSE A long-lived GET receives an endpoint event and JSON-RPC messages; separate POSTs send messages and return 202 Two channels share one legacy MCP lifecycle. A POST acknowledgment is not the JSON-RPC result. Legacy negotiation covers the four listed revisions. JSON-RPC batch arrays are supported only for 2025-03-26 using the explicit bounded batch API below; other revisions require single messages. The transport does not invent a session or silently switch protocol versions. For 2025-03-26, a missing version header is accepted only by an explicitly configured matching server; later legacy versions validate it after initialization. The version selection is deliberate: modern Tasks use get/update/cancel and per-request extension capabilities, while legacy Tasks use their own negotiated methods and result shape. Treating all revisions as one protocol loses semantics. Runnable client and server Run these commands in separate terminals from the source checkout: cargo run --locked --features std --example mcp_http -- server 8080 sse cargo run --locked --features std --example mcp_http -- client 127.0.0.1:8080 Change sse to json for a single JSON response. The example binds only to 127.0.0.1, has socket deadlines and exposes only a fixed echo tool. It is not an authenticated production daemon. It supports the Expect: 100-continue exchange; unknown expectations are rejected without waiting for their body. Its client skips a bounded number of informational responses and rejects protocol upgrades. tests/legacy_sse_network.rs demonstrates the older dual-connection exchange using actual TCP: persistent GET, endpoint negotiation, separate keepalive POSTs, initialization and a tool call. Responses arrive only through GET. A duplicate tool reply is rejected without another POST or another tool execution. Client integration Choose http::Version and create ClientSession with caller-owned session storage. Use a matching client::Client era and explicit legacy negotiation. Encode the MCP request into a bounded buffer. Use ClientSession::post_headers to generate standard headers. Modern routing names are the tool/prompt name, resource URI or task ID, depending on the method. For tools with x-mcp-header annotations, call http::parameters on the selected input schema and arguments, then write_parameter_headers. Append these headers using your HTTP stack. Add authentication separately. Send exactly once. With http_io, use write_request or write_request_with(..., Connection::KeepAlive); set deadlines on the stream before I/O. Use read_response_head for a bounded informational-head loop. Interpret the final status and Content-Type with response_mode. Read JSON into a bounded message buffer, or feed decoded HTTP body chunks to sse::Decoder. Pass complete JSON-RPC payloads to Client::receive. For a legacy initialized session, retain a valid server-issued ID with set_session_id. Validate its ownership server-side. observe_status(404) clears local session state; it does not repeat the failed tool call. A transport write failure is ambiguous: the peer might already have executed the tool. Neither reconnecting nor obtaining a new session proves a retry is safe. Applications must decide from operation semantics, idempotency controls and their own execution records. No helper automatically repeats a tool request. tests/http_session_network.rs exercises an actual truncated tool POST followed by explicit GET recovery, DELETE and expired-session cleanup. It asserts one tool execution, one replayed final result and no second tool POST. For legacy recovery, generate GET headers with get_headers(last_event_id) and let the host select and replay previously stored events. Event storage, retention, unique event IDs and ownership checks are not provided by this crate. Use delete_headers only where session termination is supported. Server integration Parse and bound the HTTP head/body before dispatch. Copy header views into a caller-owned slot array if needed; values remain borrowed. Construct Incoming { method, headers, message }, then call ServerConfig::validate with an application-defined SecurityPolicy. That policy has three separate checks: allowed Origin, authorization and session ownership. A session identifier is not a credential. The core validates media types, version-specific methods, standard singleton headers and modern header/body mirroring before returning a message/listen/terminate action. Header/body mismatch takes precedence over an unsupported modern version. For a selected tool schema, additionally call parameters and validate_parameter_headers before performing side effects. Standard validation cannot discover tool-specific annotations without that schema. Validate schemas before publishing tools over HTTP; do not advertise an invalid header annotation. Only then call mcp::Server::handle, check application permissions, perform the requested work and encode a result. An Action::CallTool or Action::Extension is a description of work, not execution. For legacy HTTP, retain the same Server across the logical session, not one Server per POST. Map HttpError through status/write_rpc; use rpc_error_status when mapping a protocol error reply. Send an Allow header with a 405 response. Accepted notifications and accepted legacy response messages receive empty 202. Keep JSON-RPC parse/invalid-request errors distinct from tool execution errors. Legacy batches (2025-03-26 only) Parse the complete JSON array into a caller-owned token tape, then call batch::Batch::parse(root, version, max_items) before any dispatch. Empty or oversized arrays, initialization inside an array, modern per-request metadata and mixed request/response categories are rejected before effects. Valid request siblings are retained when individual items are malformed. For HTTP, call ServerConfig::validate_batch once for the POST. It applies shared security, media, version and session checks and returns a BodyKind: requests (including invalid request items needing errors), notifications-only, or responses-only. Batch initialization is forbidden, so batch requests never receive the initialization exception to a required session ID. Iterate entries() explicitly. Each entry contains its borrowed raw JSON and parsed message or error. Pass valid request item bytes to Server::handle and valid response item bytes to Client::receive, using suitable scratch tokens. Return id:null/-32600 for invalid request entries; malformed response entries are local errors and must not trigger response-to-response messages. The host owns duplicate-ID policy, per-item authorization, lifecycle order and execution. encode_requests joins already encoded request/notification values. encode_responses takes optional response values; None denotes no response. Both preflight the entire output and leave it unchanged on failure. A batch with no replies emits zero bytes, never an empty array. Notification-only and response-only HTTP POSTs receive empty 202. Retain completed results for a larger output buffer; never re-execute tools after a serialization failure. Client requests already encoded before a failed batch encoding retain their pending slots: retry serialization or explicitly abandon unsent IDs. The single-message rpc::parse contract remains strict; no modern request can silently acquire batch semantics. See tests/batch.rs and tests/http_batch.rs for roundtrips and shared-envelope validation. Incremental SSE and bounded memory Decoder::new receives separate buffers for a line, joined data, event name and event ID, plus a maximum raw event-block size. Reuse them across events. feed reports exactly how many input bytes were consumed; keep the remainder. On Ready, handle event() before consume(). A pending event applies backpressure rather than overwriting data. On NeedCapacity, use the reported buffer and size with replace_buffer, then retry the unconsumed bytes. No complete event is delivered until a blank line. finish discards an incomplete trailing event; it does not turn a disconnected tool request into success. Comment heartbeats, CR/LF/CRLF, a leading BOM, multiline data and UTF-8 replacement are handled across arbitrary chunk splits. Event IDs are per block, not automatically inherited. Commit a legacy resume checkpoint only after accepting the complete block according to application policy; retain the checkpoint outside the decoder. Metadata-only blocks may carry IDs or retry hints without a JSON-RPC payload. retry_hint() can expose a complete retry field before the final delimiter. Modern HTTP ignores these legacy resumption mechanisms. write_event and write_comment preflight output capacity. Event data must be UTF-8 and cannot contain CR; LF is encoded as multiple data lines. The JSON encoder already escapes embedded string controls, avoiding field injection. Optional blocking I/O http_io supports Content-Length, chunked and close-delimited response bodies, bounded trailers, short-read/write handling, Interrupted retries and sequential keepalive reuse. Supply a buffered reader/writer to avoid one syscall per field. Consume the entire framed body before reusing a connection. It rejects ambiguous CL+TE, duplicate security/framing headers, folded headers, bare LF, HTTP/1.0 transfer coding, unsupported compression and malformed chunks. A framing/capacity failure poisons BodyReader; a partial write/flush failure poisons ChunkWriter. Close the connection after either error. ChunkWriter flushes each event and emits the final zero chunk only on explicit successful finish. This is an MCP-oriented HTTP/1.1 adapter, not a general browser stack. It does not implement HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 framing, CONNECT, upgrades, automatic redirects, compression, certificate verification or credential acquisition. Use the no-std protocol layer with an existing verified stack when those are required. The stream's timer, executor and connection policy belong to its owner. Older endpoint resolution legacy_sse::Session accepts the endpoint event before message events and resolves same-origin relative/absolute endpoints into caller storage. It rejects cross-origin endpoints, userinfo, fragments, control characters, backslashes, encoded dot segments and ambiguous repeated slashes. It does not forward a token or open the destination itself. This conservative URI resolver is not a browser URL implementation; rejected unusual URLs require an explicit host decision. References and tests Normative sources checked on 2026-11-11: https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/basic/transports/streamable-http https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-11-25/basic/transports https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-03-26/basic/transports https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2024-11-05/basic/transports https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/server-sent-events.html https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9112 See tests/http.rs, tests/sse.rs, tests/http_io*.rs, tests/http_network.rs, tests/legacy_sse*.rs and scripts/http_smoke.py. The Python peer independently checks the executable Rust server and also runs the Rust client; it is not an official conformance suite. Reproduction commands and measurement scope are in VALIDATION.md.

title: MCP protocol boundaries
body: MCP 客户端与服务端原语，连接工具调用和宿主传输。 MCP protocol boundaries Client behavior is described in CLIENT.md. Explicit legacy single-message negotiation covers 2024-11-05, 2025-03-26, 2025-06-18 and 2025-11-25. The server selects a supported requested revision or offers the latest supported legacy revision. Bounded JSON-RPC batches are supported only for 2025-03-26 through the explicit batch module; initialization is never batched. Other revisions reject arrays. Modern discovery/list responses include private, zero-TTL cache hints; the client does not cache or grant permission from those hints. Normative references checked 2026-11-11: https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28 https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/modelcontextprotocol/blob/main/schema/2026-07-28/schema.ts https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-11-25 https://www.jsonrpc.org/specification Modern requests include params._meta keys io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion and io.modelcontextprotocol/clientCapabilities. ClientInfo is optional. Discovery is available without an initialization exchange. Results contain resultType and serverInfo metadata. Unsupported version errors use -32022 and list supported versions. The caller's HTTP adapter maps the corresponding failure to HTTP 400. Legacy requests have an explicit initialize -> notifications/initialized transition, with 2025-11-25 as the supported fallback version. Ping is legacy only. Callers should use one Server per legacy connection. Modern requests are not allowed to inherit client capabilities from legacy or prior modern calls. The application implements deterministic tool ordering and pagination. Omitted arguments become {}. A present arguments field must be an object. Unknown tools and policy/schema rejection become -32602 or an application-defined permission error; actual tool failures return a tool result with isError=true. Modern structuredContent can be any JSON value. Legacy structuredContent must be an object. Input schemas must be object schemas; this API validates their wire shape, not schema correctness or tool arguments against the schema. Output-schema matching is also the application's responsibility. Notifications never receive responses. Cancellation may race completion; ignore unknown/completed IDs. Tracker permits modern ID reuse after completion or legacy connection-wide retention. Retention exhausts a caller-sized slot table rather than allocating. Progress monotonicity is enforced by Tracker when used. HTTP headers must be validated before side effects. Use http::ServerConfig::validate for standard headers and security policy, then http::parameters/validate_parameter_headers for the selected tool schema's mirrored parameters. The older mcp::HttpHeaders helper is only the original tools-profile check and is not a complete modern HTTP validator. See HTTP for version-specific status/cancellation/session rules. Resources, prompts, completion, legacy logging and callbacks, modern MRTR and subscriptions, and task messages have explicit opt-in wire boundaries; see EXTENSIONS.md. The host implements the work and only advertises capabilities it actually provides. OAuth flows, general JSON Schema validation, persistent task/replay storage and automatic execution remain outside this crate. An official discovery fixture and adversarial/independent-peer tests are checked; no claim is made of passing a complete official conformance suite.

title: 概览
body: 观测 Linux 内存压力，管理 Swap 并约束后台任务的内存预算。 zmem Memory, with room to work. A small Linux memory and Swap controller from Project Z. Website · Releases · crates.io · Rust API · Background admission · 0.4.1 acceptance · Responsiveness guide · 0.3.1 acceptance · Swap and dedup guide · 0.3.0 acceptance · 0.2.0 host acceptance zmem observes memory pressure, waits before starting new managed background work under pressure, and gives running background jobs a bounded memory budget. It brings zram setup, dynamic disk swap, automatic cleanup, opt-in memory deduplication and structured inspection into one tool. The Rust implementation has no third-party crate dependencies; the policy library uses no_std and makes no heap allocations. What it does Capability Behavior Pressure policy Reports memory pressure and IO congestion separately, using available memory, PSI and paging activity with cooldowns and recovery hysteresis. Swap management Adopts active swap, grows within capacity and free-space limits, cleans retained owned files, and retires eligible owned swap after sustained recovery. zram lifecycle Keeps the current active device during migration and prepares zram on subsequent boots. Explicit memory deduplication Registers trusted background or disposable jobs with --dedup; pauses owned KSM scanning under CPU, memory or IO pressure. Workload budgets Adjusts aggregate cgroup v2 memory.high budgets to managed background usage and available headroom; disposable jobs retain explicit hard limits. Background admission Checks available RAM and memory PSI before a background or disposable command starts; waits for stable recovery and spaces starts by the same user. Interactive protection Assigns a bounded memory.low budget to recognized desktop, terminal and remote-access scopes through their actual cgroup hierarchy. Reclaim responsiveness Caps optimistic swappiness adjustments when memory stalls, direct reclaim and anonymous refaults occur together; skips writes when current kernel readback is unavailable. User I/O controls Prepares additive I/O delegation and accounting; reports whether the calling user's existing manager has the controller available. Observability Reports daemon state, actual kernel controls, managed-workload coverage and on-demand process usage in human-readable and JSON output. Service migration Saves prior service/configuration state, replaces existing management services, and offers rollback. The Linux kernel performs actual paging, compression, page merging and final OOM handling. zmem makes earlier policy decisions using those facilities. Application checkpoints, automatic recovery of computation progress and energy optimization remain future work. Deduplication requires explicit task registration and kernel support; it does not enroll every application or deduplicate active swap files on disk. KSM uses a system-wide matching domain, so choose only workloads whose data may share that domain. The default policy preserves processes. It does not issue global cache drops or automatically kill arbitrary applications. A task explicitly started as disposable can be given a hard cgroup limit, where the kernel may terminate it if the budget is exhausted. Installation Use a Linux system with systemd, PSI and cgroup v2. Swap-file preparation uses the host's swap utilities; activation and deactivation also require nsenter from util-linux. Btrfs hosts need btrfs-progs. The daemon needs root privileges for system-wide configuration and swap management. Read-only status and policy inspection can run without root. The swap helper enters PID 1's mount namespace and root before calling the swap syscalls. It pins and verifies the target file's identity so a changed path cannot substitute a different file. The provided service unit grants CAP_SYS_CHROOT and CAP_SYS_PTRACE for this namespace/root access while retaining its other service restrictions. From crates.io cargo install zmem-manager --locked zmem doctor zmem status --json sudo "$(command -v zmem)" install --replace install --replace is the explicit system migration operation. It preserves active swap, records the prior management configuration and installs the zmem service. Existing swap that contains data is adopted in place. Changes that require rebuilding zram take effect at a normal subsequent boot. The installer also prepares I/O delegation for user managers without replacing their other delegated controllers. An existing session may need a manager refresh before user scopes can enforce I/O controls; zmem doctor --json reports the observed state. See the responsiveness guide for refresh and kernel-readback checks. The installer does not restart user sessions automatically. Active Swap created in an older service mount namespace can retain an old alias in /proc/swaps until reactivation or a normal boot. Its capacity remains available. Maintenance never infers inactivity from a missing canonical pathname: cleanup leaves active files protected by the kernel, and retirement requires the full-file headroom checks described in the lifecycle guide. Prebuilt Linux executable Download the archive and its .sha256 file for your architecture from GitHub Releases. Verify the checksum, extract the archive and run its bin/zmem executable. The release contains build.json with source identity, architecture and build libc information. Source installation is available for distributions with an older libc than the published binary requires. # In the directory containing the downloaded archive and checksum: sha256sum --check zmem-*.tar.gz.sha256 tar -xzf zmem-VERSION-linux-ARCH.tar.gz ./zmem-VERSION-linux-ARCH/bin/zmem doctor sudo ./zmem-VERSION-linux-ARCH/bin/zmem install --replace Replace VERSION and ARCH with the downloaded release name. Supported release architectures are x86_64 and aarch64. Service and rollback systemctl status zmem.service journalctl -u zmem.service sudo zmem rollback Stopping or upgrading the management daemon leaves active swap in place. Each installation captures a separate transaction snapshot; failure recovery uses it to restore the immediately previous binary, configuration and controller states. If recovery itself fails, the snapshot is retained and the error identifies its path. The explicit rollback command instead restores the original first-install baseline. Neither operation drains active swap into RAM. Keep the original configuration record until the new setup has completed a normal boot on your machine. Everyday use zmem status zmem status --json --processes zmem status --live --json zmem plan --json zmem doctor --json zmem schema status reads the report of the active daemon after checking its process identity. It retains that daemon's policy history, measured paging rates, worker state and errors. --processes adds a current process list to the same report. The observation fields identify the source, sample age, stale reports and the separate process-sampling time. Each requested process row includes its current cgroup and whether it belongs to a registered background subtree (managed_background). Both fields are null when unified cgroup membership cannot be read. Membership describes current placement: moving an existing process does not transfer its existing memory charges, so classify jobs at launch (kernel memory ownership). status --live and plan take one independent sample and show an unapplied preview. They start with a new policy state; rates remain null while the sample is unprimed. If the daemon report is unavailable, ordinary status also returns an explicitly labelled independent snapshot with the cache error. schema describes this contract for scripts and AI tools. Read the controls and coverage alongside the plan: Report field Meaning memory_pressure, io_congested Separate signals for memory pressure and IO congestion. A busy storage device alone does not establish memory exhaustion. paging Measured sampling interval, file/anonymous refaults, direct scans and available swap-rate estimates. Availability flags and null values distinguish missing observations from zero activity. controls Requested and observed swappiness, its selection reason, actual page-cluster value, protection budget, protected-scope count, and the last protection check's timestamp and errors. managed Observed background groups, populated groups, task count, memory usage and currently eligible reclaim candidates. background Requested aggregate budget, actual limits read back from populated groups, per-group limits, and sampling/application completeness. dedup Observed and target scan state, decision reason, control ownership, registered tasks, task-observation age and coverage. ksm Actual KSM controls and available kernel counters, including the signed system-wide profit estimate. Missing observations remain null. plan.background_high_percent A pressure-severity hint retained in the policy contract. Read background for the byte budget actually requested and observed. protection_complete, coverage_complete Completeness of the protection operation and managed-background observations, inside controls and managed respectively. An empty background scope has no workload to throttle or reclaim. Use zmem run --class background to place a job under that policy; arbitrary existing applications are not automatically assigned a background budget. Protection counts cover recognized scopes, and completeness flags expose incomplete scans or control operations. background.requested_budget_bytes describes the proposed aggregate budget; background.actual_budget_bytes sums the limits read back from populated groups. Check plan_available and readback_complete before interpreting a null: with complete information, it means no temporary requested ceiling or an unlimited observed group, respectively; otherwise the value is unavailable. Per-group requested_high_bytes and actual_high_bytes, together with applied_complete, expose retained external limits and partial application. To observe policy over time before applying system changes: zmem daemon --observe Start background work with its classification from the beginning: zmem run --class background -- cargo build --release zmem run --class background --wait-timeout 300 -- YOUR_BATCH_COMMAND zmem run --class interactive -- YOUR_COMMAND zmem run --class disposable --max-memory 2048 -- YOUR_BATCH_COMMAND # Explicitly register trusted, repeat-heavy memory workloads for KSM: zmem run --class background --dedup -- YOUR_TRUSTED_COMMAND zmem run --class disposable --max-memory 2048 --dedup -- YOUR_TRUSTED_BATCH_COMMAND The --max-memory value is in MiB. The disposable class is for work that can be restarted if it exceeds its explicit budget. Starting a job inside a cgroup gives the kernel a consistent accounting boundary for the job's allocations. Starting with 0.4, background and disposable commands wait for memory admission before executing. The default wait is 60 seconds; --wait-timeout 0 makes one immediate attempt, and values up to 3600 allow a longer recovery window. A timeout returns exit code 75 without starting the target. A healthy first observation can pass immediately; after pressure, recovery must remain stable for three seconds. Launch reservations by the same user are spaced at least three seconds apart. Interactive commands bypass this gate. See the admission guide for thresholds, cancellation and JSON events. Admission progress goes to stderr, leaving stdout for the target. The launcher preserves literal argument bytes and the caller's environment, working directory and standard input. It does not freeze an existing application or impose a permanent single-core or storage-bandwidth limit. Admission covers commands submitted through zmem run; it does not automatically intercept every terminal build or model loader. --dedup enables process-level KSM registration before executing the selected command and verifies that registration. It is available for background and disposable, not interactive. A kernel that rejects or cannot verify registration produces an explicit error before the target command starts. Ordinary run commands and the default managed-build wrappers do not add this flag. The default dedup_enabled = true permits the daemon to manage scanning for registered tasks. It does not register tasks by itself. When zmem owns the KSM controls, CPU, memory or IO pressure pauses scanning with run=0, preserving merged pages. Complete, fresh observations and 30 seconds of stable headroom are required before scanning resumes. The fixed scan settings are 128 pages followed by a 100 ms sleep; these are batch controls, not a hard CPU quota. Registration is refreshed through a bounded task scan every 10 seconds, with incomplete coverage reported explicitly. KSM matching crosses process, user and cgroup boundaries, including eligible memory registered by other software. zmem leaves an already running external KSM controller, an external advisor or externally changed controls alone. It never writes run=2 or PR_SET_MEMORY_MERGE=0 to force unmerging. See the dedup guide for trust boundaries, pause conditions and status interpretation. Policy and resource limits The policy core is a deterministic state machine. It receives a snapshot and a monotonic timestamp, then produces a bounded decision. The Linux adapter checks real ownership, kernel state, disk capacity and operation results before acting. Swappiness expresses the kernel's relative preference for swapping anonymous memory versus reclaiming file-backed pages. zmem uses measured paging evidence to select it. Confirmed disk-swap read pressure lowers the preference; IO congestion alone does not trigger that reduction. When file-page refaults dominate alongside direct reclaim scans, and disk-swap pressure is absent, the desired value is 80, or 100 when zram has measured useful compression headroom. Refaults count pages used again after eviction; they do not directly measure storage reads. Hysteresis and bounded steps govern changes, so the requested and actual values can differ from the desired value for a sample. Interactive protection follows recognized processes into their real nested session and application scopes. A shared, bounded memory.low budget is allocated through the required ancestors and leaf scopes. The report records how many critical scopes received protection and whether the operation completed. Recursive protection in the kernel can also pass an ancestor's protection to a child whose local memory.low is zero; interpret the full hierarchy when inspecting a session. systemd can restore an owned ancestor or service's memory.low to its configured zero baseline during reload. That can interrupt the protection path even while a leaf retains a nonzero value. zmem reapplies its budget only when the cgroup identity is unchanged, the control was already owned, and both the original baseline and current value are zero. Nonzero external values and nonzero original baselines retain external-change protection. To disable this automatic protection, set protect_sessions = false in the service configuration and restart the service; a manual zero on a currently owned node is not a persistent opt-out. controls.protection_sampled_at_unix and controls.protection_errors retain the last protection check's time and diagnostics between checks, so an intervening ordinary sample cannot hide a failed protection operation. Background jobs inherit a dynamic budget from their managed aggregate. run --class background adds no fixed half-RAM limit to each new job. During a pressure episode, the daemon calculates a shared byte budget from current managed usage, available RAM and the configured reserve plus a safety margin. Populated groups share that budget with a bounded allowance for progress; empty groups consume no share. Healthy policy removes the temporary restriction while preserving existing external limits. Budget redistribution applies tighter limits before relaxing any group. A failed tightening blocks all relaxations in that batch; a failed relaxation stops the remaining relaxations. Incomplete sampling holds existing controls, and subsequent decisions use confirmed kernel readbacks, including partial application. When measured spare headroom is available, the budget can recover in bounded steps even while memory.high throttling keeps PSI elevated. This lets work regain capacity without waiting for its own throttling stalls to disappear first. Proactive reclaim is limited to populated, managed background groups with a conservative clean-file-page budget. Empty groups and groups without eligible file pages are skipped. The worker records its requested bytes separately from observed proactive-reclaim counters or net memory reduction, then backs off when progress is absent or unavailable. A successful request write by itself is not reported as memory saved. While the daemon is running, zmem owns the aggregate memory.high policy of its dedicated zmem.slice/zmem-background.slice, including the corresponding slice below a user manager. systemd can reset that slice to max when a new scope starts. If the original baseline was unlimited and the cgroup is still the same object, zmem reapplies its policy and records a managed_background_limit_reapplied event. A manual max write to this dedicated slice is therefore temporary. Finite external memory.high limits, finite original baselines and other cgroups retain the normal external-change protection; the separate owned-zero rule above applies to memory.low. Run jobs outside the background class when another tool should own their limits. Recovery records for vanished or replaced cgroups are removed every 15 sampling cycles, or about 30 seconds with the default interval. Live control baselines and records with uncertain metadata errors remain intact. Reading a recovery journal larger than 1 MiB returns an error and retains the whole file for recovery. When growth is needed, the policy requests a full configured chunk, 2 GiB by default, bounded by the disk-swap cap. Every active swap file consumes a kernel swap slot, so creating a new small file for each minor headroom deficit can exhaust slots while disk space remains available. Full chunks provide spare headroom and use fewer slots for a given capacity. Pressure, IO and cooldown gates still determine when growth is permitted; the Linux adapter checks remaining capacity and filesystem reserve before creating a file. The disk-swap budget includes valid owned files in the configured swap directory even when allocation or activation is incomplete. Each file is charged the larger of its logical length and allocated blocks. Other active disk Swap also counts toward the cap; zram does not. An exact canonical active path is counted once. An uncertain old alias remains a separate charge, so unproven identity can conservatively reduce the room for another allocation. After a failed new-file activation, cleanup requires a confirmed kernel syscall error other than EBUSY, unchanged file identity and a successful fresh Swap inventory that does not list the canonical path as active. Setup errors, timeouts, malformed helper replies, missing observations and changed identities preserve the file. Retained allocations continue consuming the disk-swap budget. Numeric syscall errors are distinguished from helper setup errors; text that merely says a file is busy does not establish its identity or authorize cleanup. Automatic maintenance revisits owned files at most once per 60 seconds, one candidate per attempt, after higher-priority growth or reclaim work. Cleanup can remove an inactive retained allocation without calling swapoff. It requires noncritical memory pressure, no IO congestion and at least half of the configured effective RAM reserve. The final operation is an ordinary, identity-checked unlink; the kernel refuses it while the file remains active or draining. A missing /proc/swaps pathname or an EINVAL result alone never proves inactivity. Active retirement has stronger requirements: the default policy waits for 600 seconds of continuously healthy conditions and at least that long after growth. Immediately before swapoff, the worker rechecks low pressure, available RAM of at least twice the effective reserve plus the candidate's entire capacity, and enough free Swap to preserve the configured target after subtracting that entire capacity. Known used files are skipped. The whole-file bound covers an old mount alias whose usage cannot be established from its name. All zmem allocation, activation, retirement and removal operations share a lock that remains held for the lifetime of their helpers, including a helper that outlives a timeout. Maintenance never truncates, punches holes in, overwrites or applies filesystem deduplication to active Swap. Default policy setting Value Available-memory reserve Larger of 1 GiB or 10% of physical RAM, capped at total RAM Automatic launch reserve Policy reserve above, additionally capped at 25% of RAM; explicit reserves retain their meaning Background admission wait 60 seconds; --wait-timeout accepts 0..3600, timeout exits 75 before launch Desired unused Swap headroom 4 GiB when growth is needed Growth batch 2 GiB per permitted decision, bounded by remaining capacity Disk Swap cap, including retained owned allocations 32 GiB Filesystem free-space reserve 8 GiB Swap growth cooldown 30 seconds Automatic maintenance cadence At least 60 seconds between attempts; at most one file per attempt Stable healthy time before shrinking 600 seconds Dedup task registration Explicit run --dedup; daemon scanning enabled by default Dedup recovery and scan settings 30 stable seconds; 128 pages per batch, 100 ms sleep These are policy defaults, not a promise about application latency. A machine can run out of physical memory and swap, or spend time waiting for a slow storage device. zmem bounds its own actions and exposes the observed pressure so the tradeoffs remain visible. Memory and swap quantities use binary units: one MiB is 1,048,576 bytes and one GiB is 1,073,741,824 bytes. PSI measures time spent waiting for a resource. In the library, 10,000 basis points means 100% of the measurement interval. The interactive website illustrates a simplified policy decision using synthetic inputs. It runs entirely in the browser and does not connect to the daemon. Build and validate cargo test --locked cargo check --locked --lib --no-default-features cargo build --release --locked The public policy types can be embedded without the operating-system adapter. The zmem executable targets Linux; the no_std policy library does not depend on Linux. The repository includes a read-only probe for observations during ordinary work: python3 scripts/measure_responsiveness.py --duration 60 --output artifacts/before # Repeat under the candidate policy for the same duration and a comparable workload. python3 scripts/measure_responsiveness.py --duration 60 --output artifacts/after It records scheduler wakeup lateness, memory/IO/CPU PSI, paging counters, zram data, daemon status and managed-background activity. --desktop-probe adds a bounded Hyprland monitor-query round trip when available; this measures process startup plus IPC, not frame latency. The probe does not create a load or change kernel settings. Unknown measurements remain null, and counter resets are excluded from rate calculations. Output files contain reproducible samples and a summary with owner-only permissions. Natural-workload before/after observations describe the machine during those windows. Workload and cache changes remain possible causes of a difference. For a controlled comparison, identify the tested source, kernel, storage and workload, repeat comparable conditions, and assess latency together with task progress, pressure and paging activity. A lower used-memory number alone does not measure responsiveness. The published 0.2.0 acceptance record applies to its recorded binaries and observation windows. It does not validate the automatic lifecycle and dedup additions in 0.3.0 or establish a performance gain for them. The lifecycle and dedup guide separates current source behavior from measured results. Release a version Open Actions → Release zmem → Run workflow. Leave tag empty and set version to patch, minor, major, or an explicit X.Y.Z. The workflow updates Cargo.toml, Cargo.lock and the website version, validates the source, commits to main, and creates the release tag. The same run builds native Linux x86_64 and ARM64 executables, publishes the crate with the repository's CARGO_REGISTRY_TOKEN secret, and uploads the archives and checksums to GitHub Releases. A direct version-tag push runs the release pipeline too. All releases share a concurrency group to prevent overlapping version publication. To rebuild an existing tag after a failed infrastructure step, set tag to that version. An existing crate version is retained; an existing release asset must match the rebuilt file exactly. The workflow does not silently replace published artifacts. Local version editing is also available: python3 scripts/bump.py patch # Or commit, tag and atomically push a validated release from a clean main: python3 scripts/bump.py patch --release Local --release pushes a tag, which starts the official release workflow when pushed using a normal repository credential. GitHub's workflow token does not recursively start tag workflows; the one-click path therefore continues its release in the same workflow run. The Pages workflow deploys site/ directly. There is no package install, external font, analytics script or frontend build step. Daily source work is tested locally; the automated test jobs belong to the explicit release pipeline. Kernel references Pressure Stall Information cgroup v2 memory controls zram administration Virtual-memory sysctls Kernel Samepage Merging Btrfs swap files The website uses the warm graphite, linen and copper direction of oh-my-ztty. MIT licensed.

title: Background admission
body: 观测 Linux 内存压力，管理 Swap 并约束后台任务的内存预算。 Background admission Starting a large job can make an already busy machine spend more time moving pages than doing useful work. zmem 0.4 checks current memory conditions before starting a command in the background or disposable class. Waiting happens before the target command runs, so it adds no compiler or model working set during that wait. Admission and the daemon's running-task budgets serve different purposes. Admission decides when an explicitly submitted job may begin. After launch, the daemon adjusts the memory budget of managed background groups. Neither mechanism estimates an arbitrary program's future peak memory or automatically manages commands launched outside zmem run. Run a job # Wait up to 60 seconds by default, then run under the background policy. zmem run --class background -- cargo build --release --locked # Allow a longer recovery window for a batch job. zmem run --class background --wait-timeout 300 -- YOUR_BATCH_COMMAND # Make one immediate admission attempt; exit 75 if it cannot be admitted. zmem run --class background --wait-timeout 0 -- YOUR_COMMAND # Interactive commands bypass admission. zmem run --class interactive -- YOUR_INTERACTIVE_COMMAND --wait-timeout is an integer number of seconds from 0 to 3600. It bounds admission waiting, not the target command's execution time. An interactive invocation accepts a valid timeout value but does not use it or wait. A timeout exits with code 75 before the target starts. SIGINT and SIGTERM during waiting cancel that invocation with exit codes 130 and 143 when the inherited signal disposition permits delivery. Inherited ignored or blocked signals retain their meaning. zmem does not suspend or terminate another task to admit this one. The disposable class uses the same admission check and retains its explicit --max-memory MiB hard limit. Kernel OOM handling can terminate a disposable job that exceeds that limit. --dedup remains a separate opt-in for trusted background or disposable jobs. Conditions for admission The launcher reads available RAM and the kernel's ten-second memory-pressure averages. Linux PSI measures time when tasks wait for a resource: some means at least one task is stalled; full means all non-idle tasks are stalled together. Admission uses memory PSI. An I/O stall from a deliberately paced background scanner does not by itself block a new job. Check Initial healthy observation Recovery after pressure or a missing observation Available RAM At least the launch reserve At least 125% of that reserve, capped at total RAM Memory some PSI, avg10 Below 5%, or a lower configured pressure threshold Below half that threshold Memory full PSI, avg10 Below 1%, or a lower configured critical threshold Below half that threshold Stability A healthy first observation can pass immediately All recovery checks must remain satisfied for three seconds The automatic launch reserve starts with the policy's larger-of-1-GiB-or-10%-of-RAM reserve, then caps it at 25% of total RAM. This avoids an impossible 1 GiB launch floor on a small machine. An explicitly configured reserve retains its meaning; admission does not silently reduce it to the automatic cap. The 25% cap applies to launch admission, not to the daemon's other reserve calculations. The launcher samples about once per second and rechecks immediately before recording an admission. Missing, malformed or inconsistent observations do not count as healthy. Recovery uses stricter thresholds so a brief low reading does not release a burst of work. These thresholds are zmem policy choices, not kernel recommendations or a guarantee of desktop latency. Concurrent starts Launch reservations by the same user share a three-second minimum interval. A short exclusive lock protects the final observation and reservation. Waiters release the lock between attempts, and launched workloads do not retain it. This limits simultaneous admission after recovery without placing a permanent CPU quota or storage bandwidth cap on every command. The coordination record lives in the user's runtime directory; root uses /run/zmem-admission. zmem verifies ownership, permissions and file identity, and uses boot identity and a monotonic clock rather than wall time. A launcher exiting early does not erase its interval, because the command may have left descendants running. This spaces admission reservations; scheduling delays can still change the interval between actual command execution. There is no FIFO promise, declared peak-memory reservation or global cross-user launch schedule. Script and AI contract Admission events are JSON lines on stderr. They never include the command or its arguments. Stdout remains available for the target's output, and the command receives its argument bytes, environment, working directory and standard input through the normal scope launch. Event Meaning admission_wait This invocation is still waiting; the record includes elapsed time, timeout and a reason. Progress events are at least five seconds apart. admission_granted The invocation reserved a launch opportunity after a fresh observation. This is not confirmation that the target executable has started successfully. admission_timeout The wait expired; the target was not started. admission_cancelled A termination signal cancelled the wait; the target was not started. admission_error Required runtime state or launch preparation could not be validated. run_error The run arguments or configuration were invalid; the target was not started. After launch, normal command output and exit status belong to the command and systemd scope. The launcher checks the host systemd-run version: newer versions explicitly disable variable expansion, while older scope semantics already preserve literal arguments. An unknown version fails before the target starts. The compatibility distinction is documented in the upstream systemd 254 and systemd 252 manuals. zmem schema exposes the admission options and exit semantics. zmem status --json describes the running daemon and managed groups; it is not a persistent queue of pending launcher processes. What this changes in a development workflow Project Z and oh-my-ztty build helpers already submit heavy Cargo commands through zmem run --class background when a compatible local CLI and daemon are available. With zmem 0.4 those submissions also wait for admission. Cargo metadata queries remain outside that path. If admission times out, retry after pressure subsides or select a longer wait for an explicit invocation. Reuse a persistent Cargo target directory and avoid overlapping large checks when the working sets exceed RAM. Admission does not replace Cargo's dependency cache. A cache hit can remove compilation work; admission reduces the chance of adding that work at the worst moment. Neither change guarantees a faster cold build. Verification boundaries The parser, recovery transitions, deadline handling and shared-state ownership are tested independently of host load. A host acceptance record identifies which native command checks actually ran. Unit tests and a successful launch do not establish a percentage reduction in swapping, input latency or application peak memory.

title: Responsiveness, reclaim and background I/O
body: 观测 Linux 内存压力，管理 Swap 并约束后台任务的内存预算。 Responsiveness, reclaim and background I/O Available RAM and responsiveness describe different things. A machine can have spare memory while a task repeatedly faults pages back in, waits for storage, or enters direct reclaim. zmem uses measured paging and pressure alongside capacity; the pressure label alone is not a desktop-latency measurement. Read a current observation zmem status --json zmem status --json --processes Check observation.source, daemon_active, instance_verification, stale and the sample age first. The active daemon report contains measured rates and policy history. A one-shot preview starts without those rates. Field What it establishes memory.available_bytes The kernel's estimate of available RAM, including reclaimable capacity. psi.memory_full_bp Observed memory stall time, in basis points; 100 bp is 1%. paging.direct_scan_bytes_per_sec The rate of direct page scanning; this is work performed, not bytes successfully freed. paging.anon_refault_bytes_per_sec Anonymous pages becoming active again after eviction, expressed as a byte rate. paging.file_refault_bytes_per_sec File pages returning after eviction; it does not identify a foreground application. controls.swappiness_actual and swappiness_requested Kernel readback and the controller's current request. A missing request is not a successful write. Pressure is also available for individual cgroups. A background service waiting on its own bandwidth limit can contribute I/O stalls while the desktop's I/O pressure remains low. Read the relevant groups before interpreting a global I/O number as a saturated physical drive. Linux documents PSI and the cgroup v2 pressure and I/O interfaces. Avoid an unsupported cache preference File refaults establish that pages were evicted and accessed again. They do not establish that those pages belong to interactive work. A background filesystem scanner can generate refaults while causing anonymous memory to be recycled. Starting with 0.3.1, the reclaim_latency_guard prevents the file-cache and spare-zram paths from increasing swappiness when all three measured conditions hold: Memory full PSI is at least 1%. Direct scanning is at least 64 MiB/s. Anonymous refaults are at least 4 MiB/s. The resulting preference is a ceiling of 60. If the actual kernel value is already lower, the guard retains that lower value. It uses the normal 10-second evidence period, 30-second write interval and maximum change of 20 per ordinary write. Confirmed disk-swap churn retains its existing urgent path. These thresholds are a conservative starting point based on a host observation, not universal kernel recommendations or measurements of mouse latency. If current swappiness cannot be read, zmem skips the write and reports readback_unavailable with a null request. A previously cached value cannot substitute for current readback. The implementation is in swappiness.rs; the kernel's swappiness documentation describes the underlying cost preference. Wait before adding another working set A new compiler or model loader can worsen paging even while disk Swap still has space. Starting with 0.4, zmem run --class background and --class disposable check available RAM and memory PSI before executing the target. The default wait is bounded at 60 seconds, with exit code 75 if conditions do not recover. Interactive commands bypass admission. Use --wait-timeout 300 for a longer batch window or --wait-timeout 0 for a single immediate attempt. The launcher emits JSON events on stderr while waiting, rechecks conditions before admission, and spaces same-user starts. The admission guide explains the thresholds and recovery rule. This gate controls new explicitly submitted work; running-task budgets remain the daemon's responsibility. Keep a persistent Cargo target directory for repeated checks. A fresh temporary target directory discards that directory's compiled-artifact reuse, while excessive concurrent compiler working sets can turn CPU work into paging stalls. Admission and cache reuse address these separate costs. Neither requires a permanent one-core limit on ordinary builds. Make user-session I/O controls available zmem run --class background -- COMMAND requests a lower CPU and I/O weight. For a user scope, its I/O controller must be available through the user manager and its ancestors. A requested IOWeight value alone does not prove that a kernel control exists or that the storage scheduler uses weights. The installer prepares a separately owned user@.service drop-in that adds I/O delegation and accounting. The addition preserves the existing delegated controller list. Its ownership record is separate from the original installation backup, so an upgrade does not change the old backup format. Existing foreign files and later external edits remain preserved during installation and rollback. An already running user manager may retain its earlier controller availability. Follow the install diagnostic; a user-manager refresh can retain running application processes: systemctl --user daemon-reexec Confirm the relevant scope's actual cgroup.controllers, io.stat, io.weight, and any configured io.max afterwards. The installer does not automatically refresh every user's manager. The systemd resource-control manual explains delegation and hierarchical activation. Bound heavy maintenance separately Filesystem deduplication has a storage workload and its own I/O budget. KSM has a memory-scanning workload and zmem's separate registration and pressure gates. Neither operation should be treated as free background work. Per-service IOReadBandwidthMax and IOWriteBandwidthMax can bound an observed storage scanner while retaining its process and progress. Select the physical backing device and read back its actual io.max entry. Unlike a relative weight, a bandwidth cap also limits an otherwise idle device; that is a throughput tradeoff, so zmem does not install one arbitrary cap on all applications. The 0.3.1 acceptance record separates the local filesystem-scanner mitigation from the zmem policy regression tests. It records memory and I/O observations, not an input-latency benchmark or a guarantee that every source of desktop stutter has been removed.

title: Swap lifecycle and explicit memory deduplication
body: 观测 Linux 内存压力，管理 Swap 并约束后台任务的内存预算。 Swap lifecycle and explicit memory deduplication zmem 0.3.0 adds automatic maintenance of its own Swap files and scanning control for explicitly registered KSM workloads. These mechanisms address different resources: Swap maintenance returns eligible disk allocations, while KSM asks the kernel to share identical anonymous memory pages. Filesystem deduplication of active Swap is outside this design. This guide describes the current implementation and its limits. The 0.2.0 host acceptance record remains evidence for that earlier version and its recorded observation windows; it is not a performance test of these additions. Automatic Swap maintenance Growth, cleanup and retirement Operation When it may run What it does Growth The existing memory/Swap policy requests headroom and its pressure, IO, cooldown, disk-space and capacity gates permit it. Requests a full configured chunk, 2 GiB by default, capped by remaining capacity and filesystem reserve. Cleanup The controller is not critical, IO is uncongested and the immediate worker check has sufficient RAM reserve. Attempts to remove one valid owned file without calling swapoff or migrating its pages. The kernel preserves a file that is still active or draining. Active retirement The policy has sustained healthy headroom, and a fresh worker sample passes whole-file RAM and Swap checks. Deactivates one eligible owned file, verifies its identity and inventory again, then attempts ordinary unlink. Maintenance runs only when the daemon has no other worker. Growth takes priority, followed by eligible managed-background reclaim. There are at least 60 seconds between maintenance attempts, including failed or deferred attempts; each attempt selects at most one file. Candidate selection rotates, so a deferred candidate need not monopolize later attempts. A busy machine can defer maintenance indefinitely. This is a maximum action rate, not a promise to free disk space every minute. The maintenance scope is the configured swap_dir, under /var/lib/zmem. Candidates must have zmem's exact zmem-NNNNNN.swap name, be root-owned private regular files with one link, and retain their observed file identity. Symlinks, unrelated files and arbitrary adopted swap devices are not maintenance candidates. Directory traversal is bounded; exceeding the scan limit preserves the files and reports an error. See maintain_swap and its file checks and the maintenance scheduler. Cleanup without draining Swap Cleanup handles retained allocations, including files whose preparation or activation was incomplete. It skips an exact canonical path already listed in the fresh Swap inventory. For the remaining candidates, an absent path does not establish inactivity: an active file created in an older service mount namespace may appear under a different alias. The worker therefore verifies the pinned file identity and performs only an ordinary unlink. Linux's active-swap inode guard makes that final operation refuse an active or draining file. A busy or protected result is recorded as a deferral. Cleanup does not truncate the file, punch holes in it, rewrite its contents, rename it away or apply reflinks or filesystem deduplication. Let R be the effective available-memory reserve. The cleanup gate requires a valid memory sample, available RAM of at least R / 2, memory pressure below the critical threshold, IO full PSI at or below 1%, and no other detected IO congestion. The controller also requires its memory state to be noncritical. This deliberately differs from active retirement: cleanup itself does not bring swapped pages back into RAM. Retirement reserves the entire file The default policy requires 600 seconds of continuously healthy, comfortable conditions before considering active retirement, and at least 600 seconds since the last growth decision. The worker then samples again; earlier permission does not bypass current pressure checks. For a candidate whose charged size is B = max(logical length, allocated blocks), the immediate checks include: Check Required condition Memory PSI some ≤ 2% and full ≤ 1% IO PSI full ≤ 1%, with the policy's IO-congestion gate also satisfied Available RAM At least 2 × R + B Free Swap After subtracting B, at least swap_free_target_mib, 4 GiB by default Known current usage A candidate listed under its exact path with nonzero use is skipped. Subtraction or addition that cannot be represented safely defers the operation. The full B bound matters even for a currently empty file: new pages can be assigned before swapoff, and a legacy alias may hide reliable per-file usage. zmem does not infer a safe migration cost from a matching basename or file size. After a successful deactivation, or a confirmed kernel EINVAL result, the worker may proceed to the same identity, inventory and kernel-guarded unlink checks. EINVAL is not itself proof of inactivity: a concurrent deactivation can still be draining pages. An unconfirmed helper result or another failure preserves the allocation. The host helper uses the pinned file identity in PID 1's mount namespace; the implementation distinguishes syscall errno from setup, protocol and timeout failures. Serialization and accounting All zmem Swap mutations share one protected lock, including allocation, activation, retirement and removal. The descriptor is inherited by allocation commands and syscall helpers. If a helper outlives a worker timeout, it retains exclusion until its actual exit; closing the parent's descriptor does not release the child's lock. This serializes zmem operations. Unrelated administrative tools are not assumed to participate, so identity rechecks and kernel guards still matter. Retained inactive or incomplete owned files remain part of the disk-Swap budget. Each is charged the larger of logical and allocated size. Exact canonical active entries are counted once; uncertain aliases can be charged separately until identity is established. This conservative accounting can temporarily leave less growth room than a pathname-only estimate. Read decisions and outcomes with: zmem status --json journalctl -u zmem.service The journal reports swap_maintenance_idle, swap_maintenance_deferred or swap_file_removed. A removal event identifies the mode, logical bytes, allocated bytes and the kernel-guarded unlink result. Those allocated bytes describe the removed file; they are not a measured net df gain or a responsiveness improvement. Concurrent disk activity and filesystem accounting can change the observed free-space total. Explicit memory deduplication Register at launch Choose trusted workloads with repeated anonymous data, then register them explicitly: zmem run --class background --dedup -- YOUR_TRUSTED_COMMAND zmem run --class disposable --max-memory 2048 --dedup -- YOUR_TRUSTED_BATCH_COMMAND background uses the existing managed memory-budget policy. disposable also accepts an explicit hard limit, where exceeding the limit can terminate the job. --dedup is rejected for the interactive class. Default build routing through zmem run --class background does not add --dedup. The launch helper enables PR_SET_MEMORY_MERGE with value 1, verifies it with PR_GET_MEMORY_MERGE, and then executes the original command. It does not silently run an unregistered command if registration is unsupported, denied or cannot be verified. The kernel registration survives the invocation's fork/exec path; the Linux launcher places it in a marked managed scope so the daemon can discover it. The configuration default is: dedup_enabled = true This permits scanning control for registered tasks. It does not register other applications. Set it to false in the service configuration and restart zmem.service to disable zmem's scanning policy. Changing this setting does not force an unmerge, remove the process registration of an existing task, or disable an externally owned KSM controller. A shared matching domain KSM's matching domain is system-wide, subject to the kernel's existing settings. UID and cgroup boundaries do not create separate deduplication trust domains. When zmem starts an otherwise unowned scanner, it can also scan eligible memory registered by other software. The --dedup marker identifies the jobs zmem registered and observes; it does not restrict the kernel's global matching to those jobs. The kernel merges eligible identical anonymous pages and copies a shared page when a process writes to it. This can save memory, but scanning and later writes have costs. It does not merge file-cache pages or deduplicate the contents of active swap files on disk. Choose registration based on whether the workloads may share this matching domain and whether their observed benefit justifies scanning. See the kernel KSM documentation. Pause first; resume after stable observations The daemon takes ownership only of stopped, compatible KSM controls. Existing unowned scanning, an external advisor or a detected external control change produces externally_managed; zmem does not overwrite that controller's settings. Controls are journaled, compared before writing and read back afterward. For controls it owns, the policy pauses scanning when CPU, memory or IO is busy; required observations are missing; task coverage is incomplete or stale; no registered tasks remain; or dedup control is disabled. Pause means run=0, which preserves existing merged pages. zmem never uses run=2, PR_SET_MEMORY_MERGE=0 or a process-unmerge call as its response to pressure. Restoring owned scan controls also pauses scanning before changing their batch settings. The current busy gates use PSI avg10: CPU some ≥ 5%, memory some ≥ 1% or full ≥ 0.2%, and IO full ≥ 1%. Memory must additionally satisfy the daemon's healthy policy and available-RAM reserve; the IO gate includes detected paging congestion. PSI is waiting time, not CPU utilization. Missing observations are not treated as a quiet machine. Starting or resuming scanning requires 30 seconds of stable, complete observations. A sampling gap beyond the governor's allowance, a clock reversal or a failed write resets that stability history. The fixed settings are pages_to_scan=128 and sleep_millisecs=100, applied while stopped before run=1. These settings bound a scan batch and its sleep interval; they are not a hard CPU quota or a measured maximum CPU percentage. See the governor and adapter. Observe coverage and actual state The daemon refreshes registered-task discovery every 10 seconds. Discovery checks managed scope membership and stable PID identity around each process's KSM observation. It is bounded by process and task limits and does not read command lines, environments or memory contents. Enumeration limits, permission failures or malformed observations make coverage incomplete. status --processes adds the ordinary fresh process list; it does not replace the daemon's cached dedup discovery with a new scan. JSON field Interpretation dedup.state, dedup.target_state, dedup.reason Observed control state, desired next state and the decision reason. A requested pause is not reported as completed if the kernel still reports scanning. dedup.control_owned, dedup.write_succeeded Current validated ownership and the result of a write attempted in this sample. null means no write result is available. dedup.registered_tasks, dedup.tasks Observed registered process leaders and their PID/start-time identities, cgroups and available KSM fields. dedup.task_observation_age_ms, dedup.task_refresh_interval_ms Age and scheduled refresh interval of dedup discovery, separate from the report's sampling age. dedup.coverage_complete, dedup.truncated, dedup.errors Whether discovery completed within its limits, and why a partial result cannot establish complete coverage. ksm.run, ksm.pages_to_scan, ksm.sleep_millisecs, ksm.advisor Observed global kernel settings, rather than assumed policy values. ksm.general_profit_bytes A signed kernel estimate for system-wide KSM memory benefit, including accounting overhead. It may be negative and is not attributable solely to zmem. ksm.pages_sharing, ksm.full_scans, other optional counters Available kernel counters. null means unknown or unsupported; it is not an observed zero. idle with no_registered_tasks is expected until a compatible task is launched and discovered. warming indicates that the stability interval has not yet permitted scanning. paused_pressure includes a reason explaining pressure or incomplete observations. unavailable indicates incomplete or unsupported KSM control observation. Read actual controls, coverage and errors with the state: a plan alone cannot establish that a write succeeded. status --live and plan remain independent previews. They have no daemon task-discovery history and do not establish that scanning has started or that registered-task coverage is complete. Evidence and limits The source supports automatic bounded maintenance and explicit KSM registration with observable pause/resume decisions. It does not guarantee a particular amount of freed disk space, memory savings, reduced SSD wear, desktop latency or application throughput. Repeated data may be absent, merged pages can later change, external KSM work contributes to global counters, and higher-priority memory work can defer maintenance. The existing read-only measurement procedure can record comparable natural-workload windows. A future result must identify the tested version, executable, kernel, workload, KSM ownership and actual task coverage. It should assess latency and useful task progress alongside memory profit, scanning activity and paging. The 0.2.0 measurements do not supply these results for 0.3.0, and this guide claims no new performance measurement.

title: 概览
body:
解析 MIME 消息、头部与正文，并按需解码内容。 zmime A zero-dependency, no_std Rust parser for borrowed MIME message trees. Input is &[u8]; callers supply part storage and decode buffers. The library uses only core, performs no heap allocations, and never decodes an attachment during structure parsing. MSRV: Rust 1.74.0. Default builds use bounded SSE2 scans on x86_64, with runtime-selected AVX2 scans and SSSE3/AVX2 Base64 kernels. Aarch64 uses NEON when the target guarantees it. A private atomic caches CPU capability bits; the first feature detection has a separate cold-start cost. Other targets use the portable implementation. default-features = false selects portable code on every architecture. No build script, C code, FFI, or runtime is required. Parse, inspect, and decode use zmime::{Limits, Message, Part}; let input = b"Subject: Hello
\ Content-Type: multipart/mixed; boundary=demo

\ --demo
Content-Type: text/plain; charset=utf-8

Hello!
\ --demo
Content-Type: application/octet-stream
\ Content-Disposition: attachment; filename=sample.bin
\ Content-Transfer-Encoding: base64

AAEC/w==
\ --demo--
"; let mut workspace = [Part::EMPTY; 8]; let message = Message::parse(input, &mut workspace, Limits::default()).unwrap(); assert_eq!(message.parts().len(), 3); // container, text, attachment assert_eq!(message.root().headers().get(b"subject").unwrap().raw_value(), b" Hello"); let attachment = message.attachments().next().unwrap(); assert_eq!(attachment.raw_body(), b"AAEC/w=="); // borrowed, still encoded let mut decoded = [0u8; 4]; let written = attachment.decode_body(&mut decoded).unwrap(); assert_eq!(&decoded[..written], &[0, 1, 2, 255]); let mut text = [0u8; 32]; assert_eq!(message.parts()[1].text(&mut text).unwrap(), "Hello!"); Use HeaderBlock::parse for validated raw fields only. Use Part::parse_headers to also parse Content-Type, Content-Disposition, and Content-Transfer-Encoding while leaving the complete body opaque. Header names retain their original case; lookup is ASCII case insensitive. raw_value() retains leading whitespace and folds, excluding the final physical line ending. Header::unfolded removes fold CRLF/LF while retaining the following whitespace. use zmime::decode_encoded_words; let mut output = [0u8; 64]; let count = decode_encoded_words(b"=?UTF-8?Q?Caf=C3=A9?=", &mut output).unwrap(); assert_eq!(core::str::from_utf8(&output[..count]).unwrap(), "Café"); Run cargo run --example inspect for an executable example that unfolds and decodes a subject, lists the MIME tree, reads its text, and decodes an attachment on demand. All parsing and decoding buffers in the example have fixed capacity.
