Supported scope Area Behavior RFC 5322 framing Raw fields, duplicate ordinary fields, folding, CRLF and LF; explicit errors for invalid names, controls, orphan folds and missing separators MIME metadata Type/subtype, disposition, ordered parameters, comments, quoted-pairs, default text/plain and multipart/digest rules MIME structure Multipart nesting, identity-encoded message/rfc822, preamble/epilogue, ancestor boundary recognition, borrowed raw entity/body slices Base64 MIME whitespace, strict alphabet, complete quartets, canonical padding and unused-bit validation Quoted-printable Hex escapes, CRLF/LF soft breaks, trailing physical-line whitespace removal, explicit malformed-input errors RFC 2047 B/Q encoded words, adjacent-word whitespace handling, UTF-8 / US-ASCII / ISO-8859-1 Text conversion UTF-8 / US-ASCII / ISO-8859-1; other charset labels return UnsupportedCharset Delayed work Transfer decoding and charset conversion occur only on explicit decode/text calls This is a format parser, with a strict documented subset. It does not parse mailbox address lists or dates into semantic objects, convert HTML to text, or provide a mail server. RFC 2231 extended/continued parameters are available as raw attributes; requesting their decoded values returns Unsupported. Transfer-encoded message/rfc822 requires two explicit steps: parse its headers, decode its body into caller storage, then parse that buffer. Encoded multipart containers are rejected. Missing multipart closing delimiters and duplicate Content-Type/Content-Disposition/Content-Transfer-Encoding fields are errors. Raw binary access does not imply text conversion. Unknown transfer encodings and unsupported charset labels remain inspectable; decoding returns an explicit error instead of substituting text. Invalid attachment encoding is detected when that attachment is read, preserving lazy parsing. Resource and safety contract Limits bounds total input size, header bytes per part, fields per part, physical header line length, total part count, and nesting depth. Defaults are 64 MiB / 256 KiB / 256 fields / 64 KiB per line / 1024 parts / depth 32. The root has depth zero. Nested comments have a fixed depth limit of 16. Applications can tighten these values before accepting untrusted mail. Caller storage may be smaller than the configured limits; exhaustion returns WorkspaceTooSmall. Parsing uses an iterative state machine and one forward body scan. Active ancestor boundaries are checked at line-start delimiter candidates. Worst-case work is bounded by input length times configured nesting depth. No recursion or input-sized stack array is used. A Message is returned only after the complete tree validates. On failure, workspace contents may contain a partial tree; decode outputs may contain a prefix and must be ignored after an error. Only CPU feature detection and optimized scan/codec kernels use unsafe, with local bounds and target feature proofs. The portable implementation is safe Rust. The test suite checks optimized kernels against scalar references, random/truncated inputs and RFC examples. CI runs Miri, platform tests and the independent differential suite. See safety notes for the audit boundary and exact checks. Reproduce the comparison The independent comparison project pins mail-parser = "=1.0.1" and is excluded from the published crate, workspace, and dependency graph. Its toolchain requirement belongs to that project only. It compares validated headers, MIME structure with reused storage, and transfer decoding separately. Each valid fixture must produce the same raw fields, MIME parameters, parent relationships, body bytes, and decoded bytes before timing. Malformed-input recovery policies are recorded without a speed ratio. cargo test --locked cargo test --locked --no-default-features cargo +1.74.0 test --locked cargo test --locked --manifest-path comparison/Cargo.toml cargo run --release --locked --manifest-path comparison/Cargo.toml --bin compare -- \ --samples 9 --target-ms 20 > results.csv python3 comparison/summarize.py results.csv Measurements are machine- and workload-specific. Results include scenarios in which zmime is slower. The supported subset has no full-charset/full-mail performance claim. The measured results contain raw CSV, machine metadata, timing protocol, component ablations, and limits of the evidence. In the recorded complete-metadata comparison, one of eight CRLF structure cases reached 2×; the representative 2× target remains unmet. Tiny and ordinary mail were faster, while large attachments, deep multipart trees, and several decoding workloads remained slower than the pinned reference. The validation record distinguishes executed local checks from hosted CI and publication steps that still require a configured repository. CI and releases CI covers Linux, Windows, macOS, native aarch64, stable, Rust 1.74.0, formatting, clippy, docs, WASM/embedded builds, Miri, package checks and publish dry runs. The published package has no normal, optional, build, dev, or target-specific dependencies. Test programs and the independent comparison project can use std. Portable library builds additionally forbid unsafe at compile time. The manually triggered Benchmark workflow runs the same verified comparison on x86_64 or native aarch64, with SIMD or portable kernels. It uploads paired samples, summaries, and machine context as an Actions artifact. Shared hosted runner measurements are observations, with no fixed speed threshold as a CI gate. Run Release on the repository's default branch with one of none, patch, minor, or major. none publishes the current version or completes an interrupted publication; the other choices update the manifest and lockfiles. The workflow tests the exact release commit, publishes using the repository secret CARGO_REGISTRY_TOKEN, confirms the immutable registry archive, then creates its Git tag and GitHub Release. It directly calls the reusable CI workflow and does not depend on events generated by GITHUB_TOKEN. Existing versions are reused only when archive checksums match. Conflicting tags, different archive contents, yanked versions and untrusted branch/event contexts stop the release. Re-running the same Actions run reuses its version commit; a fresh recovery run should select none. See release guide. Standards and licensing The implementation targets the documented subset of RFC 5322, RFC 2045, RFC 2046, RFC 2047, and RFC 2183. It preserves unsupported RFC 2231 attributes without silently interpreting them. Licensed under either Apache-2.0 or MIT, at your option.

title: Reproducible comparison with mail-parser
body: 解析 MIME 消息、头部与正文，并按需解码内容。 Reproducible comparison with mail-parser This independent workspace compares zmime with mail-parser 1.0.1, pinned in Cargo.toml with transitive versions fixed by Cargo.lock. It does not enter the published crate's dependency graph or package. The comparison needs Rust 1.98 or newer because that is the reference library's minimum version; zmime itself has an independently tested Rust 1.74 minimum. The experiment covers borrowed RFC 5322 headers, MIME structure, and transfer decoding. It makes no full-parser or complete character-set performance claim. Both parsers receive exactly the same generated bytes. Every timed mail fixture first passes an equality check of its part tree, header names and raw values, Content-Type and Content-Disposition parameters, transfer encodings, and raw body bytes. The benchmark stops before timing if those checks fail. The timed consumers also read every supported MIME metadata field and decode every quoted parameter value into reusable scratch space. This includes work that zmime normally defers and mail-parser performs during parsing. Matching consumer checksums are asserted before timing, in addition to the full byte and tree projections; attachment transfer decoding remains separate. Reproduce From the repository root, with cargo, rustc, and Python 3.9+ on PATH: cargo test --locked --manifest-path comparison/Cargo.toml python3 comparison/run.py --output comparison/results/local --samples 9 --target-ms 20 python3 comparison/run.py --portable --output comparison/results/local-portable --samples 9 --target-ms 20 python3 comparison/report.py comparison/results/local comparison/results/local-portable > comparison/RESULTS.md The runner builds both libraries with the same release profile: thin LTO, one codegen unit, and the compiler's default target CPU. On Linux it pins the timed process to one available CPU; --cpu N selects another allowed CPU. On platforms without affinity support, it records that limitation. It records compiler versions, CPU capabilities, source revision, tracked modifications, feature selection, sampling settings, and timing scope in environment.json. The record also includes SHA-256 hashes of implementation and experiment source, benchmark executables, and every generated mail fixture. Collection fails if source or executables change during the run. compare --dump-corpus DIRECTORY validates the corpus and writes its exact .eml files without running timers. Each output directory contains every sample in raw.csv and median, minimum, and maximum timings in summary.csv. The reported ratio is mail_parser_ns / zmime_ns: values above one favor zmime, values below one favor mail-parser. Results with different storage lifecycles have an empty ratio. There is no aggregate score across different modes or input sizes. cold.csv separately measures the first flat-Base64 decode in a fresh process and a subsequent warmed loop for each library. Process creation and buffer preparation are outside those timings. No cold speed ratio is calculated: CPU feature detection, instruction-cache state, and each API's initialization are being observed separately. On x86_64, zmime caches its detected SIMD backend in a private atomic; its first decoding call may be noticeably slower on a virtualized CPU. Both libraries' dispatch caches are warmed in the main results. For a shorter targeted run: cargo run --release --locked --manifest-path comparison/Cargo.toml --bin compare -- \ --filter structure_reuse --samples 9 --target-ms 20 > structure.csv python3 comparison/summarize.py structure.csv Work performed in each mode The reference configuration keeps non-MIME headers in HeaderForm::Raw, matching the raw-header API evaluated here. It still parses Content-Type, Content-Disposition, and Content-Transfer-Encoding. Address lists, dates, Received semantics, RFC 2047 text, and character-set conversion are outside these parse timings. Both libraries preserve those header bytes. Separate differential tests cover the supported RFC 2047 character sets. Mode zmime operation Reference operation Timed output and storage headers Part::parse_headers MessageParser::parse_headers Validate and parse root headers and MIME metadata; consume every raw header and decoded parameter value; body remains opaque. The reference's public headers API allocates its result storage. structure_reuse Message::parse with reusable part storage parse_with with reusable MessageBuffers Complete supported MIME tree and metadata; consume all raw header/body views and decoded parameter values; no attachment decoding. Both receive warmed storage. structure_fresh_reference Message::parse with reusable storage parse with new storage Additional API-lifecycle observation. Storage lifecycles differ; no speed ratio is calculated. transfer_base64 decode_base64 into a caller slice Encoding::Base64.decode_append into a cleared, reserved Vec Decode every encoded byte to the same bytes; output storage is reused. Flat and MIME-wrapped inputs are separate. transfer_qp decode_quoted_printable into a caller slice Encoding::QuotedPrintable.decode_append into a cleared, reserved Vec Decode every byte; plain ASCII and escaped inputs are separate; output storage is reused. The reference builds its body-role indexes as part of parsing. zmime builds its borrowed part records. These internal representation costs remain in the measurements. Construction of the reference parser configuration, fixture generation, workspace creation, output reservation, and equality checks occur outside timed regions. Transfer output is passed to black_box; parse timings also consume header and body views so the compiler cannot discard the results. MIME parameter scratch is reserved outside timing, while parameter traversal and unescaping are timed. Header values are compared and consumed without their final physical line ending because the APIs expose that delimiter differently. Both libraries use lazy transfer decoding. In particular, parsing the large attachment fixture does not decode its Base64 body in either implementation. Using an earlier eager version of mail-parser would measure a different workload; this experiment uses the current 1.0.1 API for that reason. Inputs and correctness coverage The corpus is generated by src/corpus.rs; it contains no personal mail and requires no network downloads. Each mail category has CRLF and LF variants: Category Contents Tiny One header and a one-byte body Ordinary Common RFC 5322 fields, a folded custom field, UTF-8 text Large attachment One MiB of deterministic bytes encoded as wrapped Base64, plus a text part Nested multipart Eight nested multipart containers with sibling parts Newsletter Plain-text and HTML alternatives carried in a multipart container, with quoted-printable content Long headers A logical header with 100 folded lines and approximately 70 KiB of field data Many attachments 128 Base64 attachments with type, disposition, and filename parameters Nested message An unencoded message/rfc822 attachment inside a multipart Additional tests compare 300 generated multipart messages, 96 generated nested trees with quoted-pair filenames and folded metadata, independently encoded arbitrary-byte transfer round trips, supported UTF-8/US-ASCII/Latin-1 encoded words, and 7,200 deterministic random or mutated inputs. These tests supplement the core crate's RFC examples, resource-limit, alignment, buffer, and Miri tests. Generated fixtures exercise controlled features; they do not substitute for long-term validation on a diverse production mail corpus. Malformed and truncated inputs have explicit policy tests and no speed ratios. zmime returns structural errors and rejects malformed transfer encodings on access. mail-parser attempts recovery. For example, mail-parser 1.0.1 accepts unpadded SGVsbG8 and terminal quoted-printable abc= without a problem flag; the strict zmime decoders reject those inputs. Invalid Base64 alphabet and invalid quoted-printable hex are also exercised. Comparing rejection with recovery would measure different tasks. Character-set equivalence is also limited to shared behavior. zmime implements literal ISO-8859-1, while mail-parser maps that label to Windows-1252: an encoded word carrying byte 0x80 produces U+0080 in zmime and € in the reference. A policy regression records that difference. Character-set conversion is absent from parse and transfer timers, and the encoded-word equality cases do not claim equivalence for the differing 0x80–0x9F mapping. The reference behavior is documented on its Charset::Windows1252 variant. Sampling and the SIMD ablation Each pair has 32 warm-up iterations followed by a calibration pass. The same iteration count is used for both libraries, and sample order alternates to reduce order bias. The default records nine paired samples and targets at least 20 ms per sample for the faster library. There is no outlier deletion. The minimum and maximum accompany the median so scheduler variation is visible. --portable disables zmime's SIMD feature while retaining the identical fixtures, compiler profile, reference library, and output checks. Comparing default and portable rows measures the contribution of zmime's scanning and transfer-decoding kernels. The reference continues to select its own available kernels. This ablation does not imply equal instruction sets, and measurements on one CPU do not establish throughput on aarch64, WASM, or another x86_64 processor. Evidence and limits Claim Evidence Scope Timed mail results agree Equality checks run before the first timing Header bytes, metadata, tree, raw bodies in the generated supported subset Attachments remain lazy Parse modes access raw bodies only; transfer modes are separate Both evaluated APIs A measured scenario is faster or slower Median paired samples plus full raw CSV Recorded machine, toolchain, fixture, feature selection SIMD contributes to a result Default/portable runs with unchanged inputs The kernels enabled by zmime's feature Unsupported features are explicit Core API errors and differential policy tests No claim of all mail-parser charsets or all recovery policies The review questions are concrete: does the comparison preserve the same observable result, use a recent fixed baseline, disclose storage lifecycles, retain slow cases, and limit conclusions to measured inputs and hardware? The protocol above addresses each question. No result from this workspace supports a claim that zmime defeats mail-parser's full feature set. The reviewed measurement protocol reads decoded parameter values inside timing. Older 2026-11-10-default and 2026-11-10-portable results retained in this repository used shallower timed consumers. Their pre-timing equality checks were valid, but those rows do not establish the cost of materializing all MIME metadata and are not used for current speed claims. Current results use the reviewed- directories linked from RESULTS.md. Reference APIs and source: mail-parser 1.0.1, upstream repository.

title: Safety and resource model
body: 解析 MIME 消息、头部与正文，并按需解码内容。 Safety and resource model zmime parses untrusted mail into borrowed slices and caller-owned metadata. Its public API is safe Rust; the published crate unconditionally uses #![no_std], imports only core, and declares Rust 1.74 as its minimum supported version. The root manifest has no normal, development, build, optional, or target-specific dependencies. The independent comparison/ workspace uses its own toolchain and dependencies. These boundaries are checked by check_contract.py and the CI workflow. Ownership and bounded work The input, part array, and decoding output belong to the caller. Message::parse fills the supplied &mut [Part]; a successful Message borrows both that storage and the original &[u8]. Raw headers, bodies, attachments, preambles, and epilogues retain slices of the original input. Decoding writes only to the output slice supplied for that call. See message.rs and decode.rs. MIME nesting uses parent indices and an iterative state machine. Every parent index refers to an earlier part, so walking toward the root terminates. Descending consumes a workspace entry and checks the depth and part budgets first. Boundary scanning advances through the body; each candidate is compared with open multipart ancestors. The worst-case work is proportional to input length times permitted depth, and nesting introduces no recursive call frames. Ancestor boundaries also take precedence while a child header block is read, including delimiter strings that resemble ordinary fields. adversarial.rs exercises these cases and the RFC 2046 nesting rules. Limits bounds the amount of input the parser accepts before it consumes additional storage or scans an unbroken header line. Applications can lower the defaults to match their ingress limits. The header-byte budget includes the terminating separator; the physical-line budget excludes CRLF or LF. Resource Default Enforcement Complete message 64 MiB Checked before parsing Header block per part 256 KiB Bounds the scanner's search window Logical fields per part 256 Continuation lines retain their original field Physical header line 64 KiB Bounds each line search; set 998 for the RFC 5322 line-length restriction Tree nodes 1,024 Includes containers and the root Tree depth 32 Root depth is zero Nested comments 16 Fixed iterative limit Multipart boundary 70 bytes Fixed storage and syntax validation The supplied workspace and output slices are additional hard bounds. Insufficient part capacity returns WorkspaceTooSmall; decoding and unfolding return their documented output-capacity errors. A failed tree parse can leave partial metadata in the workspace, and a failed decoder can leave an output prefix. Use decoded bytes only after Ok; header unfolding and parameter unescaping additionally preserve output when capacity is insufficient. These behaviors are tested at exact and undersized capacities in headers.rs, mime.rs, and decode.rs. Instruction selection and shared state SIMD is an optional, default-enabled optimization. x86_64 uses its baseline SSE2 scanners and detects additional capabilities before selecting SSSE3 or AVX2 code. AVX2 selection checks both processor support and the operating system's enabled XMM/YMM state. AArch64 kernels require the target's NEON guarantee. Other targets and default-features = false use portable kernels. Rust requires the features used by an executed function to be supported by its platform; see the Rust Reference. The portable library also declares forbid(unsafe_code) at compile time. This makes the safe-Rust fallback an enforced source constraint. Test-only allocation instrumentation belongs to its separate integration-test crate. The x86 capability cache in cpu.rs is a single AtomicU8. It contains only instruction-capability bits and an initialization bit, with no pointers, mail data, output buffers, or parser state. Relaxed ordering suffices because no associated data is published with those bits; concurrent first calls can repeat feature detection and install an independently valid result. Each message's mutable parsing state remains in its own caller-provided workspace. Unsafe access arguments Unsafe code is confined to CPU detection and private instruction kernels. Every unsafe site includes its local preconditions. The memory-access arguments below apply independently of whether an input is well-formed mail; malformed octets return to the scalar validator without relaxing those bounds. Kernel Preconditions and exact access bounds SSE2 / NEON byte search A vector load requires 16 remaining input bytes. A group of four loads requires 64. Loads are unaligned, read-only, and originate from the live input slice. The tail uses safe portable code. SSE2 / NEON header-control scan Each vector load is guarded by 16 remaining input bytes. It returns the first forbidden byte and never writes memory. AVX2 byte/control scan Each load requires 32 available bytes; the byte-search group of four loads requires 128. Runtime detection establishes AVX2 and OS state support before the kernel is called. Both scanners are read-only and use bounded portable tails. SSSE3 Base64 Each vector read requires 16 input bytes and capacity for 12 output bytes. A fully valid block writes exactly eight plus four bytes. A prefix of three complete validated quartets writes exactly eight plus one byte, within the same 12-byte capacity guard. Other partial prefixes use a fixed 16-byte local array and a bounded slice copy. AVX2 Base64 Each vector read requires 32 input bytes and capacity for 24 output bytes. A fully valid block writes exactly 16 plus eight bytes. A prefix of three complete validated quartets writes exactly eight plus one byte, within the same 24-byte capacity guard. Other partial prefixes use a fixed 32-byte local array and copy only complete decoded quartets. Constant-table loads read complete 16-byte arrays. NEON Base64 Each interleaved load requires 64 input bytes and capacity for 48 output bytes. A fully valid block writes exactly 48 bytes; a partial prefix is packed into a fixed 48-byte local array and copied using bounded slices. The validity mask occupies a fixed 16-byte local array. SSE2 / NEON quoted-printable literal scan Each read requires 16 available bytes. Only printable literal runs are returned; escapes, line endings, and tails stay in the scalar decoder. CPU detection CPUID is available on x86_64. XGETBV is called only after OSXSAVE and AVX are advertised; AVX2 additionally requires XCR0 to enable XMM/YMM state and the AVX2 capability bit. These operations read processor state and do not access message memory. Input and output cannot overlap through these safe APIs because the decoder holds an immutable input slice and an exclusive mutable output slice simultaneously. SIMD emits only complete validated quartets, including valid prefixes before a fold, and may skip permitted MIME whitespace between those prefixes. Separate input-consumed and output-written counters keep whitespace from being counted as decoded data. Split quartets, padding, malformed bytes, and short tails return to the scalar state machine. Base64 padding bits are checked, and a short output receives an explicit capacity error. The implementation is in scan.rs and decode_simd.rs. UTF-8 and ASCII text decoding can use these same bounded Base64 stores because their decoded byte length is unchanged. Each produced prefix is passed through the character validator before decoding continues. UTF-8 continuation state survives vector boundaries and MIME folds. If output capacity is exhausted, the scalar path still validates the remaining decoded text and counts the exact required length. Latin-1 conversion uses the scalar sink because its UTF-8 output can expand. Quoted-printable's hexadecimal lookup and eight-byte literal copies use checked Rust array and slice operations; they add no unsafe sites. Evidence and reproduction The following instruction paths have been executed under Miri during development. Miri checks the Rust memory and intrinsic rules along the tested paths; finite test coverage complements the local bounds arguments. Its scope is described in the Miri documentation. Path Observed validation Portable parsing and decoding All 64 tests passed under strict-provenance Miri on the reviewed implementation, including headers, nested/adversarial input, decoding, and zero-allocation checks SSE2 scanner Reference-comparison tests passed under Miri on x86_64 NEON scanner All three scanner reference tests passed under strict-provenance Miri targeting aarch64 AVX2 scanner Three reference-comparison tests passed under strict-provenance Miri with +avx2 SSSE3 Base64 All seven base64_ tests passed with Miri configured for +ssse3,-avx2 AVX2 Base64 All seven base64_ tests passed with Miri configured for +avx2 NEON Base64 Two vector tests and the MIME whitespace/line-length test passed under aarch64 Miri SIMD text validation All five body_text_ tests passed under strict-provenance Miri for SSSE3, AVX2, and aarch64 NEON, including malformed text after output exhaustion SSE2 / NEON QP scan All byte values at each position 0–31 passed under Miri on both targets CPU detection Native calls exercise CPUID/XGETBV and the atomic cache. Miri selects capabilities from its target-feature configuration; it does not execute the host-detection path. The scanner tests compare every result with a scalar reference across lengths and alignments. Native header-control tests exhaust all 256 byte values; Miri uses control, whitespace, DEL, and high-bit boundary classes to bound interpreter time. Codec tests cover exact output bounds, tails, alignment, every byte in vector positions, deterministic generated data, malformed encodings, and truncation. comparison/ independently checks the supported semantic subset against its pinned mail-parser version. ci.yml runs the portable, native, differential, and Miri gates. Reproduce the principal safety checks from the repository root: cargo +1.74.0 test --locked --all-targets cargo test --locked --all-targets --no-default-features cargo test --locked --manifest-path comparison/Cargo.toml MIRIFLAGS=-Zmiri-strict-provenance cargo +nightly miri test --locked --lib --tests --no-default-features MIRIFLAGS=-Zmiri-strict-provenance cargo +nightly miri test --locked --lib --target aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu scan::tests RUSTFLAGS='-C target-feature=+avx2' MIRIFLAGS=-Zmiri-strict-provenance cargo +nightly miri test --locked --lib scan::tests RUSTFLAGS='-C target-feature=+ssse3,-avx2' cargo +nightly miri test --locked --test decode base64_ RUSTFLAGS='-C target-feature=+avx2' cargo +nightly miri test --locked --test decode base64_ cargo +nightly miri test --locked --test decode --target aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu base64_ Native runtime dispatch selects the available host backend. Setting compiler flags to +ssse3,-avx2 does not force native dispatch to ignore an AVX2-capable CPU; the Miri configuration above explicitly selects SSSE3 for interpretation. Interpretation boundaries Structure parsing is lazy: it validates framing and MIME metadata while retaining encoded body slices. Part::decode_body performs transfer decoding on request; Part::text additionally converts UTF-8, US-ASCII, or ISO-8859-1. Other character sets return UnsupportedCharset. RFC 2047 B/Q words use the same explicit charset policy. Tests verify that an unread invalid Base64 attachment does not force decoding during tree construction. The supported header subset preserves arbitrary field names and raw values without interpreting address lists or dates. RFC 2231 extended parameter bytes remain accessible, and requesting their decoded interpretation returns Unsupported. Transfer-encoded message containers require an explicit decode into a separate caller buffer before parsing that buffer; transfer-encoded multipart containers return an explicit error. These boundaries also constrain performance claims: the comparison methodology defines equivalent work for each reported mode. Claim–evidence review Claim Evidence Status The published core requires no allocator or third-party dependency Manifest, #![no_std], source imports, allocation-counting test, package/dependency contract check, embedded target build gate Enforced by source and CI checks Input cannot create recursive stack growth or unbounded metadata allocation Iterative parent chain, caller workspace, explicit budgets, depth/workspace regression tests Implemented and tested SIMD reads and writes stay within the caller's slices Per-site access proofs, exact-capacity tests, scalar comparisons, Miri runs listed above Supported for the exercised kernels Unsupported character sets are explicit Charset dispatch and unsupported-charset regressions Implemented and tested Full MIME/charset equivalence is outside the stated subset Explicit unsupported cases and mode-specific comparison eligibility Scope documented Maintenance review: contribution—does the change improve this bounded parsing API? clarity—are ownership, offsets, and error behavior still explicit? experimental strength—does an optimization have reproducible measurements? coverage—were all affected backends and malformed tails exercised? design soundness—do every feature and memory-access precondition still hold? The relevant tests and bounds arguments must change with the implementation.

title: 概览
body: 原生插件 ABI、动态库加载与可选 Wasm 沙箱。 zplugin Define a Rust trait, implement it in a cdylib, and call it through a typed host proxy. zplugin uses a frozen target-platform C ABI, cached function tables, and explicit library lifetimes. The default runtime is no_std, needs no allocator, and has zero third-party runtime dependencies. Its native system loader is shared with the Project Z zsys crate through the allocation-free dylib feature. The same interface also generates C/C++ headers; Zig imports a module translated from those headers. Additive extension records support checked structs/enums, owned resources, callbacks, and cross-library tasks that the Rust host can .await. For untrusted plugins, enable the separate wasm backend: validated Wasm32 bytecode, no host imports, finite execution fuel, and bounded guest memory. Native .so/.dylib/.dll loading still requires trusted code. Rust 1.95 or newer; edition 2024. Development toolchain: 1.100.0, the stable release published on 2026-11-12. Native loading targets Linux, macOS, and Windows; see the 0.3.0 delivery record for tested machines and compiler combinations. This is a library of primitives, with no background watcher, executor, transport, or plugin discovery service. Native loading, the optional Wasm host and the allocator-free Wasm guest SDK share the Rust 1.95 baseline required by zsys. Older release evidence remains linked above; new platform verification belongs to this version's CI run. Install Shared interface crate: [dependencies] zplugin = { version = "0.3.1", features = ["macros"] } Plugin and host crates can enable std independently. The interface itself may remain no_std. The optional procedural macro depends on syn, quote, and proc-macro2 at compile time; these are not linked into the runtime. Define an interface #[zplugin::interface(id = "example.calculator", version = 1)] pub trait Calculator { fn add(&mut self, a: u64, b: u64) -> Result<u64, zplugin::Error>; fn copy(&self, input: &[u8], output: &mut [u8]) -> Result<u64, zplugin::Error>; } The macro generates CalculatorApi, CalculatorBinding, CalculatorProxy, and CalculatorExport<T>. Argument names may change; method order, names, receiver kind, types, and results define the frozen interface. Change its version when changing that contract. Implement a plugin Use the shared interface crate as a dependency and configure the plugin: [lib] crate-type = ["cdylib"] [dependencies] zplugin = { version = "0.3.1", features = ["std", "macros"] } calculator-api = { path = "../calculator-api" } use calculator_api::{Calculator, CalculatorExport}; use zplugin::{Error, Result}; struct Implementation; impl Calculator for Implementation { fn add(&mut self, a: u64, b: u64) -> Result<u64> { Ok(a.wrapping_add(b)) } fn copy(&self, input: &[u8], output: &mut [u8]) -> Result<u64> { if output.len() < input.len() { return Err(Error::BufferTooSmall); } output[..input.len()].copy_from_slice(input); Ok(input.len() as u64) } } fn create() -> Result<Implementation> { Ok(Implementation) } zplugin::export!(CalculatorExport<Implementation>, constructor = create, version = (1, 0, 0), unload = pinned); The pinned policy keeps the image resident until process exit. To opt into cooperative unloading, implement the unsafe zplugin::export::UnloadSafe contract for the implementation, use unload = cooperative, and select the same policy when loading. The complete runnable example contains that implementation. Load and call use calculator_api::CalculatorApi; use zplugin::{Plugin, UnloadPolicy}; // SAFETY: this file and its dependencies are trusted, and obey the v1 ABI. let library = unsafe { Plugin::load_path("./libcalculator.so", UnloadPolicy::Pinned)? }; let mut calculator = CalculatorApi::create(&library)?; assert_eq!(calculator.add(20, 22)?, 42); let mut output = [0; 64]; let count = calculator.copy(b"hello", &mut output)?; assert_eq!(&output[..count as usize], b"hello"); # Ok::<(), zplugin::Error>(()) Use .dylib on macOS and .dll on Windows. load_path preserves native Unicode paths. Without std, Plugin::load(&CStr) is available; on Windows its narrow path uses the ANSI code page, and Plugin::load_wide accepts UTF-16 without alloc. The proxy borrows its library, so Rust rejects dropping that library first. For an independent owning proxy, enable alloc, put the plugin in Rc<Plugin>, and call CalculatorApi::wrap(Plugin::create_owned(&library, CalculatorApi::SPEC)?). Cloning occurs when acquiring resources; ordinary calls do not clone a lease. Run the complete example The repository includes separate interface, plugin, and host crates: cargo build --release -p demo-plugin cargo run --release -p demo-host -- target/release/libdemo_plugin.so --self-test On macOS substitute libdemo_plugin.dylib; on Windows use demo_plugin.dll. See examples/README.md for the directory structure, full Cargo configuration, explicit snapshot/restore, and owned outputs. Supported boundaries Rust interface type Boundary representation u8/u16/u32/u64, i8/i16/i32/i64, f32/f64 Fixed-width C ABI scalar &[u8], &mut [u8] Pointer and native size_t length; one call only &str Validated UTF-8 view; one call only Result<T, zplugin::Error> / zplugin::Result<T> Signed status plus initialized success output () or scalar success No output or fixed-width result record zplugin::OwnedBytes success Buffer, origin release callback, independent library lease Plugin object Opaque plugin allocation and matching destroy function #[zplugin::abi_type] struct or enum Recursive C-layout record or checked tag/payload; independent of Rust layout zplugin::OwnedResource success Versioned opaque resource with call/release table and independent library lease zplugin::CallbackRef<'_> input Borrowed callback with explicit retain/invoke/release protocol zplugin::OwnedTask<T> success Task handle with poll/cancel/release; host receives Task<T>: Future with alloc Unsupported signatures produce compile errors: generics, direct async fn, default methods, associated types, conditional methods, usize/isize, bool/char, 128-bit integers, unannotated structs, native String/Vec/Box/Arc, and native Future layouts. Stable values require Copy + Clone; reference, owned, generic and array fields are excluded. Task outputs use AbiValue, including nested structs/enums and unit. Plugin internals may use ordinary Rust facilities and dependencies. Asynchronous and cross-language plugins The interface declares a task factory, so borrowed input ends at the factory call: #[zplugin::interface(id = "example.jobs", version = 1)] pub trait Jobs { fn start(&mut self, input: u64) -> zplugin::Result<zplugin::OwnedTask<u64>>; } # #[cfg(feature = "alloc")] struct Worker; # #[cfg(feature = "alloc")] impl Jobs for Worker { fn start(&mut self, input: u64) -> zplugin::Result<zplugin::OwnedTask<u64>> { Ok(zplugin::OwnedTask::new(async move { Ok(input.wrapping_add(1)) })) } } The generated host proxy returns a lease-owning Task<u64>: use jobs.start(41)?.await?, or cancel() for cooperative cancellation. Polling, cancelling and destruction stay on the creating thread; retained wakers support concurrent notification. No native Future or Waker layout crosses the boundary. The plugin manages any runtime it needs. Dropping a future does not implicitly shut down an external executor; cooperative unloading requires workers and callback return paths to be fully joined/drained. JobsApi::write_c_header(&mut writer) emits the exact argument layouts, method signatures and descriptor helpers. C11 and C++17 include the header; Zig uses its automatically translated module. The generator itself writes through core::fmt::Write without needing an allocator. python3 scripts/async.py python3 scripts/foreign.py --install-zig See the async three-crate example, the complete C/C++/Zig example, and the extension protocol and ownership rules. Features Feature Additional capability Runtime dependency default: none ABI, native loader, borrowed instances, manual resource/factory contracts core and Project Z zsys/dylib alloc Factories, Rc leases, owned bytes/resources, closure callbacks, Future/Waker adapters Rust allocator std Native paths, error integration, panic containment std, implies alloc macros Trait-to-ABI generation Compilation-only macro crate hot-reload Bounded generations and request leases alloc wasm Import-free, fuel-metered Wasm32 sandbox; separate byte-buffer protocol alloc + Wasmi 2.0 and its dependencies; Rust 1.95+ For allocator-free plugins, implement the public ABI with application-owned object storage. export::Object<T> and the entrypoint guards also work without an allocator. Convenience export! factories deliberately require alloc. Untrusted Wasm plugins The host opts in explicitly; the default native runtime depends only on Project Z zsys: [dependencies] zplugin = { version = "0.3.1", features = ["wasm"] } use zplugin::wasm::{Interface, Limits, Plugin}; let interface = Interface { id: 0x7a70_6c75_6769_6e01, version: 1 }; // bytes is an untrusted binary Wasm module; this API is safe to call. let mut plugin = Plugin::new(&bytes, interface, Limits::default())?; let mut output = [0; 64]; let written = plugin.call(1, b"hello", &mut output)?; assert_eq!(&output[..written], b"HELLO"); # Ok::<(), zplugin::wasm::Error>(()) Implement wasm_guest::Guest, export it with export_wasm!, and compile for wasm32-unknown-unknown. The complete guest and host run with: rustup target add wasm32-unknown-unknown python3 scripts/wasm.py Wasm calls use numeric operations and bounded byte buffers. Input/output are copied across the memory boundary; native trait proxies, handles, callbacks, and async tasks are not forwarded into the sandbox. No WASI, filesystem, network, environment, clock or process capabilities are granted. Module imports and start sections are rejected. A trap exhausts/invalidates that instance, not the native host's call stack; subsequent use returns Poisoned. This is an in-process Wasm sandbox whose isolation depends on the engine. Guest-memory limits do not cap process RSS, and fuel is not a compilation-time deadline. Use additional OS process isolation for strict total-memory/time bounds or protection against engine vulnerabilities. See protocol, policy and evidence. Reproducible sandbox timings and allocation measurements are in the 0.3.0 Wasm performance report. Multiple interfaces and hot switching export_interfaces! exports independently versioned interfaces through one entry: zplugin::export_interfaces!(version = (1, 0, 0), unload = cooperative; CalculatorExport<Implementation> => create, SnapshotExport<State> => create_state, ); With hot-reload, hot::Generations::new(plugin, maximum_retired) tracks the current image and old generations. current() acquires a request/session lease. reload or reload_path loads an independent image, runs your creation/restore closure, and switches only on success. Old objects continue using their old code. Use an explicitly versioned byte snapshot for state migration. collect() asks unreferenced cooperative generations to retire; Busy generations remain and count toward the limit. No timeout forces an unload. Safety and performance Loading trusted native code remains unsafe: initializers and methods execute with the host's privileges. ABI checks detect incompatible metadata; native code must still honor memory validity, ownership, and unwind contracts. Proxies are neither Send nor Sync; all calls, including shared trait methods, require a mutable proxy. Same-object raw reentry returns Busy before a second borrow. Under std and an unwind-enabled plugin build, adapters catch Rust panics on the plugin side and poison that instance. panic=abort, foreign exceptions, and native crashes retain their process-level behavior. C++ plugins contain their own exceptions before returning; the C++ example includes that boundary. Task/callback extensions use independent size/version-prefixed tables. Failed resource cleanup prevents cooperative unloading, including a future or callback capture destructor that panics. Steady native borrowed calls use cached function pointers without forced allocation, serialization, symbol lookup, or per-call reference counting. Actual comparisons against inline/noinline calls, cached C pointers and cached libloading symbols are in the 0.2.0 performance report, including three raw runs, task initialization, reused/changed wakers, and worker shutdown. An inline static call remains a distinct, cheaper baseline for tiny functions. Validation and release python3 scripts/check.py python3 scripts/check.py --cross-version python3 scripts/legacy.py python3 scripts/foreign.py --install-zig python3 scripts/wasm.py python3 tools/bench/run.py docs/benchmarks/v0.2.0 python3 tools/bench/extensions.py CI runs actual hosts and dynamic libraries on Linux, macOS, and Windows, plus Rust 1.95.0/stable, core-only embedded/WASM compilation, negative macro fixtures, and release transaction tests. Wasm also runs on all three native host platforms, with Rust 1.95 MSRV/no_std checks and independently built guest/host pairs. The manual release workflow supports patch/minor/major/custom, dry_run, exact-commit validation, dependency-ordered publication, and recovery after a partial upload. It uses the step-scoped CARGO_REGISTRY_TOKEN secret. See release operations. Further detail: ABI and ownership, validation evidence, changelog. Licensed MIT OR Apache-2.0.

title: zplugin 0.3.0：不可信 Wasm 插件交付报告
body: 原生插件 ABI、动态库加载与可选 Wasm 沙箱。 zplugin 0.3.0：不可信 Wasm 插件交付报告 日期：2026-11-13，Asia/Taipei。 结论与范围 zplugin 0.3.0 和 zplugin-macros 0.3.0 已发布到 crates.io，并通过公开包的独立安装验收。 本轮增加可选的 Wasm 沙箱加载后端，用于运行不可信插件；原生动态库加载仍只适用于可信代码。 发布提交为 d10e9082495c8dafa2b0b0f3d19810cf5926ef02， 同一提交经过验证、打包、创建 tag 和发布，没有跳过发布门禁。 路径 适用插件 本轮交付与边界 原生动态库 可信 Rust、C、C++、Zig 插件 保留既有同步、异步任务、稳定值、资源和回调；不提供恶意代码隔离 可选 Wasm 遵循 zplugin Wasm v1 协议的核心 Wasm32 二进制 校验模块、拒绝全部导入和 start section、限制执行预算和客体资源；安全的宿主加载 API 任意 Wasm 应用 WASI、依赖 JavaScript 的 wasm-bindgen、Component Model 等 本版不支持；文件扩展名为 .wasm 不等于协议兼容 Wasm 边界只传操作码和字节缓冲，不向客体暴露宿主地址、分配器、函数指针或 Rust 布局。 没有链接文件、网络、环境变量、时钟、进程或 WASI 能力。各实例拥有独立状态，宿主类型 为 !Send + !Sync，通过可变借用串行调用。插件可以保留自己收到的数据；不同租户或 机密会话应使用新实例，不能把实例复用理解为数据遗忘。 使用 宿主显式启用沙箱： [dependencies] zplugin = { version = "0.3.0", features = ["wasm"] } use zplugin::wasm::{Interface, Limits, Plugin}; let interface = Interface { id: 0x7a70_6c75_6769_6e01, version: 1 }; let mut plugin = Plugin::new(&bytes, interface, Limits::default())?; let mut output = [0; 64]; let written = plugin.call(1, b"hello", &mut output)?; assert_eq!(&output[..written], b"HELLO"); # Ok::<(), zplugin::wasm::Error>(()) 这里的 bytes 是已按模块大小上限读取的二进制。操作 1 是示例插件的转大写方法， 不是库内置的业务功能。完整客体实现 使用 wasm_guest::Guest 和 export_wasm!，无需分配器； 宿主示例包含有界文件读取与失败用例。 rustup target add wasm32-unknown-unknown python3 scripts/wasm.py 默认/core 与原生运行时仍是 no_std、零第三方运行时依赖，MSRV 为 Rust 1.85。 可选 wasm 宿主需要 Rust 1.86，隐式启用 alloc、不隐式启用 std，增加 Wasmi 2.0.0 及其依赖共 8 个第三方运行时包。开发与稳定版 CI 使用 Rust 1.100.0、edition 2024。 编译期宏依赖与运行时依赖继续分开，不将“默认零依赖”宣传成“所有功能零依赖”。 限制和错误处理 资源 默认上限 模块二进制 4 MiB，解析前检查 客体线性内存 16 MiB，最多一个 memory 表元素 4,096，最多一个 table 输入、输出协商容量 各 1 MiB 执行预算 10,000,000 fuel；所有元数据查询共享一次预算，每次业务调用重新赋予预算 解释器值栈、调用深度 64 KiB、128 层 内存偏移、长度、缓冲区重叠、接口 ID/版本及输出长度都经过检查。调用前清零允许写入的 客体输出区；仅在成功且长度合法后复制回宿主。任何错误都保持调用者输出不变。 业务错误不自动作废实例；trap、预算耗尽或非法成功长度会将实例永久标记为 Poisoned。 释放实例不执行客体析构代码。超限 memory.grow/table.grow 返回 Wasm 的正常失败值， 允许客体自行处理。 这是依赖 Wasmi 正确性的进程内沙箱，不是操作系统进程隔离。客体内存上限不是整个宿主 RSS 上限；fuel 不限制解析/编译的墙钟时间，也不消除引擎漏洞、宿主 OOM 或硬件侧信道。 高风险多租户服务仍应叠加独立进程/容器与系统资源策略，并限制并发实例和编译请求数量。 没有声称此适配层或 Wasmi 2.0 经过独立安全审计。 Wasm 当前是同步字节缓冲协议。既有原生异步任务、waker、资源句柄、回调和 trait 代理 不会自动跨入沙箱；也未提供 WASI 授权或宿主调用桥。任何语言只要生成相同协议可兼容， 但本轮实际交付的 Wasm SDK 和独立编译示例是 Rust。现有 C/C++/Zig 生成器仍面向原生 ABI。 测试证据 正式发布工作流 43382342689 的计划、8 个验证作业和发布作业，合计 10 个作业全部成功。 验证 实际结果 Wasm 契约与对抗输入 30 项通过：畸形模块、类型错误、导入/start 拒绝、ABI/偏移/长度、fuel、栈、memory/table、trap、状态隔离及变异输入 Cargo feature 合并 显式启用引擎 memory64 后，适配层仍拒绝 memory64；回归测试通过 真实 Rust Wasm 插件 每个平台执行 8 组自检，含空、64 B、4 KiB、1 MiB、状态、错误、无限循环和 trap 独立 title: C, C++, and Zig plugins
body: 原生插件 ABI、动态库加载与可选 Wasm 沙箱。 C, C++, and Zig plugins The shared Rust interface is the source of truth for every language. ForeignApi::write_c_header generates the argument records, return records, complete method signatures, stable value layouts, and descriptor initializers. C11 and C++17 include the resulting header. Zig imports the module produced by zig translate-c from that same header. Run the complete example From the repository root, with Rust and Python 3.12 or newer: python scripts/foreign.py --install-zig The script downloads the official Zig archive into target/, verifies its pinned SHA-256 checksum before extraction, generates the declarations, builds three native dynamic libraries, and loads all three with the Rust host. The compiler pins are Zig 0.15.2 on macOS and Zig 0.17.1 on Linux/Windows. It uses the platform C/C++ compilers when available on Linux and macOS; Zig's C/C++ drivers provide the Windows fallback. No compiler or runtime is added to the published Rust runtime dependencies. The macOS pin is a compiler compatibility choice. Zig 0.17.1's native macOS translate-c exceeded the 300-second command deadline in CI, before any Zig plugin could be built or loaded. This is a translation-stage failure, not a failing plugin ABI assertion. The macOS job still generates declarations, builds and loads all three native libraries, and must pass the same contracts; no language test is skipped. On macOS, Zig emits position-independent object code with its compiler helpers, and the platform C driver links the final .dylib against the installed Apple SDK. This separates Zig code generation from SDK library resolution; the older Zig linker's unresolved libSystem symbols were observed in CI. Linux and Windows use Zig's shared-library linker directly. To use an existing installation matching the platform's pinned version: python scripts/foreign.py --zig /path/to/zig Build products and the generated foreign.h / foreign.zig files are in target/foreign/. The test writes machine, compiler, and contract results to artifacts/foreign-<platform>.json only after all three libraries pass. CI runs the same script on Linux, macOS, and Windows for stable Rust. Generate declarations for your interface interface/src/lib.rs contains ordinary shared Rust definitions: #[zplugin::abi_type(id = "foreign.point", version = 1)] #[derive(Clone, Copy)] pub struct Point { pub x: i32, pub y: i32, } #[zplugin::interface(id = "my.plugin", version = 1)] pub trait Calculator { fn add(&mut self, point: Point) -> zplugin::Result<i64>; } In a small build tool that depends on the shared crate, call CalculatorApi::write_c_header(&mut writer). The writer implements core::fmt::Write; the generator itself does not require alloc or std. The example host exposes this operation directly: cargo run --locked -p zplugin-foreign-tests -- --header target/foreign/foreign.h The C header names each method's input record Foreign_<method>_args and its output Foreign_<method>_out. Fields are arg_0, arg_1, and so on. Foreign_<method>_METHOD(function) initializes a method entry with its exact generated signature. Foreign_INTERFACE_INIT(methods, create, destroy) initializes the complete interface descriptor. The plugin exports only the version-fixed zplugin_entry_v1 entry required by the loader. plugin.c implements these adapters in C11. plugin.cpp compiles the shared implementation as C++17 and contains an exception boundary that invalidates the affected object. plugin.zig implements the same methods in Zig. Its C declarations are generated by the following build operation, which scripts/foreign.py executes automatically: zig translate-c -lc -I target/foreign examples/foreign/zig_api.h The command writes a Zig module to stdout. The test script saves it as foreign.zig and supplies it as the cabi module when compiling plugin.zig. Translation and compilation use the same native target. For cross-compilation, both operations and the Rust host must use matching target ABI settings. Contracts exercised Interface operation Wire representation and assertion calculate Named Point struct and validated u32 enum; sum and product echo Tagged union with empty, numeric, and nested-struct payloads; all variants round-trip transform Borrowed input and caller-owned output; empty input, short output, unchanged short buffer owned Origin-allocated bytes and matching release function; retained after the object drops start Independent task handle; Pending, retained waker, wake, Ready, cancellation, release resource Typed opaque resource; ID/version checks, operation dispatch, independent library lease callback Borrowed callback with explicit retain/invoke/release; Rust panic becomes an error and poisons the callback The task examples intentionally wake during the first poll and complete on the next poll. This tests the cross-library poll/waker protocol without relying on timer scheduling; the task performs no blocking wait. Rust worker-thread tests cover delayed cross-thread wakeups separately. General callbacks and resource calls remain serialized on the creating thread. The waker protocol alone permits concurrent wake/retain/release operations. Ownership and trust The caller owns borrowed input and output buffers for the duration of a call. Each returned buffer, resource, and task owns its origin allocation and must invoke its matching release function. The host wrappers keep the library loaded until those releases finish. A stored waker or callback must first be retained and later released exactly once. The examples count every plugin-owned allocation; cooperative quiescence returns Busy until that count reaches zero. Output records are initialized only on success. A successful task poll initializes its typed output only when its state is Ready. C/C++ and Zig implementations must initialize the selected tagged-union payload, reject unknown tags, contain exceptions or panics before an ABI return, and obey pointer, aliasing, thread, and descriptor-size contracts. Native libraries run with the host process's privileges; ABI validation provides compatibility checks, not execution isolation.

title: Run the independent native plugin example
body: 原生插件 ABI、动态库加载与可选 Wasm 沙箱。 Run the independent native plugin example The interface, implementation and host are separate Cargo packages. The host depends on the interface package, and loads the implementation only at runtime. cargo build -p demo-plugin cargo run -p demo-host -- target/debug/libdemo_plugin.so On macOS pass target/debug/libdemo_plugin.dylib. On Windows pass target/debug/demo_plugin.dll. With no argument, demo-host chooses the correct filename for the current platform. interface/src/lib.rs is no_std. Its #[zplugin::interface] declaration produces the typed host proxy and plugin adapter. plugin/Cargo.toml requests a cdylib; plugin/src/lib.rs implements the ordinary Rust trait and exports the versioned entry. host/src/main.rs demonstrates scalar calls, caller-owned output buffers, UTF-8 input, versioned snapshots, and a plugin-owned buffer that outlives its creating object. The plugin promises cooperative unloading through an explicit unsafe UnloadSafe implementation. It has no background activity or external registrations. A plugin with threads, tasks or callbacks must retire all such activity before making this promise. The host's unsafe load is the trust boundary. Build variants for generation tests Use separate target directories so the artifacts have independent paths: cargo build -p demo-plugin --target-dir target/first cargo build -p demo-plugin --features v2 --target-dir target/second cargo build -p demo-plugin --features fail-init --target-dir target/rejected The first version uppercases ASCII bytes; v2 lowercases them. Both preserve the same v1 application interface and snapshot schema. fail-init returns plugin status 1001 during instance construction, which exercises failed-switch rollback. All three are test variants, independent of the published crate version. Reproduce performance measurements cargo build --release -p demo-plugin --features instrument cargo run --release -p zplugin-bench -- target/release/libdemo_plugin.so Use the platform-specific library extension above. instrument adds a counting allocator inside the plugin; the benchmark also counts host allocations. The normal example does not enable this instrumentation. Raw CSV includes sample quantiles, allocation counts, Rust version, build flags and Linux RSS measurements. See docs/performance.md for the measured results and interpretation.

title: ABI v1 and ownership
body: 原生插件 ABI、动态库加载与可选 Wasm 沙箱。 ABI v1 and ownership Contract and evidence zplugin v1 connects independently compiled trusted modules on the same target platform and C ABI. The stable boundary consists of repr(C) records, fixed integer/float fields, pointers, native size_t lengths, and extern "C" functions. Rust trait objects and Rust container layouts never cross it. Rust's reference documents both the C representation and native library output types. The executable contract is src/abi.rs, the generator, and the real-library tests. the 0.2.0 delivery record records tested compiler/platform combinations. ABI compatibility also requires the same architecture, endianness, pointer width, target calling convention, system library requirements and CPU instruction support. A Linux build is not a Windows or macOS artifact. Discovery and versioning The fixed symbol is zplugin_entry_v1; its type is unsafe extern "C" fn() -> *const Header. The returned pointer must be nonnull, aligned and readable for the complete 16-byte v1 header. This minimal readability is part of loading trusted native code. Arbitrary address validity cannot be established by a metadata check. Header field Type Rule magic u64 0x315f4e4947554c50 major u16 Exactly 1 minor u16 Additive descriptor evolution only; current value 0 size u32 Bytes readable from the descriptor pointer The host checks this header before reading the plugin version, flags, interface array or quiescence callback. Descriptors shorter than the full v1 prefix are rejected. Future descriptor suffixes may be ignored; v1 prefix fields retain their offsets and meaning. Unknown flag bits are ignored; cooperative unloading requires its known flag and a present callback. An interface array contains pointers to immutable InterfaceDescriptor records. Each starts with a u32 size. The loader reads that prefix before accessing its ID, application version, method array, create or destroy functions. Array memory must contain the declared number of entries. The loader limits interface count to 4096. All descriptor memory and code addresses live at least as long as the library handle. An interface ID is an explicit ASCII name, never Rust TypeId. Macro IDs contain 1–255 ASCII letters/digits or . _ : / -. Versions are nonzero u32 values. IDs in a multi-interface export must be distinct. The host queries exact ID and version, exact method count, present function slots, and exact canonical signature bytes. It compares the actual canonical text; no collision-prone hash is trusted. For example, v1:add:mut(u64,u64)->result<u64> fixes method name, receiver, argument order/types, and success type. Parameter names are immaterial. Every interface version freezes its whole table. Add a new version or an independent extension interface for changed capabilities; do not insert optional methods into an existing frozen table. Missing entry, bad ABI, short descriptor, wrong interface version, absent method, and mismatched signature have separate error results. Four version spaces remain independent: Version Meaning zplugin crate SemVer Rust API and release package ABI major/minor Discovery and wire record contract Application interface version Frozen business method table PluginDescriptor.plugin_version Plugin business implementation Snapshot schema versions are an additional application-owned data-format version. Calls, buffers and status Each method slot has the fixed dispatcher type unsafe extern "C" fn(object, args, out) -> i32. Its canonical signature defines the generated repr(C) argument and result records. Fixed scalars retain their target C representation; slice and string fields become explicit pointer/length records. The adapters validate nullness, alignment, lengths, UTF-8 and conflicting mutable ranges before constructing Rust references. Every nonempty range must refer to one valid allocation, fit in isize::MAX, and have a nonoverflowing end address. Empty ranges may have null pointers; adapters substitute aligned dangling pointers when constructing empty Rust slices. Input bytes are initialized, readable and immutable during the call. Output slices are initialized caller memory exclusively writable during the call. No pointer may be retained afterward. Mutable ranges may not overlap inputs, other outputs, argument-record storage or scalar-result storage. Object storage and raw record validity remain explicit unsafe caller obligations. Scalar success outputs are written only after a successful return. The host reads them only after status zero. On an error the scalar output is unspecified and is not read; generated adapters leave it untouched. Unit output may be null. A mutable output slice may have partial writes before a business error or panic; zplugin does not promise transactional output rollback. The example checks short output before copying and tests that example's unchanged-buffer behavior. Status Meaning 0 Success; success output initialized -1 Invalid argument -2 Invalid UTF-8 -3 Output too small -4 Busy / rejected reentry -5 Caught Rust panic -6 Previously poisoned instance -7 Unsupported operation -8 Task cancelled -9 Task already completed Positive values Application-defined errors Other nonzero integers are preserved as Error::PluginStatus(i32), so invalid Rust enum discriminants are never read from foreign code. Returning PluginStatus(0) as an error maps to invalid argument. Objects and returned ownership An object is created in its plugin and released exactly once by the matching destroy function. A failed factory leaves its output pointer null. The generated factory allocates export::Object<T> in the plugin allocator; manual descriptors may use caller-managed storage. A successful factory returning null is rejected. The host never uses its own allocator to free plugin object memory. Binding borrows the library. An Instance either borrows it or owns an Rc lease. Its destructor calls the plugin's destroy function before releasing that lease. Buffer has a separate lease and may outlive its originating instance. Its release callback runs before releasing its own lease. An OwnedBytes result contains a data pointer, length, opaque context and the originating release function; the raw record itself carries no Rust Vec or Box layout. Custom OwnedBytes::from_raw implementations must keep both data and release context valid independently of the originating instance. They must not point into instance fields or call an already-destroyed object. OwnedBytes::from_vec provides this property by owning a plugin-allocated boxed byte slice. Its release returns to the same allocator and updates plugin resource accounting. If destroy or release reports failure, the host pins the library instead of unloading code still needed by leaked resources. A panicking factory likewise pins the candidate. This is a conservative failure path, not a successful cleanup. Low-level method() returns an unsafe function pointer; extraction does not extend the library or object lifetime. Calling such a pointer requires retaining all owners and honoring its exact records. Generated proxies handle this automatically. Threads, reentry and panic Library handles, proxies, owning leases and buffers are neither Send nor Sync. Create, use and destroy them on the same thread. Proxy methods always require &mut self, including source methods with &self. Independent instances can be used sequentially on that thread. A plugin may run its own synchronized workers; it owns their lifetime and must satisfy the selected unload policy. The raw adapter's single-thread busy guard is checked before borrowing its T. Same-object reentry returns Busy; the guard is not a cross-thread lock, and calling raw pointers concurrently violates the ABI contract. Compile-fail tests cover Send, Sync and library-borrow escape. With the plugin's std feature and unwind-enabled compilation, factory, method, destroy and buffer-release adapters contain panics on their side of extern "C". A panicking method poisons its instance; subsequent calls return Poisoned. Normal panic payloads are dropped inside a second guard. If a payload destructor also panics, only that secondary payload is deliberately leaked to prevent an unwind across the boundary. The ordinary Rust panic hook may still print. Without std, no catch is available; with panic=abort, a panic terminates the process. Foreign exceptions, segmentation faults, memory corruption and explicit process termination are outside panic containment. These behaviors follow Rust's FFI unwind rules. The extension protocol adds independently versioned task, waker, callback and resource tables. Their addition leaves the discovery header, interface descriptor, method slot, and existing v1 signatures unchanged. Cooperative close and bounded generations Pinned loading is the default. Dropping a pinned handle retains the native mapping until process exit. It can support libraries whose background activity cannot be proven quiescent. Repeated uncoordinated pinned loads intentionally retain their loader references; callers needing a bound use hot::Generations. Cooperative loading requires an explicit unsafe UnloadSafe promise for all exported implementations and a quiescence callback. No thread, task, callback, TLS/atexit destructor, buffer or escaped address may require the image after quiescence succeeds. Destructors must join workers and cancel/unregister external activity. Initializers and entry must leave no activity requiring a resident image if metadata validation fails, because that cooperative failure path closes its new handle. Failed factories must roll back their external activity. Plugin::try_close consumes exclusive ownership. Borrowed objects prevent that ownership statically, and owned objects prevent Rc::try_unwrap dynamically. The plugin's generated quiescence function also requires its object/buffer count to reach zero. Busy returns the still-owned Plugin for retry. Drop retains the handle when cooperative close fails. There is no timeout-based forced close. A generation manager reserves a retired slot before loading a candidate. It rejects a path that resolves to an already managed OS module handle. It prepares the new instance and restores an explicit versioned snapshot before publishing the new current generation. Existing objects keep their prior generation. Preparation errors or panics retain the candidate in the retired set until collect() can reclaim it; escaped candidate leases are therefore counted. Failed pinned load attempts conservatively consume a slot even if loading failed before mapping. This may stop switching early, but prevents untracked failed attempts from bypassing the configured limit. The limit counts manager-owned retired generations and conservatively retained failed attempts, in addition to one current image. It does not account for other loaders or global OS behavior. Successful dlclose/FreeLibrary releases this manager's reference; external loader references or OS pinning can keep a mapping resident. A deployment requiring actual memory reclamation must exclude such external references/pinning and verify the target system's behavior. Windows LoadLibraryExW and FreeLibrary define that platform's loader behavior. Snapshots and side effects belong to the application. zplugin switches the current library only after a successful preparation closure; it does not roll back writes to databases, files or application state performed by that closure. Quiesce the relevant business state before snapshotting if a consistent migration is required. Review and claim-evidence map Claim Evidence Limit Exact interface checks precede binding Malformed real cdylibs and contract tests Trusted readable metadata required Resources release through their origin Owned-buffer and destructor tests Custom raw resources must honor the contract Calls avoid forced allocation/refcounts Generated code plus host/plugin allocation counters Business methods may allocate Versions coexist and failure preserves current Real v1/v2 and failed-init tests Application side effects are separate Cross-compiler compatibility Independently built 1.85.0/1.100.0 combinations Same target/system ABI required Review dimensions: contribution is small typed native boundaries; terminology maps directly to records and owners; performance claims use measurements; evaluation includes failure cases and independently compiled libraries; the design keeps native-code trust and cooperative unload obligations explicit.

title: Stable values, tasks, resources and callbacks
body: 原生插件 ABI、动态库加载与可选 Wasm 沙箱。 Stable values, tasks, resources and callbacks Scope The extension protocols add richer data and execution lifetimes without changing zplugin_entry_v1, Header, PluginDescriptor, InterfaceDescriptor, Method, or any previously generated synchronous signature. A new business method still requires a new application-interface version or a separate interface. The crate version, discovery ABI, extension-table version, and application version are independent. The default crate remains allocator-free no_std. Raw tables and manual owners work with core; alloc enables convenient Rust futures, closure callbacks, allocated resources, and owning library leases. std additionally contains unwind-enabled Rust panics. There is no dependency on an executor or FFI runtime. Boundary Producer representation Host representation Retirement Stable value AbiValue::Wire Checked Rust value Copy, no resource ownership Task RawTask Task<'lib, T> Original cancel/release and independent lease Resource RawResource Resource<'lib> Original release and independent lease Callback input Borrowed RawCallback CallbackRef<'call> Retain before storage; release each retained owner Poll notification Borrowed RawWaker Runtime-local Waker adapter Thread-safe retain/wake/release Stable values and generated declarations #[zplugin::abi_type(id = "app.point", version = 1)] on a Copy + Clone struct generates a separate repr(C) wire record. Fields use fixed-width numeric types or other annotated values. Rust field layout is irrelevant: the adapter converts field by field. The complete recursive schema includes ID, version, field names, order, nested schemas, and enum tags. Binding compares full schema text. Fieldless enums use a plain u32 wire tag. Payload enums use a repr(C) record containing a u32 tag and a C union of repr(C) variant payloads. The adapter validates the tag before reading the selected payload or creating a Rust enum. The producer initializes every active field; inactive union storage and padding need not be initialized and must never be treated as serialized bytes. The schema distinguishes scalar-tag and tagged-union representations. The first extension release accepts nonempty named structs, nested values, and unit/tuple/named enum variants with literal u32 tags or sequential tags. It rejects generic declarations, reference/owned/container/array fields, bool, char, pointer-width integers, and 128-bit integers. An unsafe manual AbiValue implementation must provide a C representation with valid readable fields, checked conversion and a complete schema. Private generated wire constructors prevent safe Rust callers from forging a selected but uninitialized payload. InterfaceApi::write_c_header writes declarations, signatures and descriptor initializers to core::fmt::Write. C11 and C++17 consume the header directly. The Zig example runs zig translate-c for the target and imports its generated module. All participants must use the same platform C ABI, pointer width, architecture, endianness and compatible system-library requirements. This does not produce a platform-independent plugin binary. The validation toolchain pins Zig 0.15.2 on macOS and 0.17.1 on Linux/Windows; the example documents the macOS translator timeout behind that compiler choice. The foreign-language example includes every build configuration and the Rust host. It exercises nested payload enums, borrowed buffers, owning buffers/resources, callbacks and task polling in C, C++ and Zig. The unit/no-argument C typedefs are placeholders: the protocol writes no unit output, and callers may pass a null unit-output pointer. Task creation, polling and cancellation A task factory is a synchronous interface method returning OwnedTask<T>. The plugin can construct it with OwnedTask::new(async move { ... }), where the future is 'static and returns Result<T>, and T: AbiValue. The generated proxy returns Task<T>, which implements Future when alloc is enabled. Task::poll_raw accepts a protocol waker without requiring host allocation. An asynchronous result currently contains a stable value, not an owned buffer or another resource. General owning resources remain separate interface results. The task owns all data needed after creation. A factory receiving &[u8] or &str must finish using that borrowed input before returning, or copy the needed data into its own task state. The future cannot borrow its originating object. Consequently its host wrapper may outlive the creating proxy, and a task from an old generation can finish after a new generation has become current. RawTask contains context and a pointer to TaskVTable. The host reads the table's u32 size before its remaining mandatory prefix, requires extension version 1 and all function slots, and verifies output size, alignment and full schema against T::Wire. Invalid owned results pin the library because an unknown release path cannot safely be invoked. Operation Contract poll(context, waker, out, state) Serialized on the creating thread; waker borrowed for this call state = 0, status 0 Pending; no initialized result; arrange a wake when progress is possible state = 1, status 0 Ready; out contains one initialized T::Wire Nonzero status Error; do not read out; positive application codes remain errors cancel(context) Idempotent on completed/cancelled tasks; success stops future polling; Busy retains ownership for retry release(context) Consumes the one task owner, cancels/destroys remaining state; return only after required cleanup State and status are separate, so application error 1 cannot be confused with Pending. Generated Rust adapters preserve the output on error. Re-polling a completed task returns Completed; a cancelled task returns Cancelled; a task whose poll panicked becomes Poisoned. The independent factory remains usable. A failed release retains its library, with no timeout-forced unloading. The adapter pins the concrete future in one plugin-owned allocation. It never passes a Rust Future, Pin, Context or Waker representation through the C ABI. Waker bridges are cached while the host executor's waker is unchanged. A warmed Pending poll does not require allocation or a library-lease clone; the initial bridge setup and a changed waker can allocate. A plugin may independently allocate inside its future. Measurements distinguish these cases. Wakers and reverse callbacks RawWaker contains an opaque context and size/version-prefixed table with retain, wake, and release. All three operations are thread-safe, and wake borrows rather than consumes its owner. A poll receives a borrowed view; before storing it, the plugin retains one reference. Replacing a stored waker releases the old reference. Each retained reference keeps its context and origin callback code alive independently of the poll and task. The Rust bridge uses atomic references and contains unwind-enabled panics in host callbacks. A failed wake is latched, stops further use of that waker, and surfaces as an error at the next poll. A waker that itself fails to schedule may require the executor to poll again explicitly; zplugin cannot repair a broken executor's notification mechanism. Task polling/cancellation/destruction remains local-thread even though its notification operations may run on worker threads. General callbacks deliberately use a stricter model. Callback::new owns a 'static closure accepting borrowed input/output byte slices; as_ref() yields CallbackRef<'_>. Interface methods accept this borrowed view. The plugin may call it during the method or obtain an owned Callback through try_clone(). Retaining does not extend input-buffer borrows: each invocation gets its own call-scoped buffers. Invoke, retain and release stay on the creating thread; these callbacks are neither Send nor Sync. Same-context reentry returns Busy before a second mutable borrow, and a caught callback panic poisons that context. A raw callback constructor is unsafe: its caller retains the origin code and context for every cloned owner. Safe generated callback parameters are borrowed from the caller, and the Rust-owned callback factory participates in that origin's resource accounting. This version does not generate callback-valued returns or cross-thread general callbacks. Only the waker protocol is concurrent. Owning resources and cooperative shutdown OwnedResource::new(handler) allocates a ResourceHandler in the plugin. The handler declares a stable ID and resource version and handles a numeric operation with borrowed input/output buffers. The host receives Resource, calls check(id, version) before using its application protocol, and releases it through its original library. Its state must be independent of its originating instance. No Rust Box, trait object, file object or allocator layout crosses ABI. Each task, resource and owned buffer holds its own host library lease. Destruction runs the foreign release function before dropping that lease. Allocated Rust plugin resources also participate in cooperative quiescence. Failed future, object, or callback-capture cleanup latches the image as non-quiescent, including destructors that panic after partially running. This intentionally retains code instead of treating an interrupted cleanup as success. Physical unloading additionally requires the unsafe UnloadSafe promise. Reference-count zero alone does not establish that a worker's final waker/drop function has returned through plugin code. Workers, reactor registrations, callbacks and their return paths must be joined or synchronously drained before quiescence can succeed. The real Rust async example joins its worker in the future destructor on completion, cancellation and release, and stress-tests a wake racing cancellation. Dropping a Future does not automatically shut down Tokio or another external executor. Use pinned loading when such retirement cannot be coordinated. No async runtime is installed or entered by zplugin. Evidence and limits The executable evidence is tests/{values,tasks,failed_cleanup,resources_callbacks}.rs, compile-fail fixtures, scripts/async.py, scripts/foreign.py and scripts/legacy.py. The release report records exact executed platforms, compiler versions and counts. Tests use real independently built dynamic libraries, including both directions against the immutable published v0.1.0 source. The protocols provide compatibility and ownership checks for trusted in-process native code. They do not isolate memory faults, prevent malicious native code, catch panic=abort, or portably intercept C++ exceptions or Zig panic/abort. Foreign plugins must contain their own exceptions before an ABI return. Design review: the contribution is three additive protocols with typed bindings; the writing maps each promise to its ownership rule; measurements separate setup from warm polling; validation covers supported native platforms and failure paths; and the shutdown contract explicitly includes work that reference counts cannot prove quiescent. Unexecuted configurations receive no support claim.

The example's ready task requests 56 plugin bytes on creation. First polling creates the needed waker bridges; changing a C waker requests another 40 bytes, while changing a Rust executor waker requests 40 bytes on each side. The optimization is reuse of already-created bridges, not an assertion that every asynchronous operation requires no memory. title: zplugin 0.3.0 Wasm measurements
