new、with_roots、refresh、refresh_frequencies、cores、aggregate_times、aggregate_busy_percent、sample；CpuSample MemoryCollector new、with_proc_root、refresh、snapshot；MemorySample Processes new、with_proc_root、with_parameters、set_scan_mode、enumerate_pids、refresh、refresh_pid、details、iter/get/len/is_empty/failures、ticks_per_second/page_size；Process、ProcessChanges、ProcessFailure、Availability、Detail、DetailOptions、ProcessDetails、ScanMode DiskIoCollector new、with_proc_root、refresh、iter/get/sample；DiskDevice Filesystem／Mounts Filesystem::new/refresh/path/capacity/last_error/sample；Mounts::new/with_proc_root/refresh/refresh_capacities/iter/iter_mut/sample；Mount Networks new、with_proc_root、refresh_counters/refresh_details/refresh、iter/get/sample；Network、InterfaceDetails（含 is_up/is_running/is_loopback）、InterfaceAddress、AddressSource Hardware new、with_sys_root、四个显式刷新方法、temperatures/gpus/info/inventory_sample；Gpu、HardwareInfo、HardwareValue::value、TemperatureSensor::celsius、TemperatureSource System new、refresh_cpu/memory/processes/process/networks/network_counters/disk_io/mounts/basic；对应借用 getter、process_table 与 process_collector LinuxCollector new、with_proc_root、cpu_times、memory、processes；ProcessRecord、LinuxError::{Io, Parse} 精确签名和所有公开字段以 cargo doc --no-deps --all-features 生成的 rustdoc 为准。

title: 概览
body:
维护终端屏幕、光标、滚动历史与 VT 协议状态。 zterm A bounded terminal screen and VT state machine in Rust. zterm converts bytes from a process into character cells, cursor state, protocol replies, and input modes. A host application supplies the PTY, event loop, font rendering, window, and clipboard policy. The production library is no_std with alloc and forbids unsafe code. It uses zvte for streaming parsing, zinput for input encoding, zgraphics for Kitty and Sixel images, zgpui for optional UI scenes, and unicode-width / unicode-segmentation for character widths and cluster boundaries. Applications supply the allocator; tests and development examples use std. Use independently [dependencies] zterm = "0.5.0" use zterm::{Terminal, input::{self, Key, KeyEvent, Modifiers}}; let mut terminal = Terminal::new(80, 24, 2_000); terminal.feed(b"\x1b[38;2;99;179;237mhello\x1b[0m"); assert_eq!(terminal.cell(0, 0).ch, 'h'); assert_eq!(terminal.cell(0, 0).fg, 0x63b3ed); // Paint only the rows marked dirty, then acknowledge the rendered frame. assert!(terminal.row_dirty(0)); terminal.clear_dirty(); // A child can negotiate input modes through its output stream. terminal.feed(b"\x1b[?1h"); let encoded = input::encode_key( Key::Up, Modifiers::default(), KeyEvent::Press, "", &terminal.modes().input(), ); assert_eq!(encoded, b"\x1bOA"); // Write response bytes back to the child before clearing the queue. terminal.feed(b"\x1b[6n"); assert_eq!(terminal.responses(), b"\x1b[1;6R"); terminal.clear_responses(); feed accepts arbitrary chunk boundaries, including split UTF-8 characters and control sequences. cell addresses the live screen; view_cell addresses the same viewport with a scrollback offset. Both return a blank cell for invalid coordinates. resize clamps dimensions to 1..=1024, reflows retained primary text using recorded soft wraps, and marks all rows dirty. resize_anchored also maps requested text positions; alternate-screen content remains a fixed grid. History stays within the configured row and byte limits. Modes::input() snapshots the negotiated keyboard, mouse, focus, and paste modes into the independent zinput::Modes value. The input crate is re-exported as zterm::input; it is also usable without this terminal model. Runtime themes Terminal::set_theme applies configured default colors and the 16 ANSI palette entries to retained cells in place. It updates the live screen, scrollback, alternate screens, and saved SGR styles, then marks every screen row dirty. Terminal::theme() returns the current configuration. Applying an identical theme does no work; changing one does not allocate or restart the child process. use zterm::Terminal; let mut terminal = Terminal::new(80, 24, 2_000); terminal.feed(b"normal \x1b[31mred\x1b[0m"); let mut theme = terminal.theme(); theme.foreground = 0xe8eaed; theme.background = 0x000000; theme.palette[1] = 0xff6666; terminal.set_theme(theme); assert_eq!(terminal.cell(0, 0).fg, 0xe8eaed); assert_eq!(terminal.cell(7, 0).fg, 0xff6666); assert!(terminal.row_dirty(0)); SGR default colors and ANSI palette references follow the new configuration. Explicit truecolor and indexed colors 16 through 255 keep their values, even when their RGB values happen to equal an old default or palette entry. Color provenance is retained alongside resolved fg/bg values. The 32-byte Cell also stores an ID for complete grapheme clusters; cell_chars reads their content. The frontend still owns window padding, cursor colors, and redraw scheduling. OSC 4/10/11 queries report the current colors with their original terminator; OSC color writes remain unsupported. The SGR defaults and OSC query format follow the xterm control-sequence reference. Shell command metadata OSC 133 A/B/C/D marks expose prompt, input, output, and completion boundaries through commands(). Records have stable session-local IDs, absolute history coordinates, and optional exit codes. command_input(id, max_bytes) and command_output(id, max_bytes) extract current rendered text from retained primary-screen cells; command_scroll_offset(id) locates a retained prompt. The result reports completion and truncation explicitly. use zterm::Terminal; let mut terminal = Terminal::new(80, 24, 2_000); // These marks normally arrive from the configured shell through the PTY. terminal.feed(b"\x1b]133;A\x07$ \x1b]133;B\x07printf hello
\x1b]133;C\x07hello
\x1b]133;D;0\x07"); let command = terminal.commands().next_back().unwrap(); assert_eq!(command.exit_status, Some(0)); let output = terminal.command_output(command.id, 4_096).unwrap(); assert_eq!(output.text, "hello
"); assert!(output.complete && !output.truncated); assert_eq!(terminal.command_scroll_offset(command.id), Some(0)); Use commands().rev() to locate recent executed commands and copy their IDs before mutating the terminal. A missing command ID or output boundary returns None. A returned CommandText may be incomplete while the process is running, or truncated by the requested byte limit, history eviction, or destructive screen edits. Check both fields before labeling a copied result complete. command_scroll_offset returns a viewport offset that can be passed to view_cell; it returns None for unavailable prompts or an active alternate screen. Offsets should be queried again after more terminal output arrives. Metadata is allocated on the first marker and retains at most 128 records. Reads return at most 64 KiB of UTF-8 without duplicating the whole history. Scrolling keeps retained anchors stable. History eviction, width changes, and destructive screen operations can make a range unavailable; a reset clears records without reusing IDs. These are untrusted display markers, not proof of command identity or authorization. See the shell setup and acceptance guide. Graphics Call set_cell_size(width, height) when physical text-cell metrics change. graphics_draws(history_offset) returns the visible image placements in z-order, including source, destination and optional clip rectangles. Text-backed placements use a bounded geometry cache. The frontend preserves the full source-to-destination transform when applying Draw::clip, then performs viewport clipping and alpha compositing. Negative z-indices are behind text; values below -1,073,741,824 are also behind cells with explicit backgrounds. Types are re-exported as zterm::graphics. PTY inline RGB, RGBA and PNG support optional zlib compression, chunked transfers, image IDs/numbers, placement IDs, source cropping, scaling and deletion. PNG accepts palette, grayscale, transparency, 16-bit and Adam7 input. Metadata is discarded before decoding; invalid CRCs, oversized dimensions and decompression limits produce protocol errors. APNG remains unsupported. set_graphics_reader installs the host's bounded file, temporary-file and shared-memory reader. The host validates objects and owns unlink policy. advance_graphics advances animation from host-supplied monotonic milliseconds and returns the next deadline. Unicode placeholders and relative placements resolve through the same draw contract. The clock and external I/O remain supplied by the host. Primary and alternate screens own independent bounded image scenes. Images move with full-screen scrolling and remain available within retained history. Resizing keeps their row anchors in step with text; clearing the display removes visible placements. Dirty rows include graphics changes, so deleting an image causes the underlying text and background to be repainted. A new non-continuation command or deletion aborts a previous incomplete transfer, except that feature queries leave it intact. Normal text between completed APC chunks continues to render. An unterminated APC can be cancelled by CAN, SUB or a new ESC sequence. APC headers are capped and encoded payloads stream through a fixed-size staging buffer. Larger single-APC transfers emitted by existing kitten icat versions and unpadded final base64 are accepted without retaining the whole encoded body. Host clipboard and UI integration OSC 52 uses a dedicated bounded streaming path and request queue. The host drains next_clipboard_request, applies its clipboard policy, and checks clipboard_epoch before completing an asynchronous request. Reset and host cancellation invalidate older requests. The public MAX_CLIPBOARD_BYTES and MAX_CLIPBOARD_REQUESTS constants describe this queue independently of ordinary OSC string limits. UI scenes are re-exported as zterm::ui. Hosts opt in with set_ui_host_enabled after attaching a renderer and event router, then consume ui_scene / ui_revision. ui_action checks the expected surface and revision before returning an intent; the host applies current session and input-owner authorization. Terminal checkpoints Terminal::checkpoint() -> Result<Vec<u8>, &'static str> encodes retained terminal state for a host-controlled process replacement. Terminal::restore_checkpoint(&[u8]) -> Result<Terminal, &'static str> constructs an independent terminal for validation and restoration. The checkpoint includes primary and alternate screens, scrollback, cursors, styles, modes, tab stops, grapheme identities, shell markers and queued protocol replies. Checkpointing requires a complete parser boundary. Partial UTF-8, ESC, CSI, OSC or DCS input returns an error without changing the original terminal. A host can continue normal input processing and retry with a bounded deadline; it must keep the original session if no safe boundary arrives. Pending OSC 52 work must also finish through the host's normal clipboard handling. Terminals that have processed Kitty graphics, Sixel or native UI input are conservatively rejected, even after deleting resources or resetting the screen. The current internal format has version 1, explicit little-endian fields, bounded lengths and a corruption checksum, with a 128 MiB limit per terminal. Decoding rejects unknown versions, malformed data and invalid state references. Compatibility across builds depends on the replacement decoder accepting the format and state; validate every checkpoint in the replacement before giving up the running host. This format is intended for controlled handover rather than a stable archival interchange. The host retains ownership of PTYs, child processes, pending I/O, windows and session layout. After a successful export, stop advancing that terminal until handover completes. Reinstall process-local callbacks such as set_graphics_reader and mark restored rows dirty for a newly created renderer. Derived caches are rebuilt. Restoration preserves every retained history row while rebuilding bounded storage; allocator capacities are not part of the format. Screen and storage The visible screen is a flat cell array with a circular row origin. Full-screen scrolling rotates that origin and clears the recycled row. A partial scrolling region moves only its own rows. Dirty bits are tracked per row, including the old and new cursor rows. Scrollback is allocated as output arrives and is limited by both the requested line count and an 8 MiB retained-history budget. Once full, old line buffers are reused. The alternate screen is created on first use and retained for reuse. It does not append to scrollback; the primary screen's existing history is preserved while the alternate screen is active. Additional bounds are explicit: Storage Bound Screen dimensions 1–1024 columns and 1–1024 rows Requested history At most 65,536 lines, subject to the 8 MiB retained-history budget Ordinary OSC parser payload 4,096 bytes; OSC 52 uses its separate bounded streaming queue Pending protocol responses 65,536 bytes Hyperlink identities 1,024 entries Hyperlink URI 2,048 UTF-8 bytes Window title 256 UTF-8 bytes Working-directory value 2,048 UTF-8 bytes Kitty keyboard stack 32 entries per screen Shell command records 128, allocated lazily Command-text read 65,536 UTF-8 bytes Graphics APC staging At most a 512-byte header plus 4,096 encoded payload bytes; larger bodies stream through it Decoded graphics 32 MiB per image and per screen, counting vector capacity Pending graphics transfer 16 MiB per screen; one transfer at a time Graphics dimensions At most 8,192 pixels in either dimension, also subject to byte limit Stored images / placements 128 / 512 per screen Complete grapheme content At most 256 UTF-8 bytes per cluster, 16,384 pooled entries and a combined 1 MiB for text and reference headers The history byte limit includes cell-vector capacity and history-deque metadata. Screen arrays, parser state, titles, hyperlinks, queued responses and the bounded grapheme pool are separate allocations. Grapheme slot/tree metadata is additional to the pool's text/reference-header accounting. Passing a history limit of zero disables scrollback allocation. Image decoding uses additional bounded temporary storage. Renderer copies and buffers retained through Arc are outside the model's decoded-storage quota; frontends must bound and release those resources separately. Implemented protocol state Cursor positioning, saved cursor and attributes, scrolling regions, origin mode, delayed autowrap, insert/delete characters and lines, erasing, tabs, alternate screen, and DEC line-drawing characters. SGR attributes and 16-color, 256-color, and RGB colors. RGB accepts both semicolon and colon parameter forms; cells expose resolved RGB values. UTF-8, double-width characters and complete extended grapheme clusters within the storage limits. Editing and resizing repair split double-width cells. OSC titles, working-directory metadata, indexed/default color queries, and OSC 8 hyperlinks attached to cells and retained in scrollback. The host decides whether to open a URI. Application cursor/keypad modes, bracketed paste, focus events, independent mouse tracking and SGR mouse encoding, and Kitty keyboard protocol flags with separate primary/alternate screen stacks. Synchronized-output mode, DSR cursor/status replies, device attributes, DECRQM mode queries, character/text-area/cell pixel-size queries, and basic XTGETTCAP queries for TN, Co, and Tc. Unknown capabilities return an unsupported response. The startup compatibility environment is TERM=xterm-256color, using the standard system terminfo entry. The TN capability query returns that same name; the library does not report a ztty terminal identity. While synchronized output is enabled, the host should keep displaying its last completed frame and continue feeding bytes to the model. After reset of mode 2026, the accumulated dirty rows can be rendered together. A host with a documented timeout can call force_end_sync() to finish a stalled frame. Protocol references: xterm control sequences, Kitty keyboard protocol, Kitty graphics protocol, synchronized output, and OSC 8 hyperlinks. Current boundaries Width changes reflow retained primary-screen soft wraps while preserving hard line boundaries and requested ResizeAnchor positions. The alternate screen keeps a fixed grid. History eviction and addressed content outside the retained area remain bounded; lost anchors are reported as absent. Complete extended grapheme clusters, including emoji ZWJ sequences, are retained in bounded shared storage. cell_chars and grapheme expose the complete content. Font shaping and bidirectional layout belong to the renderer. Clipboard requests, UI actions and external image reads require host policy and host implementations. The library changes screen state and returns protocol bytes. It does not perform I/O, invoke programs, render text, or open links. Validation and measurements From this standalone workspace: cargo test --locked --lib cargo test --locked --doc cargo fmt --all -- --check cargo clippy --locked --all-targets -- -D warnings python3 tools/check_package.py cargo package --locked rustup target add wasm32-unknown-unknown x86_64-unknown-none cargo check --locked --lib --target wasm32-unknown-unknown cargo check --locked --lib --target x86_64-unknown-none The core tests cover fragmented streams, wide-cell repair, scroll regions, bounded history, screen switching, color forms, hyperlink lifetime, oversized OSC rejection, mode queries, keyboard stacks, malformed input, and response queue limits. The benchmark reports parser-plus-screen throughput, sampled latency, allocations after warmup, and initial core heap use. PTY scheduling, rendering, compositor behavior, and physical display latency are separate measurements. License MIT. See LICENSE. Sixel parsing Terminal::feed decodes bounded Sixel images from DCS streams and exposes them through graphics_draws, alongside Kitty images. DECSDM 80, private/shared palette mode 1070 and cursor-right mode 8452 are queryable with DECRQM. Sixel input commits only at ST; cancellation drops the partial decoder without moving the cursor or publishing pixels. The graphics protocol scope distinguishes tested decoding/cursor behavior from framebuffer and native-GUI compatibility limits. Repository and module layout The independent 0.5.0 workspace uses published version dependencies for zgpui, zgraphics and zinput. Its initial source was copied from ztty d0e00923; the extraction record contains the original file blobs. The subsequent split preserves public paths, method bodies and the parent data structures. Terminal module Responsibility terminal.rs Shared state, public types and construction framing.rs Byte-stream framing, cancellation and extension routing dispatch.rs VT parser callbacks and bounded replies editing.rs Cell editing, cursor movement, scrolling and history insertion style.rs, modes.rs Theme/SGR state and terminal mode negotiation view.rs Visible/retained text access, shell ranges and frontend acknowledgements graphics.rs, image_cells.rs Host image integration and cached placeholder geometry reflow.rs, grapheme.rs Resize mapping and complete-cluster editing checkpoint.rs Versioned terminal-state encoding, validation and restoration The manual candidate workflow validates one exact commit on Linux, macOS and Windows, with WebAssembly and bare-metal checks, formatting, Clippy, package boundaries and isolated release-script tests. These checks cover the library; native PTY, renderer, clipboard and display integration remain host-level validation. The separate manual release workflow prepares or resumes an exact candidate, reruns those gates, checks the crate's embedded Git identity and registry checksum, then pushes the matching tag and completes its GitHub Release. An interrupted publication resumes only when package bytes and the existing tag agree with that candidate.

title: 概览
body: 原生终端应用，在 Linux 上支持窗口、命令行与 MCP 共用会话。 ztty English · 文档 · 下载 ztty 是面向 Linux、macOS 和 Windows 的原生终端，核心用不依赖标准库的 Rust 编写。Linux 上，同一个运行中的会话可以通过窗口、命令行或 MCP 客户端使用。 本页说明 0.6.1。已发布的二进制及对应变更记录见 下载页。 Linux 安装 Arch Linux 使用 yay -S ztty。下载已发布的 x86_64 或 ARM64 预编译版： curl -fsSLO https://github.com/LIghtJUNction/ztty/releases/latest/download/install.sh sh install.sh ztty 安装器校验归档后安装到 ~/.local/bin。 在 Wayland 桌面上，X11 后端通过 XWayland 运行。当前源码默认使用 --backend auto， 其初始回退与会话兼容规则见后端选择。 从源码构建 需要 Rust 1.100.0、C 编译器和等宽字体。当前 Linux 源码的系统依赖： # Arch Linux sudo pacman -S --needed base-devel pkgconf libx11 libxft libxrender \ fontconfig freetype2 harfbuzz libglvnd ttf-dejavu # Debian / Ubuntu sudo apt install build-essential pkg-config libx11-dev libxft-dev libxrender-dev \ libfontconfig1-dev libfreetype-dev libharfbuzz-dev libegl1-mesa-dev \ libgles2-mesa-dev fonts-dejavu-core git clone --recurse-submodules https://github.com/LIghtJUNction/ztty.git cd ztty cargo build --locked --release ./target/release/ztty --font 'monospace:size=12' --geometry 100x28 ./target/release/ztty --cwd /path/to/project -e /bin/bash sh install.sh --from-binary ./target/release/ztty 已有克隆请先运行 git submodule update --init --recursive，再进行构建。 Linux/macOS 使用 SHELL，缺省为 /bin/sh；Windows 使用 COMSPEC， 缺省为 cmd.exe。用 -e 指定其他程序。安装更新后，已有共享进程仍运行原来的代码； 共享进程升级与热替换说明如何更新及路由新会话。 macOS 和 Windows 的原生构建、打包入口见发布说明。 核心能力 VT 控制序列、真彩色、鼠标报告、括号粘贴和 Kitty 增强键盘协议。 完整字符簇存储、历史重排，以及跨自动换行的文字复制。 Kitty 图片和 Sixel；Linux 增加动画、Unicode 占位符和相对位置。 Linux X11 Kitty 文件、共享内存传输，以及有界的 OSC 52 剪贴板访问。 Linux 共享会话；X11 标签页、分屏、历史搜索和命令面板。 Linux X11 GPU 文字整形、Xft 回退、配置热重载和 XIM 输入法恢复。 可选的 Shell 集成和可信文本扩展。 Linux X11 默认使用 renderer = auto：可用时选择硬件 EGL，否则使用 Xft。 配置指南和协议说明列出支持的模式与范围。 Linux X11 常用操作 操作 快捷键 复制 / 粘贴 Ctrl+Shift+C / V 在捕获鼠标的 TUI 中选择文字 Shift+拖拽 搜索历史 / 打开命令面板 Ctrl+Shift+F / P 切换会话 Ctrl+Shift+S 新建标签页 / 向右分屏 Ctrl+Shift+T / E 下一个 / 上一个标签页 Ctrl+Tab / Ctrl+Shift+Tab 放大 / 缩小 / 恢复字体 Ctrl+Plus / Minus / 0 浏览历史 Shift+PageUp / PageDown 或滚轮 打开链接 Ctrl+点击 重载配置 Ctrl+Shift+R 双击选词，三击选行。浏览历史时，点击 Back to live ↓ 回到最新输出。 日常操作、工作区和 输入兼容性说明自定义绑定、小键盘和其他操作。 Ctrl+Shift+V 粘贴文本；Ctrl+V 默认交给前台应用，Codex CLI 0.170.0 用它 添加剪贴板图片附件。从 ztty 0.5.1 开始，终端文本粘贴会拒绝只有图片的剪贴板， 避免把图片变成字符。详见图片粘贴与格式检查。 共享会话与 MCP（Linux） Linux X11 与原生 Wayland 窗口共用同一个会话进程；每个会话保留自己的 PTY、屏幕和历史。X11 窗口还共用显示连接与字体缓存。 ztty --name work -e /bin/bash & ztty attach # 列出会话 ztty attach work # 打开窗口或将已有窗口置前 ztty attach --observe work # 只读观察 ztty mcp # stdio MCP ztty mcp --transport http --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8732 MCP 支持创建会话、读取输出、输入、调整尺寸、关闭 PTY 和管理输入控制权。 MCP 创建的会话在连接断开后保留，关闭附加视图也会保留它的 PTY。 HTTP 监听非回环地址时需要令牌。 客户端配置、会话身份校验、JSON/SSE 响应与命令输出读取见会话指南； ssmcp 等工具的接入见观察模式。 SSH 终端多路复用（Linux） ztty 0.6.1 在远端共享进程中持有 shell 和 PTY。关闭窗口或断开 SSH 后， 任务继续运行；重新连接恢复屏幕与有界滚屏历史。两端安装 ztty 后即可使用： ztty ssh dev main # 使用 ~/.ssh/config 中的别名 ztty ssh ssh://alice@host:2222 build ztty ssh --list dev ztty ssh --observe dev build # 只读，不改变写入者的终端尺寸 ztty ssh --terminal dev main # 在当前终端中附着 ztty ssh --close dev build # 明确结束远端会话 Ctrl+] 分离。在 SSH 窗口中按 Ctrl+Shift+T 或分屏快捷键，会在同一主机上创建 独立的远端会话。多个面板复用同一条已认证的 OpenSSH 连接，密钥、SSH 配置与 主机密钥校验仍由系统 SSH 处理。一个会话只有一个输入控制者，--takeover 可显式接管。 SSH 会话指南说明端口、密钥和配置文件、标签页与分屏、 远端命令、本地无窗口使用及当前文本视图的支持范围。 替换运行中的程序 由 ztty 0.5.1 或后续版本启动的 Linux X11/XWayland 或无窗口共享进程支持程序热替换。 在要更新的会话内运行： ztty reload ztty reload --binary /absolute/path/to/ztty ZTTY_SOCKET 决定目标共享进程。不指定 --binary 时，目标就是本次调用的 CLI 自身的可执行文件；命令不会下载更新。替换保留共享进程 PID、原 shell 和命令的 PTY、 会话身份、输入队列与输出位置、终端屏幕和滚屏历史，以及 X11 标签页和分屏。 窗口会重建，可能短暂消失。活动原生 Wayland 视图会阻止替换；已 detach 的原生 会话保留后端来源，可在替换后重新附着。macOS 和 Windows 暂不支持此操作。 已发布的 0.5.0 旧共享进程会安全拒绝，即使用新 CLI 请求也不能原地迁移。 保留旧窗口直到工作结束，用新源码构建的共享进程开始新工作；后续可在该进程内热替换。 热替换指南说明验证过程、临时拒绝条件、 显示恢复和首次过渡步骤。Ctrl+Shift+R 仍然只重载配置。 外观 Linux 默认配置为 ~/.config/ztty/ztty.conf，也可用 --config PATH 指定文件。 font = monospace:size=11 window-padding = 16 background = #161a23 foreground = #e1e7f0 background-opacity = 92 renderer = auto Linux X11 会在原窗口中应用有效配置。配置指南 包含各平台路径、颜色、光标、快捷键和渲染器选项。 平台范围 平台 当前源码 Linux X11/XWayland GPU 或 Xft；共享会话、标签页、分屏、Attach、MCP Linux 原生 Wayland Auto 回退或显式选择 EGL/GLES；共享会话、Attach/MCP、剪贴板与 text-input 输入法 macOS 原生 AppKit/CoreText 窗口与 Darwin PTY；本地会话 Windows 原生 Win32/GDI 与 ConPTY；本地标签页和分屏 macOS 无需 X11，Windows 无需 WSL。Windows 支持字体与工作区快捷键； macOS 复制粘贴使用 Command+C/V 或 Ctrl+Shift+C/V。 共享会话、Attach 与 MCP 当前属于 Linux 功能。 各平台实际测试范围见验收说明。 试用实验性原生 Wayland 后端： cargo build --locked --release --features wayland ./target/release/ztty --backend wayland --name work 官方 Linux 包的构建会启用 Wayland 支持。当前源码默认 Auto，先完整初始化 X11/XWayland，再在兼容条件下考虑原生 Wayland 初始回退。 Wayland 会拒绝标签页、分屏和工作区容器。Wayland 配置 说明额外依赖，以及尚未实机验证的物理 GPU、桌面输入法与显示缩放。 性能与开发 本轮运行时报告记录启动 %、 INCR 粘贴、Auto、查询后 reload、最终原生验收和实际安装。固定 Xvfb GPU 路径下， 按需分配软件回退 pixmap 每窗口节省约 3.66 MiB 的 X server 资源；这不代表整进程 RSS 或硬件显存的同等降幅。大段粘贴进入 ZLE 后的编辑耗时仍然存在。 输入发送完毕或明确取消后，当前源码释放容量超过 64 KiB 的输入缓冲， 较小的缓冲继续复用。输入缓冲回归记录 中，一次 8 MiB 输入清空后保留的容量由 8 MiB 降为 0。这是队列的分配容量； 本次改动尚未测量整进程 RSS/PSS 或吞吐变化。 2026-11-20 性能与热替换报告 提供固定源码、可执行文件哈希、全部原始样本和验收范围。与保留的旧版对照， 软件渲染的 ASCII/彩色输出吞吐：单窗口从 171.7 提高到 257.5 MiB/s， 10 窗口从 158.5 提高到 229.2 MiB/s；独立 Unicode 滚屏测试的三轮成对增益 中位数为 53.4%。报告也保留无窗口 ASCII 路径的小幅负向结果。 三应用比较使用私有 Xvfb，统一强制软件 OpenGL；ztty 实际驱动为 llvmpipe。 10 个窗口保持打开，每次只测一个输出生产者。它测量 PTY/DSR 逻辑处理， 不能代表物理帧率或真实 GPU 桌面排名。 10 窗口共享实例 应用 PSS，MiB 输出，MiB/s ztty 326.9 150.4 Ghostty 809.0 140.1 Kitty 354.6 53.0 Xvfb 与 llvmpipe 下的十窗口比较 表中为三次独立运行的中位数；字体度量、像素尺寸、宿主内存压力与渲染器选择 均限制结果的适用范围，报告保留全部波动。单窗口 ztty/Ghostty 吞吐区间重叠， 不能据此声称稳定排名。软件与 GPU 路径也通过了记录中的标签切换完整帧、 同步输出保持与提交检查；物理桌面及合成器行为仍需单独验证。 本地开发检查使用 sh tools/check.sh。 可复用库 库 在 ztty 中的职责 发布状态 zgpui UI 场景与布局 已发布 0.1.5 zinput 键盘、鼠标与粘贴编码 已发布 0.1.3 zpty PTY / ConPTY 进程管理 已发布 0.2.3 zgraphics 图片协议与放置 已发布 0.2.0 zterm 终端屏幕与协议状态 已发布 0.5.2 这些正式库版本包含 ztty 0.5.2 使用的终端状态保存、恢复与 PTY 接管 API。 开发源码通过 GitHub 默认分支消费这些库，由 Cargo.lock 记录本次提交； 子模块固定点与这份源码快照一致，用于独立库检查。上表记录已发布的注册表版本。 应用保持 zgpui 的 std 和 native 特性关闭。 可独立使用的 Project Z 库见架构说明； 使用指南与验收记录集中在文档索引。 MIT © LIghtJUNction

title: ztty
body: 原生终端应用，在 Linux 上支持窗口、命令行与 MCP 共用会话。 ztty 中文 · Documentation · Releases ztty is a native terminal for Linux, macOS and Windows. Its terminal core is written in Rust without the standard library. On Linux, the same live session can be used from a window, the CLI or an MCP client. This page documents 0.6.1. Published binaries and their release notes are available on the download page. Install on Linux On Arch Linux: yay -S ztty. For a published x86_64 or AArch64 binary: curl -fsSLO https://github.com/LIghtJUNction/ztty/releases/latest/download/install.sh sh install.sh ztty The installer verifies the archive and installs to ~/.local/bin. On Wayland desktops, the X11 backend runs through XWayland. Current source uses --backend auto; see backend selection for its initial fallback and session compatibility rules. Build and run Use Rust 1.100.0, a C compiler and a monospace font. Install the current Linux source's native dependencies with the command for your distribution: # Arch Linux sudo pacman -S --needed base-devel pkgconf libx11 libxft libxrender \ fontconfig freetype2 harfbuzz libglvnd ttf-dejavu # Debian / Ubuntu sudo apt install build-essential pkg-config libx11-dev libxft-dev libxrender-dev \ libfontconfig1-dev libfreetype-dev libharfbuzz-dev libegl1-mesa-dev \ libgles2-mesa-dev fonts-dejavu-core git clone --recurse-submodules https://github.com/LIghtJUNction/ztty.git cd ztty cargo build --locked --release ./target/release/ztty --font 'monospace:size=12' --geometry 100x28 ./target/release/ztty --cwd /path/to/project -e /bin/bash sh install.sh --from-binary ./target/release/ztty For an existing clone, run git submodule update --init --recursive before building. Linux/macOS use SHELL (falling back to /bin/sh); Windows uses COMSPEC (falling back to cmd.exe). -e chooses another program. Installing an update leaves existing brokers running their current code; see broker upgrades and reload. Native build and packaging details cover macOS and Windows. What it does VT sequences, true color, mouse reports, bracketed paste and Kitty keyboard input. Unicode grapheme storage, history reflow and copy across wrapped lines. Kitty images and Sixel; Linux adds animation, Unicode placeholders and relative placement. Linux X11 Kitty file/shared-memory transport and bounded OSC 52 clipboard access. Linux shared sessions; X11 tabs, splits, history search and a command palette. Linux X11 GPU text shaping, Xft fallback, live configuration and XIM recovery. Optional shell integration and trusted text actions. The Linux X11 renderer defaults to renderer = auto: hardware EGL when available, otherwise Xft. Configuration and the protocol reference describe supported modes and limits. Linux X11 controls Action Shortcut Copy / paste Ctrl+Shift+C / V Select text inside a mouse-driven TUI Shift+drag Search history / open command palette Ctrl+Shift+F / P Switch sessions Ctrl+Shift+S New tab / split right Ctrl+Shift+T / E Next / previous tab Ctrl+Tab / Ctrl+Shift+Tab Increase / decrease / reset font Ctrl+Plus / Minus / 0 Scroll history Shift+PageUp / PageDown or mouse wheel Open a link Ctrl+click Reload configuration Ctrl+Shift+R Double-click selects a word; triple-click selects a line. The Back to live ↓ button returns from history to current output. Daily workflow, workspaces and input compatibility cover custom bindings and keypad behavior. Ctrl+Shift+V pastes text. Ctrl+V goes to the foreground application; Codex CLI 0.170.0 uses it to attach clipboard images. Since ztty 0.5.1, terminal text paste rejects image-only selections. See image paste and format checks. Shared sessions and MCP (Linux) Linux X11 and native Wayland windows use the same session broker. Each session keeps its own PTY, screen and history. X11 windows also share a display connection and font cache. ztty --name work -e /bin/bash & ztty attach # List sessions ztty attach work # Open or raise its window ztty attach --observe work # Read-only view ztty mcp # MCP over stdio ztty mcp --transport http --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8732 MCP can create sessions, read output, send input, resize and close PTYs, and manage input ownership. MCP-created sessions survive transport disconnects; closing an attached view preserves their PTY. HTTP outside loopback needs a token. See sessions and MCP for client setup, session identities, JSON/SSE replies and command-output reads; observer mode covers tools such as ssmcp. SSH terminal multiplexing (Linux) ztty 0.6.1 keeps remote shells in a headless session broker. Closing an SSH connection or its window leaves those shells running; reconnecting restores their screen and bounded scrollback. Install ztty on both Linux machines, then: ztty ssh dev main # SSH alias from ~/.ssh/config ztty ssh ssh://alice@host:2222 build ztty ssh --list dev ztty ssh --observe dev build # Read-only; does not resize the writer ztty ssh --terminal dev main # Attach in the current terminal ztty ssh --close dev build # Explicitly terminate a remote session Ctrl+] detaches. Ctrl+Shift+T and the split shortcuts in an SSH window create independent remote sessions on the same host. OpenSSH reuses one authenticated connection for these panes and continues to manage keys, SSH config and host-key checks. Input has one owner; --takeover explicitly transfers it. SSH sessions covers ports, identity/config files, native tabs and splits, remote commands, local headless use and the text-view scope. Reload the running executable A broker started from ztty 0.5.1 or later can replace its executable on Linux X11/XWayland or without windows. Run this inside the session you want to update: ztty reload ztty reload --binary /absolute/path/to/ztty ZTTY_SOCKET selects the broker. The default target is the executable of the CLI you invoked; the command does not download an update. It keeps the broker PID, existing shells and command PTYs, session identities, queued input, output byte cursors, terminal screens and history, and X11 tabs/splits. Windows are rebuilt and may briefly disappear. Active native Wayland views block this handover; detached native sessions retain their backend for later reattachment. macOS and Windows do not support this handover. A broker from the published 0.5.0 release safely refuses reload, even when asked by a newer CLI. Keep its windows until their work finishes and use a new source-built broker for new work; that broker can support later reloads. The reload guide covers validation, temporary refusal, display recovery and the one-time transition. Ctrl+Shift+R continues to reload configuration only. Appearance On Linux, edit ~/.config/ztty/ztty.conf; use --config PATH for another file. font = monospace:size=11 window-padding = 16 background = #161a23 foreground = #e1e7f0 background-opacity = 92 renderer = auto Linux X11 reloads valid changes in place. Configuration covers platform paths, colors, cursor behavior, bindings and renderer selection. Platforms and verification Platform Current source Linux X11/XWayland GPU or Xft; shared sessions, tabs/splits, attach and MCP Linux native Wayland Auto fallback or explicit EGL/GLES; shared sessions, attach/MCP, clipboard and text-input IME macOS Native AppKit/CoreText window and Darwin PTY; local sessions Windows Native Win32/GDI and ConPTY; local tabs and splits macOS runs without X11; Windows runs without WSL. Windows supports font and workspace shortcuts; macOS uses Command+C/V or Ctrl+Shift+C/V for copy/paste. Shared sessions, attach and MCP are Linux features. Platform verification records the tested scope. To try the experimental native Wayland backend: cargo build --locked --release --features wayland ./target/release/ztty --backend wayland --name work The official Linux package build enables Wayland. Current source defaults to Auto and tries the complete X11/XWayland view before a compatible native fallback. Wayland rejects tabs, splits and workspace containers. Wayland setup covers dependencies and the unverified physical GPU, desktop IME and scaling behavior. Performance and development The runtime iteration report records the startup marker and INCR paste fixes, Auto selection, query-safe reload, final native checks and installation. In its fixed Xvfb GPU-path test, lazy software backing pixmaps save about 3.66 MiB per window of X-server resources; this is not a whole-process RSS or hardware VRAM claim. Large-paste ZLE editing time remains. After input is fully sent or explicitly cancelled, this source releases an input buffer whose allocated capacity exceeds 64 KiB; smaller buffers remain available for reuse. The input-buffer regression records an 8 MiB queue retaining 0 bytes after clearing, compared with 8 MiB before the change. This measures queue allocation capacity; process RSS/PSS and throughput were not measured for this change. The 2026-11-20 performance and reload report includes fixed source and executable hashes, every raw sample, and test limits. Compared with the retained baseline, software-rendered ASCII/color throughput rose from 171.7 to 257.5 MiB/s with one window and from 158.5 to 229.2 MiB/s with ten windows. A separate scrolling Unicode test improved by 53.4% using the median of three paired ratios. Small negative headless ASCII results are also recorded. The three-terminal comparison uses a private Xvfb display and GPU code paths under a forced Mesa software-GL environment; ztty reports llvmpipe. Ten windows stay open, with one output producer measured at a time. These are logical PTY/DSR timings, not physical frame rates. Ten-window shared session Application PSS, MiB Output, MiB/s ztty 326.9 150.4 Ghostty 809.0 140.1 Kitty 354.6 53.0 Ten-window comparison under Xvfb and llvmpipe Values are medians of three independent runs. Font metrics, pixel dimensions, host memory pressure and renderer choice limit generalization; the report keeps all ranges. Single-window ztty/Ghostty throughput overlaps and is not a stable ranking. Software and GPU paths also pass the recorded complete-frame tab-switch and synchronized-output checks; physical desktop compositors need separate validation. Run sh tools/check.sh for the local development checks. Reusable libraries Library Role in ztty Status zgpui UI scenes and layout Published 0.1.5 zinput Keyboard, mouse and paste encoding Published 0.1.3 zpty PTY / ConPTY process ownership Published 0.2.3 zgraphics Image protocol and placement Published 0.2.0 zterm Terminal screen and protocol state Published 0.5.2 These published versions include the terminal checkpoint and PTY handover APIs used by ztty 0.5.2. Development builds use the libraries' GitHub default branches, with exact source commits recorded in Cargo.lock. Library submodule pins match that snapshot for independent checks; the table records published registry versions. The application keeps zgpui's std and native features disabled. The architecture describes the reusable Project Z libraries; the documentation index links usage guides and verification records. MIT © LIghtJUNction

title: Configuration
body: 原生终端应用，在 Linux 上支持窗口、命令行与 MCP 共用会话。 Configuration ztty reads a UTF-8 file with one key = value per line. Lines beginning with # are comments. Omitted keys use built-in defaults. File locations Platform Default path Linux ~/.config/ztty/ztty.conf macOS ~/Library/Application Support/ztty/ztty.conf Windows %APPDATA%\ztty\ztty.conf On Linux and macOS, setting XDG_CONFIG_HOME selects $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/ztty/ztty.conf. ztty --config PATH selects a file explicitly. --font overrides the configured font. The Linux X11 backend reloads the file when it changes, including atomic saves. Ctrl+Shift+R reloads it manually. Invalid changes leave the previous configuration active and show a temporary error. macOS and Windows read settings at startup. Fonts, colors and cursor font = monospace:size=11 window-padding = 16 background = #161a23 foreground = #e1e7f0 background-opacity = 92 background-blur = true cursor-shape = underline cursor-color = #b1ccff cursor-blink = true cursor-blink-interval = 500 selection-foreground = #f0f4fa selection-background = #394969 palette = 1=#e06c75 palette = 4=#61afef Setting Values window-padding 0–128 pixels background-opacity 0–100 percent background-blur true or false cursor-shape block, underline, bar cursor-blink true or false cursor-blink-interval 100–5000 ms per phase palette INDEX=#RRGGBB, with index 0–15 Terminal applications can change the active cursor through DECSCUSR and DEC private mode 12. On Linux X11, opacity applies to the default background; explicit ANSI backgrounds, selection and glyph colors retain their own opacity. Blur is supplied by the compositor. background-blur sends the KWin-compatible X11 request; Hyprland uses its own window rules. Set opacity to 100 for an opaque window. macOS uses a native visual-effect view for blur. Windows uses an opaque GDI surface. The platform backends implement these settings through different native APIs. Linux X11 renderer The current source supports these values: Setting Behavior renderer = auto Default; try hardware EGL, use Xft when only software GL is available renderer = gpu Use EGL/GLES, including software GL drivers renderer = software Use Xft/XRender The GPU path uses HarfBuzz for shaping and FreeType/Fontconfig for fonts. Linux X11 can switch renderer through a configuration reload while keeping its window and PTY. A GPU failure schedules a complete software redraw. See the renderer verification for tested text and frame behavior. Native Wayland (experimental) This section describes the backend included in ztty 0.5.2; its published artifacts and acceptance are recorded in the release report. Native Wayland uses xdg-shell, EGL/GLES and XKB, with the same Linux session broker and PTY ownership as X11. Enable the Cargo feature when building from source. The official Linux package build enables it. Current development builds default to --backend auto: they initialize the complete X11 view first, which retains tabs, splits and executable reload on X11 and XWayland desktops. If X11 initialization fails, Auto can initialize a native Wayland view before starting the command. This selects the best supported path; it is not a claim that one backend is faster on every machine. Automatic native fallback is allowed for a new broker or a pool that already has a native Wayland view. It is refused for an existing pool of only X11 or headless sessions, because adding a Wayland view would remove executable reload from that pool. Workspace launches require X11 and validate their target before starting a child. Explicit --backend x11 and --backend wayland do not fall back. Neither a later display failure nor a request timeout replays the command. ztty attach also defaults to Auto and keeps an existing view's backend. Each session remembers its last successfully attached backend across detach. Auto reattaches that backend to the same PTY, including restoring the last native Wayland view when no X11 display is available. It does not migrate a known view to another backend after an initialization failure; an explicit backend can request that change. A headless session that has never had a view still uses the new-view selection and compatibility checks above. New clients use a concrete backend name plus an optional Auto flag on the broker protocol; an older broker retains its legacy concrete-backend behavior until it is updated. The optional last_view_backend checkpoint field preserves detached-view provenance across executable reload. Older checkpoints without this field infer X11 only from an attached X11 view; detached provenance stays unknown. Reload of active native Wayland views remains unsupported. The default Cargo feature set remains unchanged. Install these dependencies in addition to the Linux build dependencies in the README: # Arch Linux sudo pacman -S --needed wayland wayland-protocols libxkbcommon # Debian / Ubuntu sudo apt install libwayland-dev libwayland-bin wayland-protocols libxkbcommon-dev A separate configuration such as wayland.conf can select the renderer: font = monospace:pixelsize=16 renderer = gpu window-padding = 8 background-opacity = 100 cargo build --locked --release --features wayland ./target/release/ztty --backend wayland --config ./wayland.conf --name work ./target/release/ztty attach --backend wayland --observe work ./target/release/ztty attach --backend wayland work Each session has its own PTY. Detach and reattach preserve the session; X11 and Wayland views can coexist on one broker. MCP retains the existing input ownership checks. Tabs, splits and workspace containers are rejected on Wayland; open separate session windows instead. Clipboard and primary selection use bounded asynchronous transfers. Text-input-v3 handles focus, cursor position, visible preedit and UTF-8 commits. The terminal does not own the shell's editable buffer, so it does not invent surrounding text or turn IME deletion requests into arbitrary backspaces. Both renderer = auto and gpu use EGL/GLES on Wayland; software is rejected. Mesa software GL still uses that EGL/GLES path. Renderer selection is a configuration setting, not a --renderer command-line option. The shared Wayland report records the earlier feature-owner candidate. The 0.5.2 release report records 65 Wayland checks for each released Linux architecture, bound to its own source and ELF. Those checks use headless Sway/software EGL and an IME protocol peer. Physical GPU behavior and real desktop IME combinations remain unverified. Output-scale and fractional-scale protocol handling are not implemented; HiDPI and cross-monitor scale changes are therefore not accepted features. Active native Wayland views remain outside the supported ztty reload handover scope. Detached native sessions preserve their backend provenance across a supported handover and can then reattach to the same PTY. Key and mouse bindings keybind = ctrl+shift+x = search keybind = alt+f12 = sessions keybind = ctrl+shift+t = none mousebind = ctrl+button3 = palette A custom binding takes priority over the default for that chord. none consumes the chord. Supported modifiers are ctrl, shift, alt and super; the command palette shows active shortcuts. See binding names and input rules. Text actions on Linux X11 ztty-plugin-api 0.1.0 is published; the registry verification record records the archive and independent consumer checks. The host and shared API both use zplugin 0.3.1; the locked graph includes zsys 0.1.1. These library releases are separate from the ztty application release. Register a trusted native library with: text-plugin = dedent=/absolute/path/libdedent.so Open Ctrl+Shift+P and choose Copy using dedent. The action transforms the selection, or the visible text when there is no selection, and copies the result. The text extension guide documents the interface, worker limits and an independently buildable example.

title: Architecture
body: 原生终端应用，在 Linux 上支持窗口、命令行与 MCP 共用会话。 Architecture ztty separates terminal state from operating-system integration so its libraries can be embedded in other applications. zpty owns a child process and native PTY resources, zterm owns text and screen state, zgraphics owns images and placements, and zinput encodes events without owning a session. The platform frontend supplies native input, cell metrics, window management, and rendering. flowchart TD A["Shell or TUI"] <--> B["zpty: PTY session"] B --> C["zterm::feed"] C --> D["zvte: text and VT parsing"] C --> E["zgraphics: Kitty APC stream"] D --> F["Text cells and modes"] E --> G["RGBA images and placements"] F --> H["Native platform renderer"] G --> H H --> I["zinput: event encoding"] I --> B Ordinary text and control sequences use zvte. Kitty APC sequences take a bounded streaming path into zgraphics; they do not accumulate in the title/OSC buffer. Both paths update terminal state, and protocol replies return through the same ordered PTY write queue as keyboard input. Source entry points are zterm::Terminal and zgraphics::CommandStream. Shared process ownership (Linux) On Linux, ordinary launches and MCP servers connect to one session broker for the current user. The broker owns the PTYs and terminal state; each foreground launcher waits on its session without creating another display or font stack. MCP stdio and HTTP listeners remain separate protocol processes and use the same broker. Session implementation, local IPC and X11 resources define these boundaries. Owner Resources Broker Session registry, event loop and shared read/encoding scratch buffers Display connection X11 connection, atoms and XIM context, shared by its windows Font selection on a display Base and fallback Xft fonts and their glyph caches Terminal session PTY child, screen, history, input queue and retained output Visible window Xft draw target, pixmap, input context, selection and cursor state Launcher Caller metadata and foreground completion wait The broker opens a display only when a window is needed. Windows with the same font selection reuse its font set. Closing the last window releases unused font sets. The broker keeps its opened X11 connection until it exits, so headless MCP sessions can later be attached without rebuilding Xlib state. The per-window pixmap and each session's contents remain independent allocations. One single-threaded loop polls PTYs, display connections and local IPC peers. XIM filters an event before its destination window selects the session. Output-heavy sessions have a read budget per iteration so other windows and control requests receive service. The local protocol uses an abstract Unix socket and checks the connecting user with SO_PEERCRED. ZTTY_SOCKET=@name selects an isolated broker namespace, which the test tools use. Creator argv, working directory and environment are carried with each launch; the first creator's environment does not become the default for all later sessions. Session control An ordinary window owns a local session whose lifetime ends when its window closes or its child exits. MCP-created sessions retain their output and exit status until explicitly closed; a window can attach to and detach from that state. The broker exits after its last session and pending work are gone. Sessions and MCP documents the exact names and lifecycle. The MCP transports translate six terminal tools into the same broker operations. They use bounded no_std JSON handling. Stdio uses newline framing; Streamable HTTP uses JSON responses with independent transport sessions. Session reads return byte cursors and UTF-8-safe text pages, with retained output bounded separately from terminal history. Screen state A screen is a contiguous array of fixed-size cells. A row origin index maps logical rows onto that array. Full-screen upward scrolling changes the origin and clears the newly exposed row; it does not move the entire visible screen. Partial scrolling regions copy only the affected rows. Each cell stores a Unicode scalar, two optional combining scalars, foreground and background RGB values, attributes, width, and a hyperlink identity. The tested x86_64 layout is 28 bytes. There is no per-cell heap pointer. Wide glyphs have a leading width-two cell and a width-zero continuation cell; edits repair any pair cut by their boundaries. History is lazy and bounded by both the requested number of rows and 8 MiB of cell storage. Once the bound is reached, old row allocations are reused. The alternate screen is allocated on demand and cached for reuse. Titles, links, control strings, and protocol reply queues have explicit finite bounds. These properties are implemented in zterm and covered by its core tests. Image lifecycle and memory An image transfer is invisible until it completes and validates successfully. The APC receiver holds at most a 512-byte header and 4096 encoded bytes, decoding larger payloads incrementally. The pending binary transfer has a separate 16 MiB limit. This accepts both protocol chunks and larger APCs emitted by current kitten icat clients without retaining the full base64 representation. zgraphics converts RGB, RGBA, and PNG input into straight-alpha RGBA8 pixels. It validates dimensions, container structure, and PNG checksums before invoking zune-png; optional zlib transmission compression uses zune-inflate. Nonessential PNG metadata is removed before decoding. An invalid transfer is discarded while previously stored images remain usable. The implementation is in decode.rs. Each screen has its own graphics scene. The default limit is 32 MiB per decoded image and 32 MiB of retained decoded storage per scene, counting vector capacity, with at most 128 images and 512 placements. Width and height are each limited to 8192 pixels and must also satisfy the byte limit. A scene allocates no image storage until needed. The independent primary and alternate scenes prevent an alternate-screen application from showing or deleting primary-screen images. Placements store an image identity, a cell anchor, source rectangle, requested size, pixel offset, and z-order. Scrolling updates anchors, history trimming removes expired placements, and cell-size changes recompute display geometry. Draw iteration borrows a sorted placement list and does not allocate or sort a new list on each damaged row. Source cropping and aspect-preserving scaling are resolved by the scene; the frontend clips each destination to the text viewport. The protocol scope specifies the supported commands. Pixel buffers use Arc<Vec<u8>> so a native graphics API can retain immutable pixels until it has finished drawing, even if the terminal deletes or replaces the image. The scene revision signals mutations; each image also has a generation value so replacement under the same ID invalidates converted pixels. Generations are local to a scene, so frontend caches are cleared when switching scenes. The Linux Xrender upload cache has a separate 64 MiB bound and releases obsolete server resources. macOS retains an Arc through its CoreGraphics data-provider release callback; Windows composites from canonical RGBA into its display buffer. Quota accounting covers the decoded pixels retained by a scene. It does not include decoder temporaries, retained external Arc references, converted renderer pixels, or native graphics resources. A host embedding zgraphics must release its own references and caches when they are no longer needed. Input and output The platform frontend maps native input into shared event types. Linux uses XIM commits, macOS implements AppKit's text-input interface, and Windows receives Win32 key and text messages. zinput combines text, key identity, and modifiers according to the negotiated protocol. Main and alternate screens have separate Kitty keyboard flag stacks; mouse tracking and mouse encoding are independent modes. PTY writes keep an offset into a bounded queue. Partial writes advance the offset; EAGAIN waits for writability. Reads are drained with a per-iteration budget so heavy output cannot indefinitely starve window events. Query replies share the same ordered write path as keyboard input. The platform event loops wait on native readiness mechanisms rather than continuously polling the terminal model: Platform PTY readiness and input Rendering path Linux poll over X11, PTY and broker IPC descriptors; XIM commits Xft text and Xrender images into a retained X pixmap macOS AppKit events and a Core Foundation file-descriptor source for the Darwin PTY CoreText text and CoreGraphics images in an AppKit view Windows Win32 messages plus ConPTY output/process events in MsgWaitForMultipleObjectsEx GDI text and direct RGBA compositing into a retained DIB Linux Expose events can present the retained pixmap without rebuilding screen state. Synchronized output delays drawing until completion, with a 150 ms recovery timeout. Cursor blink and synchronization deadlines can wake an otherwise idle event loop. Native frontend correctness is a separate question from shared-core correctness; acceptance coverage records the environments actually exercised. Windows ConPTY uses synchronous pipe endpoints. zpty services them with two native worker threads and bounded queues, each limited to 1 MiB plus a 16 KiB worker buffer. Public reads and writes remain nonblocking with respect to pipe I/O, and callers retain unwritten bytes. This is distinct from the descriptor readiness model on Linux/macOS. The PTY API documentation also describes platform-specific process shutdown behavior. Runtime boundary The application and Project Z libraries compile with #![no_std]. alloc remains available through the host allocator. The third-party PNG, DEFLATE, checksum, and Unicode-width dependencies compile with their no_std features; none of the enabled production dependencies requires Rust std. Tests and benchmark harnesses use std for orchestration. Rust dependency Purpose zvte 0.1.3 Streaming ANSI/VT parsing unicode-width 0.2.3 Character-cell width rules zune-core 0.5.3, zune-png 0.5.2 PNG decoding primitives and decoder zune-inflate 0.2.54 DEFLATE/zlib decoding simd-adler32 0.3.10 Transitive checksum implementation The exact resolved graph is in Cargo.lock; manifests disable default features on direct normal dependencies. The no_std audit checks enabled features and crate attributes, including conditional no_std declarations. The platform-independent libraries can also be checked for x86_64-unknown-none, which has no Rust standard library. zgraphics requires pointer-width atomics because it uses Arc. The native frontend still links operating-system C ABIs. Linux uses libc/libutil, X11, Xft, Xrender, and the compiler unwinder required by the stable Rust alloc archive. macOS uses the Darwin runtime and Apple frameworks; Windows uses Win32 and ConPTY. Panic handling terminates the process. These dependencies belong in runtime and memory accounting even though Rust std is absent. On Linux and macOS, the PTY library exposes spawn as unsafe because forkpty has process-wide safety preconditions. The application prepares argv, environment, and PATH resolution before the fork. The child then performs only descriptor closure, execve, a bounded error write, and _exit. Memory accounting Core heap measurements describe one terminal model. The Linux multi-window report sums PSS and private memory across the broker and all waiting launchers. PSS apportions shared mappings; adding process RSS values would count shared pages repeatedly. Code, system libraries, font data and allocator state remain part of process memory. Decoded image quotas and renderer cache quotas describe retained resources, not peak RSS. A large image can temporarily require its compressed bytes, decompressed bytes, canonical RGBA, and a native upload at the same time. The retained X pixmap and Xrender image uploads belong to the X server and must be counted separately. Apple and Windows graphics resources likewise have native lifetimes beyond the core heap. Full history, both screens, and image-heavy use are different workloads from an empty startup window. The performance report distinguishes these measurement boundaries; the graphics core comparison records a local paired benchmark with its own host and compiler metadata.

title: Sessions and MCP
body: 原生终端应用，在 Linux 上支持窗口、命令行与 MCP 共用会话。 Sessions and MCP On Linux, ztty keeps terminal sessions in one process for the current user. Ordinary launches, attached windows and MCP tools use that same process. Each session owns its PTY, screen and history; windows on the same display reuse the display connection and font caches. See architecture for ownership and performance for measured memory. The shared broker, attach command and MCP transports described here currently require Linux. Native macOS and Windows terminal backends are implemented separately; see the platform table. Open, list and attach Run a named terminal from an existing shell: ztty --name work -e /bin/bash & ztty --name logs -e /bin/sh & ztty attach ztty attach work Each ordinary launch opens its window and waits until that window closes or its command finishes. The & in the example leaves the launching shell available. The waiting launcher is small and is included in the multi-window memory measurements. ztty attach without an argument prints the session list. With a name or complete address, it opens the session's window, or raises the existing window, and waits for that window to close. There is one visible window per session. Attaching a completed MCP session lets you inspect its retained screen. Names use 1–64 ASCII letters, digits, dots, underscores or hyphens; . and .. are reserved. Omitting a name assigns session-N. A complete address is unique within the local broker. The same short name may exist in different namespaces; an ambiguous short name produces an error and requires its complete address. Created through Example address Ordinary terminal ztty://local/work MCP stdio ztty://mcp/stdio/work MCP HTTP ztty://mcp/http/127.0.0.1:8732/work MCP HTTP on IPv6 ztty://mcp/http/[::1]:8732/work ztty attach ztty://mcp/stdio/work ztty attach ztty://mcp/http/127.0.0.1:8732/work These addresses identify sessions in the local broker. The HTTP portion records which MCP listener created the session; attaching the address does not connect to a remote machine. Session lifetime Event Ordinary local session MCP session Window closes Hang up the child and remove the session Detach the window; keep the PTY and history Child exits Close the window and remove the session Retain output, screen and exit status for inspection MCP transport exits or HTTP transport session is deleted Unaffected Keep the terminal session session_close tool Close the session and release its resources Close the session and release its resources The first row applies to a local operator view. Closing a read-only view, or a view whose input is owned by another actor, detaches it and keeps the PTY alive. This also applies to the window manager's close action. An observing attach to an existing workspace leaves its active tab and X input focus unchanged. Detaching removes that session's window resources. The broker drops unreferenced font sets after their last window closes, but keeps opened X11 connections until it exits. It exits after approximately three seconds with no remaining sessions, pending clients or children to reap. Completed MCP sessions count as retained sessions until explicitly closed. The broker owns the PTYs, so stopping that process closes its sessions. Each creator supplies its own command arguments, working directory and environment. A later launch uses its caller's environment even when the broker was started by another terminal or an MCP server. MCP over stdio ztty mcp # Equivalent: ztty mcp --transport stdio The server reads one JSON-RPC message per input line and writes protocol responses to stdout. Tool requests run concurrently; match each response by its JSON-RPC ID because completion order can differ from submission order. Diagnostic output uses stderr. A client configuration using the common mcpServers format can launch it with: { "mcpServers": { "ztty": { "command": "ztty", "args": ["mcp"] } } } MCP starts without opening a desktop window. Use session_create to start a PTY, then ztty attach to view it. MCP over Streamable HTTP ztty mcp --transport http --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8732 Connect an MCP client to http://127.0.0.1:8732/mcp. The defaults are loopback and port 8732. IPv4, IPv6 and hostnames are supported; port 0 selects an available port and reports the actual URL on stderr. --http is shorthand for --transport http; streamable-http is also accepted as the transport name. A listener outside loopback requires a bearer token. Prefer the environment variable so the token is absent from the process argument list: ZTTY_MCP_TOKEN='replace-with-a-long-random-token' \ ztty mcp --transport http --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8732 Clients send Authorization: Bearer <token>. --token TOKEN is also supported. The listener implements plain HTTP; use a TLS terminator or secure tunnel across an untrusted network. The default is the JSON response form of Streamable HTTP. Select SSE responses for POST requests with: ztty mcp --transport http --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8732 --http-response sse --http-response json explicitly selects the default. Both modes require clients to accept application/json and text/event-stream. Accepted notifications return HTTP 202 with no body. GET returns HTTP 405. Initialization returns an Mcp-Session-Id; subsequent requests include that ID and the negotiated Mcp-Protocol-Version. DELETE removes that HTTP transport session while leaving its terminal sessions available. Idle HTTP transport sessions expire after 30 minutes; retained terminals remain available. In SSE mode, an accepted tool request sends its response headers and an initial comment before waiting for the broker. While it waits, the connection sends a comment every five seconds. Completion sends one event: message containing the complete JSON-RPC response, finishes the HTTP chunked body and closes the connection. This lets clients observe a live connection while session_read waits for output. Each request still delivers one bounded output page, including its cursor and timeout status. JSON-RPC request errors use the same response stream; HTTP errors retain ordinary HTTP status codes and JSON error bodies where applicable. These streams are scoped to a POST request. GET subscriptions, event IDs and Last-Event-ID replay are not implemented. After an interrupted read, start a new request with a fresh request ID, the last confirmed next_cursor, and expected_session. The terminal's retained output remains available. A cancelled or overloaded stream may end without a final event or terminating HTTP chunk; treat it as an interrupted request. The server validates Origin, Host headers on every bind address, content types and protocol versions. It supports 2025-11-25, 2025-06-18 and 2025-03-26, with negotiation following the MCP lifecycle. Tools Tool Arguments Result session_create Optional name, command, cwd, cols, rows, history URI, child/broker PIDs, dimensions and state session_list None All local and MCP sessions session_read session; optional cursor, max_bytes, expected_session, wait_ms Output page, screen snapshot, next cursor, output_eof and state; positive waits also return timed_out session_commands session At most 128 OSC 133 records, exit status and availability session_command_read session, command_id; optional part, max_bytes Rendered command input/output, complete and truncated session_write session, data; optional expected_session Queued input and session state session_resize session, cols, rows; optional expected_session Updated PTY and screen dimensions session_close session; optional expected_session Closed session metadata session_control session, action; optional takeover, expected_session Acquire/release input ownership; takeover is explicit Guarding session changes session_write, session_resize, session_control and session_close accept the same optional expected_session object as session_read. Copy uri, id, created_at and broker_pid from the session you intend to change. The broker checks all four fields before queuing input, resizing the PTY, changing its owner or closing it. If a name or URI was reused, the mutation returns the tool error session identity changed; refresh session metadata and leaves the replacement session unchanged. The guard also works with a short-name selector; its uri field remains the canonical creation URI. Omitting the guard preserves existing behavior and selects the session currently matching that name. These public identifiers do not grant input ownership. A matching guard does not deduplicate requests: sending a write twice still delivers its bytes twice. After a mismatch, inspect the replacement before deciding whether a previously planned action still applies. Observation and input ownership Run ztty mcp --read-only to expose only the four session/command reading tools. For an HTTP listener that accepts both roles, set ZTTY_MCP_TOKEN for operators and a different ZTTY_MCP_OBSERVER_TOKEN for observers. When either is configured, every request must authenticate; a transport session cannot switch roles by changing its bearer token. Observers cannot create, resize, write, close or acquire control, even if they manually submit a hidden tool name. Each MCP connection receives an independent trusted actor identity. Creation grants input ownership to that actor. A replacement connection can read retained output immediately; it must call session_control with action: "acquire" and takeover: true to replace a previous owner. A plain acquire refuses an existing owner. The broker clears unsent input and cancels pending GUI paste transfers when ownership changes. Bytes already delivered to the child cannot be recalled. The actor identifier in metadata is not the HTTP transport-session credential. Local GUI input resumes after Ctrl+Shift+G, or ztty control NAME acquire --takeover. Input authority and visibility are separate: read-only viewing does not grant typing, paste, mouse reports, focus reports or PTY resize. The child still receives normal terminal protocol replies such as DSR while observed or detached. --allow-host name:port adds an explicit HTTP authority, for example behind a trusted reverse proxy. An Origin header must agree with the request Host. The transport implements the 2025-11-25 JSON and POST SSE response lifecycle; it does not claim conformance with newer MCP revisions or provide an unsolicited SSE subscription. Command reads use the terminal's retained physical cells. They are bounded text extraction, not a second raw stdout archive. A resized or overwritten region can be unavailable, and completed commands can leave the history buffer. Check both complete and truncated; see daily workflow. command is an executable-and-arguments array. Use an explicit shell when shell expansion, pipelines or redirection are needed. With no command, the server uses its inherited SHELL, falling back to /bin/sh. The default grid is 120×32 with 2,000 history rows; dimensions are limited to 2–512 columns and 2–256 rows. For example, after initialization: { "jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 2, "method": "tools/call", "params": { "name": "session_create", "arguments": { "name": "checks", "command": ["/bin/sh", "-lc", "cargo test"], "cwd": "/path/to/project" } } } Follow the returned URI with session_read, or open it with ztty attach ztty://mcp/stdio/checks. Send a newline in session_write.data to submit a command to an interactive shell; \u0003 sends Ctrl+C. A write accepts at most 65,536 UTF-8 bytes. Output cursors and memory bounds session_read.cursor is a raw byte offset; start at zero and pass the returned next_cursor to the next call. cursor in the response is an alias for that next offset. max_bytes accepts 1–65,536. A text page may extend by up to three bytes to finish a UTF-8 character. An incomplete trailing character is held until more PTY output arrives. Already available bytes beyond the requested page are checked before deciding to wait: a malformed prefix followed by ASCII or another character advances the cursor, even with a one-byte page. Only a genuinely incomplete suffix waits for more output; EOF releases that suffix using replacement characters. MCP sessions retain a rolling 256 KiB of raw output, separate from screen history. When a cursor precedes the retained range, truncated is true and first_cursor identifies the retained range's start. has_more reports additional available output. The screen snapshot and screen_truncated flag provide a separate view of the current terminal contents. Actual invalid byte sequences use replacement characters in the text representation. Screen history grows on demand and has its own 8 MiB cell-storage cap. The broker allows 128 terminal sessions; close completed sessions to release their retained state. Each HTTP server allows 64 transport sessions and 64 concurrent connections, with a 1 MiB message limit and a 4 MiB budget for in-flight payloads and retained broker buffers. Allocator capacity, parsed JSON, session state and operating-system buffers are separate memory costs. HTTP request receiving and response sending each have their own ten-second deadline; a pending output wait has a separate deadline. At most 32 HTTP connections may wait for output, preserving slots for management requests. Each stdio process accepts 32 concurrent tool requests, including at most 24 positive output waits, and bounds its aggregate queued data to 4 MiB. A stdio writer that makes no progress for five seconds terminates the transport and releases its pending requests. SSE framing and queued comments count against the same HTTP payload budget. Only one heartbeat can be queued at a time, and its send deadline is not extended by further heartbeats. A slow consumer therefore cannot accumulate comments without limit. If the payload budget is exhausted after SSE headers have been sent, the connection closes; no second HTTP response is inserted. Guarded resume and output termination A canonical URI can be reused after its old session is closed. A byte offset alone cannot distinguish that replacement from the previous output stream. When resuming or reconnecting, send expected_session with exactly the four identity fields from the original create/list/read response: { "session": "ztty://mcp/stdio/checks", "cursor": 4096, "expected_session": { "uri": "ztty://mcp/stdio/checks", "id": 7, "created_at": 1794988800000, "broker_pid": 12345 } } These numbers are illustrative; copy the actual returned values. The guard is checked before output or screen data is read. A different URI, session ID, creation time or broker process returns a tool error. Renaming the display name preserves the original URI and identity, so a guarded read can continue. Missing, unknown, duplicate or incorrectly typed identity fields are rejected. The identifiers prevent accidental stream confusion; transport authentication and input ownership still determine authority. Existing calls without expected_session remain supported and have no instance guard. A reconnecting client should retain both its original identity and its own next_cursor; independent observers do not consume each other's position. After an identity mismatch, explicitly start a new read at zero only if the new session is the intended one. Do not silently replace the saved identity. output_eof means this endpoint's PTY reader has terminated, either at EOF or after an unrecoverable read error, so no more bytes will be appended. A direct child can already have exited while a descendant still holds the PTY and writes later. Therefore running: false and an exit_code do not prove that output has finished. Use output_eof && !has_more to identify a drained retained stream, and still check truncated for expired bytes. This condition does not guarantee a successful child exit or lossless transport. Waiting for output Set wait_ms to a value from 1 to 30,000 to park an empty read until output becomes available. Omitting it, or passing zero, keeps immediate-read behavior. The same byte cursor, page size, observer permissions and optional identity guard apply in either mode: { "session": "ztty://mcp/stdio/checks", "cursor": 4096, "max_bytes": 16384, "wait_ms": 30000, "expected_session": { "uri": "ztty://mcp/stdio/checks", "id": 7, "created_at": 1794988800000, "broker_pid": 12345 } } A positive wait completes when it can deliver bytes, report an expired cursor, or report output_eof. These responses have timed_out: false. At the deadline, an otherwise empty live stream returns timed_out: true with its current screen and unchanged cursor. An incomplete UTF-8 suffix stays pending until it becomes decodable, the reader terminates, or the deadline expires. Direct-child exit alone does not end a wait while a descendant still owns the PTY. Every parked read binds to the PTY instance selected when the request was accepted. Closing that PTY produces a tool error, even if a new terminal reuses its name before the reply is sent. A rename preserves the instance and URI. Keep sending expected_session when issuing later requests or reconnecting so the identity check also covers the interval between requests. The broker, stdio transport and HTTP listener drive these reads through their existing poll loops. Other clients can list, write, resize and close sessions while a read waits. A parked broker read retains only its session ID, cursor, page limit and deadline; its screen response is built on completion. The broker caps combined window and output waiters at 128 while retaining management connection capacity. HTTP supports JSON or opt-in POST SSE responses; unsolicited output subscriptions remain separate work. Cancelling a pending request Send the MCP cancellation notification using the original request ID: { "jsonrpc": "2.0", "method": "notifications/cancelled", "params": {"requestId": 42} } String IDs match their decoded characters exactly. Numeric IDs match their exact integer value, so 42, 42.0 and 4.2e1 identify the same request, and -0 matches 0. Strings and numbers stay separate: "42" is not 42. Matching never rounds large integers through floating point; replies preserve the original request's ID token. Both transports reject a second request whose ID matches a currently pending request. Clients must still issue a new ID for every request within an MCP session, as required by the base protocol. Cancellation drops that request's broker connection and produces no result for the cancelled request. Unknown, malformed and already completed cancellations are ignored. On HTTP, cancellation is restricted to the same authenticated MCP transport session; another session using the same request ID has no effect. Disconnecting its connection or deleting the HTTP session also releases pending reads. Keep the input direction open while a positive wait is pending: input EOF cancels it, including HTTP shutdown(SHUT_WR). Accepted ordinary requests still complete after input EOF while the response direction remains available. These operations leave terminal processes alive. Bytes already sent by a write operation remain subject to the existing input-ownership rules and cannot be recalled. Clients should ignore responses that raced with a cancellation. Verify python3 tests/mcp_transport.py --binary ./target/release/ztty python3 tests/mcp_sse.py --binary ./target/release/ztty --output artifacts/mcp-sse/report.json python3 tests/mcp_sessions.py --binary ./target/release/ztty python3 tests/mcp_security.py --binary ./target/release/ztty python3 tests/mcp_wait.py --binary ./target/release/ztty --output artifacts/mcp-wait/report.json python3 tests/daily_workflow.py --binary ./target/release/ztty python3 tests/shared_gui_smoke.py --binary ./target/release/ztty The MCP tests cover transport lifecycle, IPv6, concurrent requests, real PTYs, UTF-8 cursor boundaries, guarded reconnection across transports, same-name session replacement, independent observers, delayed descendant output, creator environment isolation, namespaced addressing, exit status and persistence. The GUI test covers shared-window behavior on a private Xvfb display. These shared-session tests exercise Linux X11/XWayland; native macOS and Windows frontends have their own acceptance records. Split output and byte cursors Output reads preserve an incomplete UTF-8 suffix until its remaining bytes or EOF arrive, including when earlier bytes are malformed. A returned cursor counts raw bytes. A nonadvancing cursor with has_more=true can mean an incomplete character, so wait before retrying it. Independent observers do not consume one another's cursor. See the bounded output contract and real PTY regression. Upgrading a running broker Installing a replacement executable leaves existing brokers running their current code. ztty 0.5.1 adds an explicit Linux process handover for brokers started from a reload-capable executable. Installing it does not add this capability to a broker that is already running the 0.5.0 executable. Reload the running broker A broker started from reload-capable source supports: ztty reload ztty reload --binary /absolute/path/to/ztty The command targets the broker selected by ZTTY_SOCKET. Inside a ztty shell, that variable identifies its own broker; from another shell, copy the target session's broker socket path explicitly. Without --binary, the target is the executable of the CLI process you just invoked. Use an absolute path to select another local build. The command does not download, install or select a newer release. Reload replaces the broker executable with exec while retaining its PID and owned PTY descriptors. Existing shells and commands continue with the same child PIDs and PTYs. The checkpoint preserves session identities, input ownership and queued input, retained raw output and byte cursors, primary/alternate screens, scrollback and viewport positions, terminal cursors/styles/modes, and X11 tabs/splits. Output retention limits still apply; reload cannot recover bytes that were already evicted. The target ELF first runs as a separate validator. It decodes the complete checkpoint and returns an acknowledgement tied to that attempt's random nonce. Only after the broker checks that acknowledgement does it hand over to the validated executable. An unsupported state or failed preflight keeps the current broker and terminal models in control; it does not restart the shell or replay a bounded output tail to reconstruct the screen. The supported hosts are Linux X11, XWayland and headless brokers. A broker with active native Wayland views cannot perform this handover. Detached native sessions retain their last backend across a supported handover and can reattach to the same PTY. macOS and Windows do not support it. Ctrl+Shift+R continues to reload configuration, and does not replace the executable. Refusal conditions and bounds The whole broker must be ready for handover. One unsupported session or active operation causes the request to be refused before exec.
